bait: Cut clam; squid; crab
rig: Deep drop rig with electric reel
explanation_cold: Golden tilefish are deep-dwelling bottom fish found in submarine canyons; they remain in deep water year-round.
explanation_warm: Golden tilefish are prized for their sweet flesh; they live in burrows on the outer continental shelf at 400-1200 ft depths.
lures: Heavy jigs near deep structure

name: Red porgy
bait: Cut squid; shrimp; small crabs
rig: Double-drop bottom rig (chicken rig)
explanation_cold: Red porgy hold near hard bottom and reef structure in deeper water during cooler months.
explanation_warm: Red porgy feed actively around ledges and artificial reefs; they travel in schools and provide steady action.
lures: Small jigs (1-2 oz), soft plastics near bottom structure

name: Yellowtail snapper
bait: Small pieces of shrimp; glass minnows; pilchard chunks; cut squid
rig: Light spinning outfit; free-line or small weight with chum
explanation_cold: Yellowtail snapper slow down in winter but remain near reefs in the Keys and South Florida.
explanation_warm: Yellowtail snapper are aggressive feeders around reefs and wrecks; chumming brings them to the surface for exciting light-tackle fishing.
lures: Small jigs, Clouser minnows, shrimp imitations near structure

name: Sheepshead (Gulf)
bait: Live fiddler crabs; shrimp; oysters; barnacle-covered debris
rig: Knocker rig tight to pilings; short fluorocarbon leader
explanation_cold: Gulf sheepshead stack around bridge pilings, jetties, and docks in winter, feeding on barnacles and crabs in the cooler water.
explanation_warm: Sheepshead move nearshore around structure before scattering to offshore reefs for spawning.
lures: Rarely caught on lures; small jigs near pilings occasionally work

name: Redfish (Gulf red drum)
bait: Live shrimp; cut mullet; live crab; pogies (menhaden)
rig: Carolina rig or popping cork with live bait
sinker: 1-3 oz egg sinker or popping cork
explanation_cold: Gulf redfish hold in deeper marsh channels and near warm-water outflows during winter cold fronts.
explanation_warm: Redfish aggressively tail on grass flats and prowl shorelines; bull reds gather at passes during the fall spawn run.
lures: Gold spoons, paddle-tail swimbaits, topwater at dawn/dusk; same as red drum

name: Barred surfperch
bait: Sand crabs (mole crabs); bloodworms; Gulp! sandworms; small pieces of mussel
rig: Carolina rig with light leader; sliding sinker rig
explanation_cold: Barred surfperch are actively spawning and feeding aggressively in the winter surf zone -- this is peak season on the Pacific Coast.
explanation_warm: Barred surfperch are present but less concentrated; they move to deeper water as surf warms.
lures: Small paddle-tail swimbaits (2-3"), Berkley Gulp Sand Crab, tube jigs in the surf zone

name: Redtail surfperch
bait: Sand crabs; sand shrimp; pile worms; Gulp! sandworms
rig: Carolina rig or double dropper loop rig
explanation_cold: Redtail surfperch school up in the surf zone during winter and early spring, feeding heavily on sand crabs in the wash.
explanation_warm: Redtail surfperch are less common in the surf during warmer months; try rocky areas and jetties.
lures: Small paddle tails, Gulp Sand Crab in the surf; same tactics as barred surfperch

name: Calico surfperch
bait: Sand crabs; bloodworms; small pieces of shrimp
rig: Carolina rig with light line
explanation_cold: Calico surfperch are abundant in the Northern California and Oregon surf during winter months.
explanation_warm: Calico surfperch move to slightly deeper water but can still be found near jetties.
lures: Small jigs, Gulp lures in the surf

name: Rubberlip seaperch
bait: Pile worms; mussels; small pieces of shrimp; sand crabs
rig: Light Carolina rig; hi-lo rig around structure
explanation_cold: Rubberlip seaperch hold near rocky structure and pilings during winter.
explanation_warm: Rubberlip seaperch feed actively around piers, jetties, and rocky shorelines; they are one of the largest surfperch species.
lures: Small jigs near structure

name: California halibut
bait: Live anchovy; live smelt; squid strips; Gulp! grubs; swim baits
rig: Sliding sinker rig with fluorocarbon leader; Carolina rig; jig head
sinker: 1-3 oz sliding egg or banana sinker
explanation_cold: California halibut are in deeper water during cold months and less accessible from shore.
explanation_warm: California halibut move into shallow sandy areas near piers, jetties, and in the surf zone to ambush baitfish; cast parallel to shore and retrieve slowly along the bottom.
lures: Live bait-style swimbaits, paddle tails on 3/8-3/4 oz jighead, Berkley Gulp grubs drifted on bottom

name: Starry flounder
bait: Pile worms; sand shrimp; clam necks; cut anchovy
rig: Sliding sinker rig; spreader bar
explanation_cold: Starry flounder move into bays and estuaries during winter and are a popular pier catch from NorCal through Washington.
explanation_warm: Starry flounder retreat to deeper, cooler water during summer months.
lures: Small paddle-tail swimbaits, Gulp grubs on jighead

name: Lingcod
bait: Live bait (smelt, anchovy); large swimbaits; jigs tipped with squid
rig: Heavy jig head or dropper loop rig with large swimbait
explanation_cold: Lingcod move into shallower rocky reefs during fall and winter to spawn; they are aggressive ambush predators accessible from jetties and rocky points.
explanation_warm: Lingcod retreat to deeper water offshore during warm months; less accessible from shore.
lures: Large swimbaits (5-8"), heavy jigs (4-8 oz), plastic eels; very aggressive; retrieve with erratic action

name: Vermilion rockfish
bait: Squid strips; cut anchovy; shrimp; Gulp! baits
rig: Hi-lo rig; dropper loop rig; shrimp fly rigs
sinker: 4-8 oz bank or cannon ball sinker
explanation_cold: Vermilion rockfish are deeper and less accessible in cold months.
explanation_warm: Vermilion rockfish (red snapper of the Pacific) are found around rocky structure; they're a prized catch from deepwater piers and jetties.
lures: Heavy jigs (2-4 oz), soft plastic shrimp/grubs near rocky structure

name: Blue rockfish
bait: Small pieces of squid; cut anchovy; shrimp; Sabiki rig (artificial)
rig: Hi-lo rig; shrimp fly rigs; small jigs
explanation_cold: Blue rockfish hold deep during winter but can be caught from deep piers.
explanation_warm: Blue rockfish are common around kelp beds, piers, and rocky structures in NorCal and Oregon; they school up and can be caught readily on small baits.
lures: Jigs, soft plastics near rocky structure

name: Copper rockfish
bait: Squid strips; shrimp; cut anchovy; live bait
rig: Hi-lo rig; dropper loop rig
explanation_cold: Copper rockfish hold near rocky structure year-round but are less active in cold months.
explanation_warm: Copper rockfish are solitary ambush predators found around kelp and rocky reefs; they're accessible from deep piers and jetties.
lures: Small-medium jigs, swimbaits near rocky bottom

name: Grass rockfish
bait: Pile worms; shrimp; cut squid; mussels
rig: Sliding sinker rig near rocks; hi-lo rig
explanation_cold: Grass rockfish hunker in rocky crevices during winter.
explanation_warm: Grass rockfish inhabit shallow rocky areas and tide pools; they are common from piers and jetties along central and northern California.
lures: Small jigs, paddle tails near kelp and grass beds

name: Cabezon
bait: Shrimp; squid; mussels; cut fish; pile worms
rig: Sliding sinker rig near rocks; dropper loop
explanation_cold: Cabezon move into shallower water during fall and winter to spawn; they're one of the largest sculpin family fish on the Pacific Coast and are aggressive biters.
explanation_warm: Cabezon are present but in deeper water; focus on rocky jetties and deepwater piers.
lures: Large swimbaits and jigs near rocky structure; aggressive on large rubber baits

name: Pacific mackerel (chub mackerel)
bait: Small pieces of cut squid; Sabiki rigs; small chrome jigs; cut anchovy
rig: Sabiki rig; small metal jig on light line
explanation_cold: Pacific mackerel move offshore during winter.
explanation_warm: Pacific mackerel run in large schools around piers and harbors in SoCal; they're fun to catch on Sabiki rigs and make excellent live bait for larger fish.
lures: Metal spoons, small jigs; caught on sabiki rigs or small fast-retrieved lures

name: Jack mackerel (Spanish jack)
bait: Sabiki rigs; small jigs; cut squid; cut anchovy
rig: Sabiki rig or light jig setup
explanation_cold: Jack mackerel are offshore and not typically available from piers in winter.
explanation_warm: Jack mackerel school around SoCal piers in summer and fall; they are aggressive feeders and excellent for bait or eating.
lures: Small jigs, metal spoons; same as Pacific mackerel

name: Pacific bonito
bait: Live anchovy; Sabiki-caught bait; metal jigs; feathered lures
rig: Live bait on sliding sinker; casting jig; trolling feather
explanation_cold: Pacific bonito are offshore during cool months.
explanation_warm: Pacific bonito (a small tuna relative) chase baitfish schools past SoCal piers; they fight hard and are great on light tackle.
lures: Metal spoons, fast jigs, feather lures; excellent topwater action when schooling

name: Yellowtail (California yellowtail)
bait: Live sardine; live mackerel; iron jigs; surface poppers
rig: Live bait on heavy fluorocarbon leader; yo-yo iron jig
sinker: None (free-lined live bait) or 1-2 oz sliding sinker
explanation_cold: Yellowtail migrate south to Baja during cold months.
explanation_warm: Yellowtail cruise past SoCal piers and kelp beds chasing baitfish; these are powerful fighters and one of the most prized pier catches on the West Coast.
lures: Swimbaits (6-9" kite-fish style), iron jigs (flylined), Yo-Zuri/Rapala plugs; premier lure target

name: White seabass
bait: Live squid; live sardine; cut squid; swimbaits
rig: Live bait rig with fluorocarbon leader; heavy sliding sinker rig
explanation_cold: White seabass are offshore during cold months.
explanation_warm: White seabass move inshore to spawn in spring; they follow squid runs near piers and kelp beds and are a trophy catch from shore.
lures: Large swimbaits (5-7"), iron jigs, trolling lures near kelp and structure at night

name: Corbina
bait: Sand crabs; bloodworms; mussels; clam
rig: Carolina rig with light fluorocarbon leader
explanation_cold: Corbina move to deeper water and are hard to reach from shore in winter.
explanation_warm: Corbina cruise the SoCal surf zone rooting for sand crabs and worms in the wash; they are the prized surf species of Southern California.
lures: Berkley Gulp Sand Crab, small swimbaits, Yamamoto Senko-style worms in the surf

name: Spotfin croaker
bait: Sand crabs; mussels; bloodworms; ghost shrimp
rig: Carolina rig; sliding sinker rig
explanation_cold: Spotfin croaker move to deeper bays and offshore during cold months.
explanation_warm: Spotfin croaker feed in the SoCal surf zone; their distinctive high-pitched croaking and golden body make them easy to identify.
lures: Small paddle-tail swimbaits, tube jigs in the surf

name: Yellowfin croaker
bait: Sand crabs; mussels; bloodworms; cut squid
rig: Carolina rig; sliding sinker rig
explanation_cold: Yellowfin croaker are deeper and less active during cold months.
explanation_warm: Yellowfin croaker are common in the SoCal and central CA surf zone; they school up and feed aggressively on sand crabs.
lures: Small swimbaits, Gulp lures

name: Leopard shark
bait: Squid; cut mackerel; anchovy; shrimp; sand crabs
rig: Sliding sinker rig with wire or heavy fluorocarbon leader
explanation_cold: Leopard sharks are in deeper water and less active during winter.
explanation_warm: Leopard sharks cruise shallow bays and surf zones in summer; La Jolla and Pacifica are famous spots. They are beautiful, spotted sharks and fight well.
lures: Primarily bait-caught; large soft plastic swimbaits near bottom

name: Shovelnose guitarfish
bait: Sand crabs; squid; cut fish; shrimp; bloodworms
rig: Sliding sinker rig; Carolina rig
explanation_cold: Shovelnose guitarfish are in deeper water during winter.
explanation_warm: Shovelnose guitarfish are common in SoCal surf and bays; these ray-shark hybrids root through sand for crabs and worms.
lures: Not typically targeted with lures

name: Bat ray
bait: Squid; shrimp; cut mackerel; ghost shrimp; mussels
rig: Heavy sliding sinker rig with wire leader
explanation_cold: Bat rays are in deeper water and less accessible during winter.
explanation_warm: Bat rays are powerful fighters caught from piers and surf in California bays; they can exceed 100 lbs and will test your tackle.
lures: Not typically targeted with lures

name: Thornback ray
bait: Squid; shrimp; cut fish; sand crabs
rig: Sliding sinker rig; heavy Carolina rig
explanation_cold: Thornback rays are deeper during cold months but occasionally taken from piers.
explanation_warm: Thornback rays are a common catch from NorCal piers; they have distinctive thorny spines on their back and tail.
lures: Not typically targeted with lures

name: Kelp greenling
bait: Shrimp; pile worms; mussels; cut squid; small crabs
rig: Hi-lo rig; dropper loop near bottom
explanation_cold: Kelp greenling hold near rocky structure year-round but bite less aggressively in winter.
explanation_warm: Kelp greenling are colorful bottom fish found around kelp and rocky piers from Central CA to Washington; the males have bright blue spots.
lures: Small jigs, Gulp shrimp near kelp

name: Rock greenling
bait: Shrimp; pile worms; mussels; cut fish
rig: Hi-lo rig; dropper loop near rocks
explanation_cold: Rock greenling shelter in rocky crevices during cold months.
explanation_warm: Rock greenling are common along Oregon and Washington rocky shores and jetties; they are aggressive biters on natural baits.
lures: Small jigs near rocky bottom

name: Pacific staghorn sculpin
bait: Pile worms; small shrimp; cut fish; sand crabs
rig: Hi-lo rig; small hook near bottom
explanation_cold: Staghorn sculpin are abundant year-round in bays and off piers; they're one of the most common catches in Pacific NW.
explanation_warm: Staghorn sculpin are in slightly deeper water during warmer months but still common from piers.
lures: Not typically targeted with lures

name: Pacific herring
bait: Sabiki rigs; small hooks with herring roe; small jigs
rig: Multi-hook Sabiki rig
explanation_cold: Pacific herring spawn in bays during winter, creating huge schools that are easy to catch on Sabiki rigs from piers; great for bait.
explanation_warm: Pacific herring are offshore during warm months.
lures: Not typically targeted with lures; incidentally caught on sabiki rigs

name: Jacksmelt
bait: Small pieces of pile worm; tiny shrimp; Sabiki rigs; small dough balls
rig: Multi-hook Sabiki rig or float rig with small hook
sinker: Split shot or small torpedo sinker
explanation_cold: Jacksmelt are less concentrated near shore in winter.
explanation_warm: Jacksmelt are one of the most common pier fish in California; they school near the surface and are fun on ultra-light tackle.
lures: Small jigs, sabiki rigs

name: Walleye surfperch
bait: Pile worms; small shrimp; Gulp! baits; small pieces of mussel
rig: Hi-lo rig; float rig; light Carolina rig
explanation_cold: Walleye surfperch move to deeper water in winter.
explanation_warm: Walleye surfperch are a staple pier catch in California; they school around pilings and rocky areas and are fun on light gear.
lures: Small paddle tails, jigs in the surf

name: White croaker (tomcod)
bait: Cut squid; cut anchovy; pile worms; shrimp; almost anything
rig: Hi-lo rig; Carolina rig
explanation_cold: White croaker are deeper during winter months.
explanation_warm: White croaker (tomcod/kingfish) are one of the most abundant fish at SoCal and central CA piers; they eat almost anything.
lures: Small jigs, soft plastics

name: Kelp bass (calico bass)
bait: Live anchovy; cut squid; swimbaits; artificial grubs
rig: Sliding sinker rig near kelp; jig head with swimbait
sinker: 1-2 oz sliding sinker or jig head
explanation_cold: Kelp bass are less active in cold water and hold tight to structure.
explanation_warm: Kelp bass are the most popular gamefish from SoCal piers and jetties; they ambush baitfish around kelp beds and rocky structure.
lures: Swimbaits, topwater poppers, rubber worms near kelp; voracious lure fish

name: Sand bass (barred sand bass)
bait: Live anchovy; cut squid; swimbaits; Carolina-rigged plastics
rig: Dropper loop rig; jig head; Carolina rig with swimbait
explanation_cold: Sand bass move to deeper water during winter.
explanation_warm: Sand bass school over sandy bottoms and around structure in SoCal; they aggregate in large spawning groups in summer.
lures: Swimbaits, drop-shot rigs with small plastics; excellent jig target

name: California sheephead
bait: Mussels; shrimp; sea urchin; cut squid; crab
rig: Dropper loop rig near rocks; hi-lo rig
explanation_cold: California sheephead are less active and in deeper water during winter.
explanation_warm: California sheephead are colorful, hard-fighting wrasse found around rocky reefs and kelp; they have powerful jaws that crush shellfish.
lures: Heavy jigs, swimbaits near rocky structure

name: Opaleye
bait: Frozen peas; moss; mussels; small pieces of shrimp
rig: Float rig with small hook; light hi-lo rig
sinker: Split shot or small egg sinker
explanation_cold: Opaleye are less active but still present near rocky shorelines in winter.
explanation_warm: Opaleye are herbivorous fish found around rocky shorelines and jetties in SoCal; they're surprisingly hard fighters for their size.
lures: Small jigs, Gulp shrimp near kelp; not a strong lure target

name: Halfmoon (Catalina perch)
bait: Mussels; frozen peas; moss; small pieces of shrimp
rig: Float rig; light hi-lo rig
explanation_cold: Halfmoon hold near rocky structure during winter.
explanation_warm: Halfmoon are found along SoCal rocky shores and kelp beds; they're similar to opaleye and share the same habitat.
lures: Small jigs and soft plastics near structure

name: Pacific sardine
bait: Sabiki rigs; tiny jigs; small pieces of squid on tiny hooks
rig: Multi-hook Sabiki rig
explanation_cold: Pacific sardines move offshore during winter.
explanation_warm: Pacific sardines school in massive numbers around SoCal piers; they're prized as live bait for yellowtail, white seabass, and halibut.
lures: Not typically targeted with lures; bait species

name: Northern anchovy
bait: Sabiki rigs; tiny hooks with small squid pieces
rig: Multi-hook Sabiki rig
explanation_cold: Northern anchovies are deeper and less concentrated near piers in winter.
explanation_warm: Northern anchovies are the backbone of the California baitfish; catching them on Sabiki rigs provides the best live bait for nearly every gamefish.
lures: Not typically targeted with lures; bait species

name: Giant trevally (ulua)
bait: Live akule (bigeye scad); live opelu; large cut bait; whole octopus
rig: Heavy sliding sinker rig with 100+ lb leader; ulua setup
explanation_cold: Giant trevally are present year-round in Hawaii but slightly less active during cooler months.
explanation_warm: Giant trevally (ulua) are the ultimate shore-fishing trophy in Hawaii; they're powerful predators caught from rocky shores and piers on heavy tackle.
lures: Large poppers, stickbaits (GT poppers), heavy swimbaits; very powerful fighter

name: Bluefin trevally (omilu)
bait: Live baitfish; cut squid; poppers; metal jigs
rig: Sliding sinker rig; popping/spinning setup; papio rig
explanation_cold: Bluefin trevally are present year-round but slightly less active in winter.
explanation_warm: Bluefin trevally (omilu) are strikingly beautiful blue-finned jacks found around reefs and rocky shores in Hawaii; they hit lures and bait aggressively.
lures: Poppers, jigs, stickbaits; aggressive lure fish

name: Papio (juvenile jack)
bait: Live opelu; cut squid; shrimp; small crabs; poppers
rig: Light papio rig; float rig; small sliding sinker
explanation_cold: Papio are present year-round in Hawaii; smaller jacks are always near shore.
explanation_warm: Papio are the most popular shore-fishing target in Hawaii; these juvenile jacks roam reefs and harbors and are a great family fishing species.
lures: Small jigs, spoons, swimbaits; juvenile jacks are aggressive

name: Bonefish (oio)
bait: Shrimp; sand crabs; small crabs; squid strips; fly fishing (Christmas Island specials)
rig: Light Carolina rig with fluorocarbon leader
explanation_cold: Bonefish are present year-round in Hawaii flats but slightly less active in winter.
explanation_warm: Bonefish (oio) feed on shallow sand flats in Hawaii; they are the ghosts of the flats -- fast, wary, and an incredible fight on light tackle.
lures: Clouser minnows, shrimp fly imitations, Crazy Charlie flies; almost exclusively sight-fished with lures/flies

name: Menpachi (soldierfish)
bait: Small shrimp; cut squid; aku belly (skipjack tuna belly); bread
rig: Small hook dropper rig; float rig near rocks
sinker: Split shot or small bank sinker
explanation_cold: Menpachi are active year-round in Hawaii, feeding at night around rocky areas.
explanation_warm: Menpachi (soldierfish/squirrelfish) are a prized eating fish in Hawaii; they come out at night to feed around rocks and reef edges near piers.
lures: Small jigs near structure at night

name: Moi (Pacific threadfin)
bait: Sand crabs; shrimp; cut squid; small crabs
rig: Sliding sinker rig in the surf; Carolina rig with fluorocarbon
explanation_cold: Moi are present in cooler months but less concentrated in the shallows.
explanation_warm: Moi (Pacific threadfin) is Hawaii's most revered eating fish; once reserved for royalty, they feed in the sandy surf zone and are caught from beaches and piers.
lures: Small jigs, soft plastics; delicate fighters

name: Mu (bigeye emperor)
bait: Shrimp; squid; small crabs; cut fish
rig: Bottom rig with fluorocarbon leader; dropper loop
explanation_cold: Mu are present year-round around reef structure but less active in cooler months.
explanation_warm: Mu (bigeye emperor) are prized bottom fish in Hawaii caught from rocky shores and piers over reef; they are excellent eating.
lures: Small jigs, soft plastics near bottom structure

name: Kaku (barracuda)
bait: Live baitfish; cut fish strips; silver spoons; jigs
rig: Wire leader with live bait; casting spoon or jig
sinker: None (cast and retrieve) or 1-2 oz sliding sinker
explanation_cold: Kaku are present year-round in Hawaii harbors and reefs.
explanation_warm: Kaku (great barracuda) patrol Hawaii harbors, piers, and reef edges; they strike fast and fight hard on light tackle.
lures: Long tube lures, needlefish-style jigs, large silver spoons; fast retrieve

name: Aholehole (Hawaiian flagtail)
bait: Bread; small shrimp; dough balls; bread flies; palu (chum)
rig: Float rig with small hook; light bottom rig
explanation_cold: Aholehole are active year-round in Hawaii harbors and rocky shorelines.
explanation_warm: Aholehole are one of Hawaii's most popular panfish; they school around piers, harbors, and river mouths and are great eating.
lures: Small jigs near structure

name: Longfin inshore squid
bait: Squid jigs (luminous or chrome); small sabiki rigs baited with fish flesh; small spoons
rig: Squid jig rig with a small sinker; light spinning or jigging rod
hook_size: Size 2-4 squid jig; no hook — jig has prongs
explanation_cold: Longfin squid are most abundant inshore during fall and winter as they follow cold-water baitfish schools; jigging at night under lights near piers produces steady action.
explanation_warm: Longfin squid have largely moved offshore into cooler deep water; occasional catches still occur near inlets on overcast days or at night.
lures: Not a typical lure target; caught on sabiki/squid jigs

name: Blue shark
bait: Whole mackerel; bluefish; menhaden; squid; chunk bait
rig: Float rig with 6-9 ft of wire or heavy mono leader; or bottom rig with large circle hook
sinker: None for float rig; 4-8 oz for bottom rig
explanation_cold: Blue sharks are pelagic and move offshore or south in cold water — nearshore catches are uncommon below 55°F.
explanation_warm: Blue sharks are among the most abundant pelagic sharks from Cape Hatteras to New England in summer; they cruise near the surface offshore and occasionally come within a few miles of shore following baitfish and menhaden schools.
lures: Primarily caught on bait offshore

name: Great hammerhead shark
bait: Live stingrays (preferred); live bluefish, jack, or ladyfish; large cut baits
rig: Heavy conventional tackle (50-130 class); 10-15 ft of 480-lb steel cable leader; large circle hook
sinker: 4-8 oz egg sinker or fish-finder rig
explanation_cold: Great hammerheads move south to warmer Florida and Gulf waters as temperatures drop — rarely encountered north of Florida below 65°F.
explanation_warm: Great hammerheads patrol nearshore flats, surf zones, and inlets along the Southeast US and Gulf; they are particularly attracted to stingray-rich sandy flats and are one of the most prized shark targets from shore.
lures: Primarily caught on bait; large swimbaits near bottom

name: Pacific barracuda (California barracuda)
bait: Live anchovies; small mackerel; chrome surface iron jigs; white swimbaits
rig: Light to medium spinning or casting rod; wire or heavy fluorocarbon leader (single strand wire preferred)
sinker: None for surface jigs; split shot for live bait
explanation_cold: Pacific barracuda move south into Mexican waters or offshore when temperatures drop below 60°F; catches are uncommon in Southern California from December through February.
explanation_warm: Pacific barracuda school near kelp paddies, the surface, and nearshore reefs from San Diego to Point Conception; they hit chrome surface iron jigs and live anchovies aggressively on light tackle from boats and piers.
lures: Long tube lures, Rapala plugs, large needlefish-style jigs; fast retrieve

name: Toau (blacktail snapper)
bait: Cut squid; small fish chunks; shrimp; live small fish
rig: Bottom rig with light to medium sinker; slip sinker rig near reef structure
explanation_cold: Toau are active year-round around Hawaii's shallow reef flats and rocky shorelines; water temperature in Hawaii rarely limits the bite.
explanation_warm: Toau (blacktail snapper) are one of Hawaii's most common and easily caught shore fish; they congregate around reef structure, rocky points, and reef edges — great eating and fun on light tackle.
lures: Small jigs, soft plastics near reef structure

name: Roi (peacock grouper)
bait: Live small fish; cut fish; squid strips; lures near structure
rig: Bottom rig near reef structure; small jig or drop-shot rig around rocky habitat
explanation_cold: Roi are active year-round in Hawaii; this invasive grouper occupies reef habitat year-round and can be caught on most bottom rigs near structure.
explanation_warm: Roi (peacock grouper) are an invasive species in Hawaii introduced in the 1950s; they are abundant on coral reefs, rocky bottoms, and rubble zones — anglers are encouraged to keep all they catch as part of control efforts.
lures: Jigs, swimbaits near reef

name: Weke (goatfish)
bait: Small shrimp; pieces of squid; cut fish; sandworms
rig: Light bottom rig with small hook; two-hook bottom rig in sandy areas
explanation_cold: Weke are year-round Hawaii residents; they forage along sandy bottoms and reef edges using their chin barbels to detect buried invertebrates.
explanation_warm: Weke (goatfish) are a beloved Hawaiian table fish found in schools over sandy flats, grass beds, and mixed reef-sand edges; they are excellent eating and bite readily on small baits fished on the bottom.
lures: Small jigs, soft plastics near sandy bottom

name: Atlantic halibut
bait: Large whole or chunk baits — whole herring, mackerel, large squid, haddock belly strips; bait must be very fresh
rig: Heavy single hook bottom rig with 80-100 lb fluorocarbon leader; hi-lo rig for smaller fish
sinker: 16-32 oz bank sinker depending on depth
lures: Heavy metal jigs (400-800g) worked slowly near the bottom at depth
explanation_cold: Atlantic halibut inhabit very deep, cold water (200-2000 ft) in winter and are only accessible on specialized deep-water charter trips; they are the largest flatfish in the Atlantic.
explanation_warm: Spring through early summer is the prime season when halibut move to slightly shallower grounds (100-400 ft) on Stellwagen Bank and similar offshore ledges; they are critically endangered and all must be released.

name: Black marlin
bait: Large rigged baits — whole mackerel, bonito, large squid, or live blue runner; skip baits at speed
rig: Heavy offshore trolling spread; 130-200 lb leader; IGFA-class heavy gear (50-130 lb class)
sinker: None for trolling; live bait fished in current
lures: Large offshore lures — Ilander, Islander, skirted ballyhoo; dark colors work well in warm water
explanation_cold: Black marlin are warm-water billfish rarely found in US waters in winter; they are primarily encountered in tropical and subtropical offshore waters of the Gulf Stream.
explanation_warm: The peak US east coast encounter for black marlin is during the summer months in the Gulf Stream corridor; they are a prized catch-and-release trophy requiring serious offshore tackle.

name: Chinook salmon (king salmon)
bait: Whole or plug-cut herring trolled with flasher; anchovies; sand lance; cured roe near river mouths in fall
rig: Mooching rig with 2-hook herring setup; downrigger trolling with flasher-herring at 40-120 ft
sinker: 4-12 oz mooching sinker; downrigger ball to depth
lures: Spoons (Coho Killer, Coyote, Apex), hoochies on 36-in leader behind flasher, spinners near river mouths
explanation_cold: Fall and winter Chinook (blackmouth) school nearshore in Puget Sound and coastal bays; they feed near the bottom in 60-200 ft and are targeted on downriggers with herring.
explanation_warm: Spring ocean Chinook feed aggressively on herring and anchovies; trolling cut-plug herring with a 4-6 oz mooching sinker near bait balls at 40-80 ft produces the most fish.

name: Chum salmon (dog salmon)
bait: Pink or chartreuse shrimp flies; chum entry flasher rigs; small herring near estuaries
rig: Light jig or shrimp fly below a small float; drift fishing near river mouths
lures: Pink or chartreuse shrimp flies, Buzz Bombs in pink, small spoons, Clouser minnows in pink/white
explanation_cold: Chum salmon return to estuaries and rivers from September through December; they stack up in tidewater and respond well to pink shrimp flies near staging areas.
explanation_warm: Ocean chum can be encountered offshore in summer but are rarely targeted specifically; the main fishery is in fall when they congregate near river mouths.

name: Coho salmon (silver salmon)
bait: Whole herring, anchovies, sand lance; pink shrimp; cured salmon eggs near estuaries in fall
rig: Trolling with flasher and 36-inch leader; mooching rig with whole herring; surface trolling in summer
sinker: 2-6 oz mooching weight or no weight at surface
lures: Spoons (Krocodile, Coyote), hoochies in pink/chartreuse/white, buzz bombs, Stingsilda jigs; Clousers on fly
explanation_cold: Coho stage in estuaries and near river mouths in fall before their spawning run; they feed heavily and are accessible from river-mouth jetties and near-shore structure.
explanation_warm: Summer coho feed aggressively near the surface and upper water column; surface trolling with flasher-hoochie at 20-60 ft is standard, and fish will smash spoons and jigs near bait schools.

name: Haddock
bait: Fresh surf clams (top choice), sandworms, squid strips, cut herring or mackerel; clam is the gold standard for haddock
rig: Hi-lo bottom rig with 2 dropper loops on 30-50 lb leader; single hook fish finder rig on rough bottom
sinker: 6-12 oz bank or sea anchor sinker
lures: Slow-pitch jigs (100-300g) in white or pink, Norwegian-style diamond jigs, spreader bar rigs with squid
explanation_cold: Haddock school tightly over rocky and gravelly bottom at 100-300 ft in winter; they feed actively in cold water and clam bait fished straight down is highly effective.
explanation_warm: Haddock fishing tapers as water warms above 52°F; early spring (April-May) and fall produce the best catches before temperatures peak and fish move deeper.

name: Pacific halibut
bait: Whole or plug-cut herring; fresh salmon belly strips; octopus pieces; large chunk bait on heavy jigs
rig: Spreader bar rig or slip sinker with 80-150 lb fluorocarbon leader; drift fishing over sand/gravel bottom
sinker: 8-32 oz depending on depth and current
lures: Heavy metal jigs (Crippled Herring, Buzz Bomb, Point Wilson Dart), large paddle-tail swimbaits on 4-8 oz jighead
explanation_cold: Pacific halibut move into deep water 200-400+ ft in late fall and winter; targeting them is difficult and largely confined to commercial operators outside of summer season.
explanation_warm: Peak season runs May through September when halibut migrate into nearshore shallows of 60-250 ft to feed on herring and sand lance; drifting cut herring over sandy bottom is the classic method.

name: Pink salmon (humpy)
bait: Small herring, krill, shrimp; pink shrimp flies near estuaries
rig: Small jig or shrimp fly under a bobber; light spinning gear works well
lures: Pink spoons and spinners, small pink jigs, shrimp flies; nearly anything pink works during a pink salmon run
explanation_cold: Pink salmon runs occur on odd years in most areas; outside of their late-summer run window they are not present.
explanation_warm: Pink salmon return July through September, often in enormous numbers; they readily hit small pink lures and can provide explosive action near river mouths and tidal flats.

name: Sablefish (black cod)
bait: Squid, octopus pieces, herring, cut rockfish; sablefish are opportunistic deepwater scavengers
rig: Deep-drop rig with multiple dropper loops; heavy leaders; electric reels commonly used at depth
sinker: 16-32 oz or heavier depending on depth and current
lures: Heavy slow-pitch jigs (300-600g) in deep water; flutter jigs worked near the bottom
explanation_cold: Sablefish inhabit very deep water (1000-5000 ft) in winter and are rarely targeted by recreational anglers outside of specialized deep-drop charter trips.
explanation_warm: Shallower sablefish (300-800 ft) can be encountered on deep-drop trips in spring and summer; they are prized for their rich, buttery flesh and fight well on heavy tackle.

name: Swordfish
bait: Whole rigged squid (top choice), large mackerel or bluefish belly strips; deep-drop with 8-inch squid rig
rig: Heavy stand-up tackle; 200-400 lb monofilament or wire leader; chemical light sticks on deep-drop rig
sinker: 32-64 oz on deep-drop daytime rig; 8-16 oz at night in shallower water
lures: Natural bait is primary; large swim-head lures with squid skirt used at night on surface
explanation_cold: Swordfish move offshore to warmer Gulf Stream waters in winter; accessible only via overnight deep-drop trips to 1500-2000 ft on the stream edge.
explanation_warm: Daytime swordfish are targeted with deep-drop squid rigs at 1000-2000 ft on the Gulf Stream; at night, fish migrate shallower (100-400 ft) and can be targeted more easily near structure.

name: Atlantic bluefin tuna
bait: Chunk mackerel, butterfish, herring, squid; live bait (bluefish, pogies) for giants
rig: Chunking: hi-lo heavy mono rig; kite-fishing: specialized kite rod; live-bait: circle hook free-line
sinker: None for chunking; 8-16 oz for deep presentations
lures: Large cedar plugs, jet heads, vinyl skirted lures at trolling speed 7-9 kts
explanation_cold: Bluefin move south along the coast in late fall; the November Hudson Canyon bite for giants is legendary but weather-dependent.
explanation_warm: School bluefin (under 73 in) work bait balls near the surface June-October; giant bluefin (over 73 in) arrive on inshore lumps in fall. Strict NOAA quota — verify your vessel's category before fishing.

name: Atlantic mackerel
bait: Sabiki rigs (best); small pieces of clam, squid, or any shiny flash
rig: Sabiki rig with 6-8 size 8-10 hooks; drift in the current over schools
sinker: 1-4 oz to get rig to depth
lures: Tiny metal jigs (1/4-1/2 oz), small spoons, Sabiki rigs
explanation_cold: Atlantic mackerel overwinter offshore in deep water; they return to coastal waters in spring as the biggest schools of the year push north.
explanation_warm: Mackerel are a schooling species accessible from piers, jetties, and boats spring through early summer; they are one of the best live baits for stripers, blues, and tuna — and excellent eating.

name: Steelhead trout (sea-run rainbow)
bait: Cured salmon roe (top choice); sand shrimp; nightcrawlers; small herring near estuary
rig: Drift rig with pencil lead; bobber-and-jig; float rig with sand shrimp or roe
sinker: Pencil lead 1/4-3/4 oz; split shot on light gear
lures: Jigs in pink/chartreuse/white, spoons (Little Cleo), spinners (Mepps, Blue Fox), egg-sucking leech flies
explanation_cold: Winter steelhead (Dec-Mar) are the primary run in most Pacific NW rivers; they hold in deep pools and runs and respond to slow-drifted roe or jigs in low, clear water.
explanation_warm: Summer steelhead (Jun-Oct) enter rivers while water is still warm; they are more active and will chase lures — swinging flies and spinners through runs produces aggressive strikes.

name: Pacific cod
bait: Squid, herring, clams, cut fish; any fresh bait on a bottom rig
rig: Hi-lo bottom rig with two dropper loops; heavy single-hook bottom rig on rocky ground
lures: Heavy diamond jigs (6-12 oz) in silver; Norwegian-style pirks worked near the bottom
explanation_cold: Pacific cod are most active in cold winter water at 100-400 ft; they are the West Coast equivalent of Atlantic cod and school over rocky and sandy bottom in deeper bays and offshore.
explanation_warm: Pacific cod fishing tapers as water warms above 52°F; fall and winter are prime, especially in Puget Sound and along the Washington coast.

name: Black rockfish
bait: Live or cut herring; tube worms; squid strips; live anchovies
rig: Light to medium tackle; drift-fishing with a single hook on 20-30 lb leader; jig straight down to schools
lures: Tube jigs in black/purple, soft plastic paddle tails, metal jigs (Crippled Herring), and Buzz Bombs — black rockfish readily hit surface lures
explanation_cold: Black rockfish hold near rocky reefs and kelp at 30-150 ft year-round; they are less active in winter but can be found schooling tight to structure.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer are prime for black rockfish along the Pacific coast; they school near the surface around kelp beds and rocky points and aggressively hit surface poppers, tube jigs, and cut herring.

name: Yelloweye rockfish
bait: Squid, cut herring, octopus; any oily bait fished on the bottom in deep water
rig: Heavy bottom rig with 60-80 lb leader; deep-drop setup with electric reel for depths over 300 ft
lures: Heavy slow-pitch jigs (200-400g) in orange/red/gold; flutter jigs worked near rocky bottom
explanation_cold: Yelloweye rockfish inhabit very deep rocky reefs (200-1200 ft) year-round; they are slow-growing and extremely long-lived (up to 120 years) making them heavily protected.
explanation_warm: Yelloweye are targeted by deep-drop anglers year-round; spring and summer are preferred due to calmer seas. Oregon and Washington allow limited harvest — verify current rockfish complex rules before fishing.

name: Quillback rockfish
bait: Live herring, cut squid, tube worms fished near rocky structure
rig: Medium tackle bottom rig; single hook on 20-30 lb leader near rocky reefs at 30-150 ft
lures: Tube jigs, small metal jigs, soft plastic paddle tails in brown/orange
explanation_cold: Quillback rockfish are resident on shallow rocky reefs year-round; they are territorial and solitary, typically found as singles or pairs near the bottom.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall is the most accessible season as seas calm and fish become more active near reef structure at 30-120 ft depth.

name: Olive rockfish
bait: Live anchovies or small herring; tube worms; small cut squid
rig: Light to medium spinning or conventional; drift over kelp and rocky reefs
lures: Small tube jigs, soft plastic paddle tails, Buzz Bombs
explanation_cold: Olive rockfish congregate near the bottom of rocky reefs and kelp beds year-round in nearshore waters.
explanation_warm: Most active spring through fall near kelp canopy at 20-80 ft; a common catch on inshore rockfish trips along the Oregon and Washington coast.

name: Opakapaka (pink snapper)
bait: Fresh whole fish, squid, octopus, or cut bait fished deep on bottom rigs
rig: Deep-drop bottom rig with multiple dropper loops; heavy 100-200 lb leader; electric reel at 600-1200 ft
sinker: 32-64 oz or heavier for deep drops
lures: Heavy slow-pitch jigs (400-800g) in red/pink/silver near deep rocky ledges
explanation_cold: Opakapaka are Hawaii's most prized bottomfish, inhabiting deep rocky ledges at 600-1200 ft; they are targeted year-round on deep-drop trips.
explanation_warm: Fall through winter is considered peak season; opakapaka feed actively at depth and are excellent table fish — one of Hawaii's finest eating species.

name: Onaga (long-tail red snapper)
bait: Fresh whole fish, squid, octopus fished very deep on heavy bottom rigs
rig: Deep-drop rig at 900-1800 ft; electric reel required; multiple hook dropper loops
lures: Heavy jigs (500g+) in red/pink for shallower encounters; mostly bait at depth
explanation_cold: Onaga are found at extreme depths (900-1800 ft) in Hawaii year-round; they require specialized deep-drop gear and electric reels.
explanation_warm: Winter and early spring produce the best onaga fishing; this deep, ruby-red snapper is among the most prized and valuable of Hawaii's bottomfish.

name: Uku (gray snapper / jobfish)
bait: Live baitfish (small akule, nehu), fresh squid, or cut fish near mid-depth reefs
rig: Live bait rig with 40-60 lb fluorocarbon leader; light to medium bottom rig at 100-300 ft
lures: Vertical jigs in blue/silver/white (100-200g), soft plastic swimbaits, live bait on light gear
explanation_cold: Uku hold near mid-depth reefs and bottom structure at 100-400 ft year-round and are accessible throughout winter.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer are peak uku season in Hawaii; they school near rocky bottom and pinnacles and hit jigs and live bait aggressively — one of Hawaii's most popular nearshore targets.

name: Hapu'upu'u (Hawaiian grouper)
bait: Fresh whole fish, large squid, octopus fished deep on heavy bottom rigs
rig: Heavy bottom rig with 150-300 lb leader; multiple dropper loops; electric reel at 300-900 ft
lures: Heavy jigs (300-600g) in dark colors near rocky deep ledges
explanation_cold: Hapu'upu'u inhabit deep rocky ledges at 300-900 ft in Hawaiian waters; they are one of Hawaii's deepwater bottomfish species.
explanation_warm: Winter through early spring produces the best catches; this Hawaiian sea bass can grow to 50+ lbs and is a prized trophy and table fish.

name: Striped marlin
bait: Whole rigged ballyhoo, mackerel, small bonito; skip baits trolled at 7-9 kts
rig: Medium to heavy offshore trolling spread; 150-300 lb leader; 30-50 lb class tackle
lures: Skirted lures in blue/white/pink, cedar plugs, swim-head lures behind teasers
explanation_cold: Striped marlin are most common in fall along the US West Coast; they follow warm water currents and are primarily encountered offshore of Southern California.
explanation_warm: Late summer through fall is the peak window for striped marlin off the California coast; they are an exciting catch-and-release billfish requiring serious offshore tackle.

name: Opah (moonfish)
bait: Squid, herring, or small mackerel fished at mid-water depths offshore
rig: Slow trolling with a spreader bar or deep-set trolling rig at 150-400 ft depth
sinker: None for trolling; 16-32 oz for deep-drop
lures: Heavy slow-pitch jigs at mid-water depth; opah are caught incidentally on albacore and swordfish trips
explanation_cold: Opah are year-round offshore residents that migrate with warm-water eddies; they are rarely targeted directly but frequently caught as bycatch on tuna and swordfish trips.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall is the peak season when opah are most abundant near the surface in warm Pacific waters; they are exceptional eating fish and highly prized.

name: Porbeagle shark
bait: Fresh whole mackerel, herring, or bluefish; large chunk baits on heavy mono or wire leader
rig: Heavy shark rig with 300-400 lb wire or heavy mono leader; balloon float for drifting bait
sinker: None for drifting; 4-8 oz to sink bait
lures: Large soft plastic swimbaits trolled slowly; primarily a bait fishery
explanation_cold: Porbeagle are cold-water sharks that stay active year-round in the North Atlantic; they are found at the surface and near bottom over offshore banks in cool water.
explanation_warm: Spring through early summer is peak season when porbeagle approach the continental shelf; they are a powerful, acrobatic catch and must be released in US waters (prohibited to harvest).

name: Acadian redfish (ocean perch)
bait: Fresh or frozen squid strips, sandworms, clams, small cut herring
rig: Hi-lo rig with small dropper loops; fish in schools at 200-600 ft depth
lures: Small diamond jigs (4-6 oz) in silver; Norwegian-style jigs with tube tails
explanation_cold: Acadian redfish are year-round residents of deep offshore banks (200-600 ft); they school densely and provide fast action — a 20-fish bag on a drift is common.
explanation_warm: Spring trips to Stellwagen Bank and Georges Bank produce the best Acadian redfish fishing; they are a great eating species that are underutilized by recreational anglers.

name: Petrale sole
bait: Squid strips, sand lance, small herring, clams; any fresh bait fished on sandy bottom
rig: Light bottom rig with two small dropper loops; drift over sandy or mud bottom at 60-200 ft
lures: Small jigs or blade baits tipped with squid fished near the bottom
explanation_cold: Petrale sole move into deeper water (200-400 ft) in winter to spawn; fall through winter offshore trips can target them specifically.
explanation_warm: Spring and early summer petrale sole move into shallower nearshore grounds (60-150 ft); they are the most prized of West Coast flatfish for the table.

name: Pacific sanddab
bait: Clams, sand lance, squid strips, small shrimp; tiny baits on small hooks are best
rig: Light multi-hook bottom rig with 4-6 small dropper loops; drift over sandy bottom at 20-100 ft
lures: Very small jigs tipped with bait
explanation_cold: Pacific sanddabs are found on sandy bottom year-round at 20-300 ft; they are accessible from piers and party boats throughout the year.
explanation_warm: Summer and fall are the best times for sanddabs on party boats; limits of these small but delicious flatfish are common — they are considered one of California's finest eating fish.

name: English sole
bait: Sandworms, clams, squid strips; small baits presented near bottom in bays and estuaries
rig: Ultra-light bottom rig with very small hooks; fish in bays and estuaries near eelgrass beds
lures: Very small jig heads tipped with worm or squid
explanation_cold: English sole are bay and nearshore residents found year-round on sandy and mud bottoms; they are active in cold water and accessible from shore in winter.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer are the most productive seasons for English sole in bays and estuaries; a fun light-tackle species great for introducing beginners to flatfish fishing.

name: Arrowtooth flounder
bait: Herring, sand lance, small squid; the same baits as halibut but for a smaller target
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 60-300 ft on sandy or soft bottom; standard halibut-style setup
lures: Small metal jigs, paddle-tail swimbaits near the bottom
explanation_cold: Arrowtooth flounder are abundant on the West Coast at 100-400 ft over sandy and soft bottom; they are common bycatch on halibut and other bottomfish trips.
explanation_warm: Available year-round; most commonly caught spring through fall on bottomfish trips off Oregon and Washington. Often misidentified — arrowtooth have large, arrow-shaped teeth unlike halibut.

name: Cusk
bait: Fresh clams (top bait), squid, herring, sandworms; bait must be fresh for cusk
rig: Single-hook bottom rig with 40-60 lb leader; fish near the bottom over rocky ledges and wrecks
lures: Heavy diamond jigs (8-12 oz) worked slowly near the bottom; cusk occasionally hit jigs
explanation_cold: Cusk are deepwater cod-relatives found at 100-600 ft over hard rocky bottom; they are most active in cold water from fall through spring.
explanation_warm: Cusk are primarily a winter and early spring target in New England; they fight well and are excellent eating — an underappreciated sportfish on deep cod and haddock trips.

name: China rockfish
bait: Live or cut herring, squid strips, tube worms near structure
rig: Light to medium bottom rig; drift near vertical rock walls and caves at 20-150 ft
lures: Tube jigs in black/yellow, small metal jigs; China rockfish are visual strikers
explanation_cold: China rockfish are year-round residents on shallow rocky reefs and are not strongly seasonal; they sit in caves and crevices waiting for prey.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall produces the most accessible fishing for China rockfish along rocky shores of the Pacific Northwest coast; they are easily recognized by their distinctive yellow racing stripe.

name: Black-and-yellow rockfish
bait: Tube worms, small live herring, squid strips near structure
rig: Light tackle; single hook on 15-20 lb leader; fish near kelp and rocky substrate at 10-60 ft
lures: Small tube jigs, tiny metal jigs, soft plastics
explanation_cold: Black-and-yellow rockfish are shallow-water residents on rocky reefs and kelp beds, present year-round in California.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer are most productive in the upper water column around kelp; they are a popular pier target in central and northern California.

name: Surf smelt (Pacific)
bait: Sabiki rigs; very small hooks with tiny bait are ideal; they also beach-spawn and can be scooped
rig: Sabiki rig in the surf zone; fine-mesh scoop net during beach spawning events
lures: Tiny metal flash jigs or sabiki rigs
explanation_cold: Surf smelt overwinter offshore and are largely inaccessible; they are a bycatch species on winter pier outings.
explanation_warm: Summer spawning runs bring surf smelt onto sandy beaches in the Pacific Northwest; they are excellent live bait for salmon and halibut and good table fare when pan-fried.

name: Gray triggerfish
bait: Small blue crabs or fiddler crabs (best); squid strips; clam pieces on very small hooks
rig: Small hook on light 20-30 lb fluorocarbon leader; free-line bait near structure
hook_size: #1-1/0 small strong hook — triggerfish have hard beaks and strip bait from large hooks
lures: Small jigs with crab or squid trailer; triggerfish rarely hit lures but will sometimes investigate
explanation_cold: Gray triggerfish retreat to deeper offshore reefs in winter and are rarely caught nearshore.
explanation_warm: Summer and fall around nearshore artificial reefs, live bottoms, and offshore wrecks; triggerfish are clever bait-stealers that require tiny hooks and fresh crab — one of the most fun and frustrating reef fish to target.

name: Lehi (amberjack / silvermouth jack)
bait: Live baitfish (small akule, nehu, opelu); fresh squid or cut fish near deep ledges
rig: Live bait rig with 80-100 lb fluorocarbon leader; drift or vertical presentation near structure
sinker: None for live bait; 2-4 oz to keep bait near structure
lures: Large vertical jigs (150-300g) in blue/silver near ledges and pinnacles
explanation_cold: Lehi are deep-reef amberjack found at 200-600 ft on Hawaiian rocky ledges; they are less accessible in winter but present year-round.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer are peak lehi season in Hawaii; these powerful, deep-dwelling amberjack run hard when hooked and are excellent eating — one of Hawaii's prized but less-known sportfish.

name: Atlantic salmon
bait: Cured salmon roe; sand shrimp; small herring near estuary mouths
rig: Fly rod with sink-tip line is the traditional approach; drift rig with roe near river mouths
sinker: Split shot or light pencil lead for drift
lures: Classic Atlantic salmon wet flies (Green Highlander, Jock Scott, Rusty Rat), tube flies, spey flies; small spinners near estuary
explanation_cold: Atlantic salmon overwinter at sea and are not a freshwater target in winter; they return to rivers in spring and fall.
explanation_warm: Wild Atlantic salmon are critically endangered in the US; most Maine rivers hold very few fish. The traditional Maine salmon flies fishery is a catch-and-release cultural institution. Verify all current rules — harvest is generally prohibited.

name: Sockeye salmon (red salmon)
bait: Tiny red or orange spinners, small jigs, or sockeye flies; they do not actively feed in fresh water
rig: Light spinning or fly rod; small hook presentations that aggravate territorial instinct
hook_size: #6-#4 small colored hook or spinner treble
lures: Small red/orange spinners (size 0-2), tiny bright-colored jigs, short-shank sockeye flies; sockeye must be aggravated into striking
explanation_cold: Sockeye are not a freshwater target outside their summer return; they are unavailable at other times.
explanation_warm: Sockeye return to Pacific NW rivers July-August in massive numbers; they are notoriously difficult to catch on rod-and-reel because they stop feeding on return — very small aggravation presentations are the only reliable method.

name: Rock sole
bait: Clams, sandworms, squid strips; any fresh bait on small hooks near bottom
rig: Light multi-hook bottom rig; drift over sandy and gravel bottom at 30-200 ft
lures: Small jigs tipped with bait
explanation_cold: Rock sole are most active in cold water; they move into shallow estuaries and bays in spring to spawn.
explanation_warm: Spring spawning aggregations bring rock sole into accessible shallow water; they are a tasty and commonly caught flatfish on Pacific NW party boats.

name: Bocaccio
bait: Live or cut herring, squid strips, anchovies near deep rocky reefs
rig: Bottom rig or dropper loop at 100-400 ft on rocky structure
lures: Heavy jigs (150-300g) in red/orange, soft plastic swimbaits near deep structure
explanation_cold: Bocaccio hold in deeper rocky habitat year-round; winter finds them concentrated in 200-400 ft over hard bottom.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer are most productive at 100-250 ft; bocaccio are a rebuilding species with retention limits — verify current rockfish complex rules before fishing.

name: Widow rockfish
bait: Herring, anchovies, squid; widow rockfish school mid-water and take bait readily
rig: Mid-water dropper loop rig at 150-400 ft; jig straight down to schooling fish
lures: Heavy diamond jigs (200-400g) in silver, flutter jigs worked mid-water column
explanation_cold: Widow rockfish school in mid-water at 150-500 ft year-round along the Pacific coast.
explanation_warm: Spring and early summer produce the best fishing as fish school densely over offshore banks; a mainstay catch on Pacific NW party boat rockfish trips.

name: Tiger rockfish
bait: Live or cut herring, tube worms, squid strips fished tight to rocky structure
rig: Single hook bottom rig at 30-200 ft on hard rocky bottom; territorial fish found one at a time
lures: Tube jigs in orange/black/red, small metal jigs worked near crevices and ledges
explanation_cold: Tiger rockfish are solitary territorial fish on shallow to mid-depth rocky reefs year-round.
explanation_warm: Accessible from spring through fall at 30-150 ft on rocky PNW reefs; recognized by distinctive tiger-stripe pattern.

name: Treefish
bait: Tube worms, small herring or anchovies, squid strips near structure
rig: Light to medium tackle; single hook near rocky bottom at 10-80 ft
lures: Small tube jigs, tiny metal jigs near rocky ledges and caves
explanation_cold: Treefish are shallow-water residents on rocky reefs and kelp beds year-round in central and northern California.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall near shallow rocky structures; striking yellow/black striped pattern makes them unmistakable.

name: Gopher rockfish
bait: Tube worms, small anchovies or herring, squid strips near bottom structure
rig: Light bottom rig on rocky reef at 10-100 ft; single hook close to structure
lures: Small tube jigs, soft plastic grubs in brown/white/pink
explanation_cold: Gopher rockfish are resident on shallow rocky reefs and kelp beds year-round.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer are the most accessible season for gopher rockfish near shallow rocky structure of central California; commonly caught from kayaks and small boats.

name: Kelp rockfish
bait: Live anchovies or small herring, tube worms; must be presented in or near kelp canopy
rig: Lightweight float or free-line rig in the kelp canopy at 10-40 ft
lures: Small swimbaits, tube jigs, small surface lures worked through kelp gaps
explanation_cold: Kelp rockfish inhabit kelp forests year-round but are less active in winter when kelp senescence reduces cover.
explanation_warm: Summer is prime for kelp rockfish suspended in the kelp canopy at 5-30 ft; they are a top kayak and small-boat target in southern and central California kelp forests.

name: Dover sole
bait: Clams, squid strips, sand lance, tube worms on very small hooks near soft bottom
rig: Ultra-light multi-hook bottom rig; drift over soft mud or sandy bottom at 60-400 ft
lures: Tiny jig heads tipped with bait
explanation_cold: Dover sole inhabit deeper soft-bottom habitat (100-400 ft) year-round and are most accessible in winter on offshore party boat trips.
explanation_warm: Spring and early summer catch rates improve as fish move to shallower grounds; Dover sole are exceptional eating — one of the best-tasting flatfish on the West Coast.

name: Rex sole
bait: Very small baits — clams, tube worms, tiny squid strips; rex sole have tiny mouths
rig: Ultra-light multi-hook bottom rig at 30-200 ft on sandy-mud bottom
hook_size: #6-#4 hook — small mouth requires small hook
lures: N/A; bait-only due to small mouth size
explanation_cold: Rex sole are available year-round on sandy and soft bottom in nearshore waters; they concentrate in bays in winter.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer on sandy bottom at 30-150 ft; caught alongside other flatfish species on party boat bottomfish trips.

name: Pacific spiny dogfish
bait: Herring, squid, clams, cut fish; dogfish are opportunistic and will eat almost anything
rig: Medium bottom rig at 30-200 ft; wire leader not required but 40-60 lb mono helps with abrasion
lures: Heavy metal jigs, large swim shads worked near the bottom
explanation_cold: Pacific spiny dogfish are year-round residents on the West Coast and are most commonly encountered in Puget Sound and along the Oregon/Washington coast.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall produces the most active dogfish schools near bait balls; they are the most abundant shark in Pacific NW waters and a prolific bycatch species — very good eating if prepared fresh.

name: Sixgill shark
bait: Large cut baits — whole herring, squid, salmon carcasses, large chunk fish; sixgills are deep scavengers
rig: Heavy shark rig with 200-400 lb mono or wire leader; deep-drop from anchored boat at 100-600 ft at night
lures: Not a lure target; bait-only deep-drop fishery
explanation_cold: Sixgill sharks inhabit deep cold water (300-6000 ft) year-round but come to relatively shallow water at night in Puget Sound and Hood Canal.
explanation_warm: Summer night-fishing in Puget Sound produces the best sixgill encounters at 100-300 ft; these prehistoric-looking sharks can exceed 15 ft and 1,300 lbs — a bucket-list catch in the Pacific NW.

name: Sevengill shark
bait: Fresh cut fish — herring, mackerel, jacksmelt, fresh squid; strong-smelling fresh bait is best
rig: Medium-heavy rig with 80-200 lb mono leader; fish from shore or boat in bays and estuaries
lures: Large swimbaits fished slowly near the bottom; sevengills occasionally hit lures
explanation_cold: Sevengill sharks use bays and estuaries as pupping grounds in fall; they are present in San Francisco Bay and similar habitats year-round.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer produce the best sevengill fishing in California bays; they are a popular shore-fishing target from bridge pilings and bay shores, particularly in the SF Bay Area.

name: Tope shark (soupfin)
bait: Fresh herring, mackerel, squid; tope sharks prefer fresh, oily baitfish
rig: Medium shark rig with 80-150 lb mono leader; drift bait near bottom or mid-water
lures: Large swimbaits slowly retrieved near the bottom; occasional lure takes in kelp areas
explanation_cold: Tope (soupfin) sharks are migratory, moving south in winter and returning to California bays and nearshore in spring.
explanation_warm: Summer and fall are peak tope season along the California coast; they are a strong fighter and excellent food fish — one of California's most underrated sportfish.

name: Kumu (whitesaddle goatfish)
bait: Small shrimp, tiny crab pieces, sandworms; kumu root around in sand for invertebrates
rig: Very light bottom rig with tiny hooks near sandy bottom; light 10-15 lb fluorocarbon
lures: Very small jigs tipped with shrimp; micro soft plastic grubs
explanation_cold: Kumu are found year-round in Hawaiian waters on sandy flats and rubble near reef edges.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall produces the best kumu fishing near sand patches adjacent to shallow Hawaiian reefs; they are highly prized table fish and a traditional Hawaiian subsistence species.

name: Nenue (Hawaiian chub)
bait: Sea lettuce and other algae (natural food); bread balls, cooked rice, or dough bait work best
rig: Ultra-light float rig with tiny hooks and dough bait or algae; light 8-12 lb line
lures: Not a lure target; requires natural or dough bait presentations
explanation_cold: Nenue (chub) are resident on shallow Hawaiian reefs and surge zones year-round.
explanation_warm: Summer is peak nenue fishing around Hawaiian pier pilings, rocky shores, and shallow reef areas; they respond to bread and dough bait and are a fun light-tackle species.

name: Pacific ocean perch
bait: Squid strips, herring, clams, sandworms; any fresh bait on a bottom rig
rig: Hi-lo bottom rig at 200-600 ft; deep-drop on offshore banks and ridges
lures: Medium diamond jigs (100-200g) in red/silver worked near deep bottom
explanation_cold: Pacific ocean perch inhabit deep rocky habitat (200-900 ft) year-round; they are a common catch on offshore bank fishing trips.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer are most accessible on offshore party boat trips to Pacific NW banks; they school densely over rocky bottom and provide fast-paced action when located.

name: Rougheye rockfish
bait: Squid, herring, cut fish fished deep on heavy bottom rigs; an extremely slow-growing deep species
rig: Deep-drop bottom rig at 400-1500 ft; electric reel may be needed for greatest depths
lures: Heavy slow-pitch jigs (300-500g) near deep rocky bottom
explanation_cold: Rougheye rockfish are among the longest-lived rockfish (up to 205 years); they inhabit very deep cold water year-round and are rarely targeted specifically.
explanation_warm: Encountered as bycatch on deep-drop trips for sablefish and halibut; regulations are very conservative due to extreme age and slow recovery time — verify all current rockfish rules.

name: Longspine thornyhead
bait: Squid, cut fish, herring; any fresh bait on a deep-drop rig
rig: Deep-drop bottom rig at 600-2000 ft; electric reel typically required
lures: Heavy slow-pitch jigs (400-800g) at extreme depth
explanation_cold: Longspine thornyheads (idiots) live at extreme depths (600-2000 ft); rarely targeted specifically and encountered mainly as deep-drop bycatch.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer are the most practical time to deep-drop for thornyheads; they are prized for their excellent flavor and sold commercially as 'idiot fish' or 'channel rockfish'.

name: Brown rockfish
bait: Live or cut herring, tube worms, squid strips near shallow rocky habitat
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 20-120 ft in bays, estuaries, and nearshore rocky areas
lures: Small tube jigs, soft plastic grubs in brown/red, small metal jigs
explanation_cold: Brown rockfish are year-round residents in bays and nearshore waters, tolerating warmer and brackish conditions better than most rockfish.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer near shallow rocky structure in California bays and estuaries; commonly caught from docks, piers, and kayaks — one of the most accessible rockfish species.

name: Rosy rockfish
bait: Small herring or anchovies, squid strips, tube worms near rocky structure at moderate depth
rig: Light bottom rig at 50-200 ft on rocky or mixed bottom
lures: Small tube jigs in pink/red, tiny metal jigs worked near rocky bottom
explanation_cold: Rosy rockfish inhabit rocky reefs at 50-200 ft year-round along the California and Oregon coast.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall on nearshore rocky reefs; a brightly colored species often caught alongside vermilion and copper rockfish on inshore trips.

name: Canary rockfish
bait: Herring, anchovies, squid strips near rocky mid-depth reefs
rig: Medium bottom rig at 100-350 ft on rocky bottom
lures: Diamond jigs (150-300g) in orange/gold near the bottom
explanation_cold: Canary rockfish inhabit rocky reefs at 80-400 ft year-round; they are a rebuilding species with very restrictive retention rules.
explanation_warm: Encountered on offshore rockfish trips spring through fall; canary rockfish are often prohibited from retention — verify current rockfish complex rules and area closures before keeping any.

name: Starry rockfish
bait: Anchovies, small herring, squid strips; presents best near rocky structure at moderate depth
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 30-150 ft on rocky and mixed bottom
lures: Small tube jigs, soft plastics in orange/red/white
explanation_cold: Starry rockfish are resident on shallow to mid-depth rocky reefs year-round in California.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer near rocky structure at 30-150 ft; recognized by their distinctive star-shaped white spots on bright orange body — a visually striking southern California rockfish.

name: Kala (unicornfish)
bait: Limu (seaweed), bread bait, or tiny invertebrate pieces near reef edges
rig: Ultra-light float or bottom rig with very small hook; light 10-15 lb line
lures: Not a lure target; requires plant-based or dough bait
explanation_cold: Kala (bluespine unicornfish) are resident on Hawaiian reefs year-round, grazing on algae along reef edges and surge zones.
explanation_warm: Year-round target on Hawaiian reefs; most active in warmer months near surge channels and reef edges where algae grows abundantly — a light-tackle challenge on small hooks.

name: Manini (convict tang)
bait: Limu (algae), bread balls, cooked noodles, or rice compressed on a tiny hook
rig: Ultra-light float rig with size 8-12 hook; 6-10 lb line; fish in tide pools and shallow reef
lures: Not a lure species; requires plant-based bait
explanation_cold: Manini are schooling surgeonfish resident on shallow Hawaiian reefs year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round shallow-water target in Hawaii; often seen in large schools over rocky reef and tide pools — challenging to hook due to small mouth but a traditional Hawaiian subsistence fish.

name: Shortspine thornyhead
bait: Squid, cut fish, shrimp; any fresh bait at deep-water depths
rig: Deep-drop rig at 400-1800 ft; similar setup to sablefish fishing
lures: Heavy slow-pitch jigs (400g+) in red near deep rocky bottom
explanation_cold: Shortspine thornyheads inhabit deep rocky bottom (400-1800 ft) year-round; commonly sold in Asian markets as 'channel rockfish.'
explanation_warm: Occasionally targeted specifically by deep-drop anglers; more often caught as bycatch alongside sablefish — superb eating fish with rich, flaky white flesh.

name: Pile perch
bait: Mussels, small clams, sandworms, tube worms near pilings and rocky structure
rig: Light float or bottom rig at 5-30 ft near dock pilings, rocky jetties, and kelp
lures: Small tube jigs, tiny grubs near structure
explanation_cold: Pile perch are a schooling species around pilings and jetties year-round; they are less active in coldest winter months.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall is peak for pile perch near harbor pilings and rocky structure; one of the most common pier perch in California and good eating when kept fresh.

name: Shiner perch
bait: Sandworms, tiny clam bits, very small shrimp pieces; tiny baits on tiny hooks
rig: Ultra-light float or bottom rig; 4-6 lb line with size 8-12 hooks
lures: Micro tube jigs, tiny grubs
explanation_cold: Shiner perch are extremely abundant in California bays and estuaries year-round; they are easiest to catch near eelgrass beds.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer in eelgrass beds and near pilings; shiner perch are excellent live bait for larger halibut and are great fun for kids on ultra-light gear.

name: Rainbow seaperch
bait: Mussels, sandworms, small clams, shrimp pieces near rocky reef and kelp
rig: Light float or bottom rig at 10-40 ft near rocky structure
lures: Very small soft plastic grubs, tiny tube jigs
explanation_cold: Rainbow seaperch inhabit rocky reefs and kelp beds year-round along the California and Oregon coast.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall near rocky shorelines and kelp canopy; one of the most colorful Pacific surfperch with stunning red/blue/orange markings.

name: Striped seaperch
bait: Mussels, tube worms, sandworms, tiny shrimp near exposed rocky coast
rig: Light to medium surf rig or float rig near rocky jetties and surge zones
lures: Small metal jigs, tube jigs near rocky structure
explanation_cold: Striped seaperch favor exposed rocky shorelines and jetties; they are active year-round but most accessible spring through fall.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer on rocky exposed coastline at 5-30 ft; one of the deeper-reaching surfperch, sometimes caught to 80 ft near offshore rocky pinnacles.

name: Pink seaperch
bait: Small sandworms, clams, mussels, shrimp pieces on tiny hooks
rig: Ultra-light float rig or surf rig near sandy and mixed bottom
lures: Tiny soft plastic grubs, micro tube jigs
explanation_cold: Pink seaperch favor sandy-bottom nearshore areas and are present year-round along the Pacific coast.
explanation_warm: Spring and summer from surf and piers over sandy bottom; often caught alongside barred surfperch in the surf zone.

name: Chilipepper rockfish
bait: Herring, anchovies, squid strips at mid-depth on offshore banks
rig: Mid-water dropper loop rig at 150-400 ft; jig straight down to schools on sonar
lures: Heavy diamond jigs (150-300g) in pink/red/silver worked mid-water
explanation_cold: Chilipepper rockfish school densely at 150-450 ft over offshore banks fall through spring.
explanation_warm: Spring and early summer party-boat rockfish trips to Pacific banks produce limits of chilipeppers; they school tightly and once found, the action is fast.

name: Shortbelly rockfish
bait: Small herring, anchovies, squid; shortbelly are small and school in huge numbers mid-water
rig: Sabiki rig worked at 100-300 ft mid-water on offshore trips
lures: Small sabiki-style jigs in the water column
explanation_cold: Shortbelly rockfish are mid-water schoolers at 100-400 ft year-round on the Pacific coast; they are an important baitfish for larger predators.
explanation_warm: Commonly caught as bycatch on offshore rockfish and tuna trips; not often targeted specifically but make excellent live bait for halibut and lingcod.

name: Painted greenling
bait: Small crabs, mussels, sandworms; painted greenling are ambush predators near structure
rig: Light bottom rig at 5-40 ft near rocky reef and kelp; very short leader stays near bottom
lures: Very small tube jigs, tiny grubs worked slowly near the bottom
explanation_cold: Painted greenling are year-round residents on shallow rocky reefs along the Pacific coast.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall near exposed rocky shores and tidal zones at 5-30 ft; a beautifully marked species with striking crimson and white bars.

name: Oceanic whitetip shark
bait: Large whole fish, squid, or chunk bait; this is an offshore open-ocean species
rig: Heavy shark rig with 300-400 lb wire or heavy mono leader; drift bait at surface offshore
lures: Large slow trolled baits; rarely hits artificial lures
explanation_cold: Oceanic whitetip sharks are confined to warm offshore blue water and are rarely encountered closer than 30 miles from shore.
explanation_warm: Summer encounters in the Gulf Stream and Gulf of Mexico offshore; prohibited from harvest in US waters — release all immediately.

name: Silky shark
bait: Large chunk fish, whole rigged bait, or fresh cut bait offshore
rig: Heavy shark rig with wire or heavy mono leader; free-line or slow troll offshore
lures: Large trolling lures occasionally; primarily a bait fishery
explanation_cold: Silky sharks are offshore blue-water residents most common in summer near the Gulf Stream and in the Gulf of Mexico.
explanation_warm: Summer through early fall offshore; silky sharks are prohibited from harvest in US Atlantic waters — catch and release only.

name: Common thresher shark
bait: Fresh whole bluefish, mackerel, or bunker (menhaden); threshers stun prey with their long tail
rig: Heavy shark rig with 200-400 lb leader; drift bait at surface or mid-water
lures: Large swimming plugs or soft plastic swimbaits trolled slowly; primarily a bait fishery
explanation_cold: Common thresher sharks move south and offshore in winter; they return to Mid-Atlantic and New England waters in summer.
explanation_warm: Summer through early fall along the Mid-Atlantic and New England coast; common threshers are acrobatic jumpers and one of the most exciting sharks on rod-and-reel.

name: Shortbill spearfish
bait: Whole rigged ballyhoo, squid, or small mackerel trolled at 7-9 kts
rig: Medium offshore trolling spread; 100-200 lb leader; 20-30 lb class tackle
lures: Skirted lures in blue/white, cedar plugs
explanation_cold: Shortbill spearfish are rare offshore visitors along the US East Coast; encounters are uncommon compared to white marlin or sailfish.
explanation_warm: Summer offshore in the Gulf Stream; they are the least common Atlantic billfish and a notable catch for offshore anglers.

name: Sand drum
bait: Small shrimp, sand fleas, fiddler crabs, cut mullet near sandy bottom in the surf or inlets
rig: Light to medium surf rig or fish-finder rig on sandy bottom
lures: Small paddle-tail jigs near bottom; sand drum occasionally hit slow-moving soft plastics
explanation_cold: Sand drum are year-round Gulf/SE residents; they are less active in cooler months but present year-round.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in the surf and around inlet mouths; a smaller relative of the black drum, they hit similar baits and are underrated table fare.

name: Southern puffer
bait: Shrimp, fiddler crabs, clams, sand fleas; puffers will eat almost any bottom bait
rig: Light bottom rig with small hooks near sandy/grassy bottom in bays and inlets
lures: Not a lure target; bait-only
explanation_cold: Southern puffers are warm-season visitors in northern parts of their range; year-round in South Florida.
explanation_warm: Summer and fall in the Gulf and SE coast; called 'sea squab', they are excellent eating when properly cleaned.

name: Gulf toadfish
bait: Any dead bait — shrimp, cut mullet, clams; toadfish are extreme bottom-dwellers
rig: Bottom rig fished directly on sand or mud near shell rubble and oyster reefs
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Gulf toadfish are year-round residents in warm Gulf waters, living in shell middens, oyster reefs, and under rocks.
explanation_warm: Year-round bycatch in Gulf bays; they make a loud whistle call during spawning and are commonly hooked while targeting sheepshead and flounder.

name: Sea raven
bait: Fresh clams, squid, sandworms, cut herring; sea ravens are aggressive bottom feeders
rig: Heavy bottom rig at 60-300 ft over rocky or mixed bottom
lures: Heavy jigs worked near the bottom; sea ravens strike hard and fight well for their size
explanation_cold: Sea ravens are year-round cold-water residents on rocky bottom at 30-300 ft; most active fall through spring.
explanation_warm: Fall through spring on deeper rocky structure; a common bycatch on New England cod and haddock trips with dramatic puffing behavior when landed.

name: Akule (bigeye scad)
bait: Sabiki rigs with small hooks; also caught by cast net
rig: Sabiki rig fished near the surface or mid-water in Hawaiian harbors and bays
lures: Tiny metal jigs in silver; primarily a sabiki rig target
explanation_cold: Akule school year-round in Hawaiian harbors and nearshore waters; large schools are visible at the surface at dawn.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall produces the largest schools of akule nearshore; prized as live bait for ulua and other large predators, and excellent eating when salted and dried (traditionally).

name: Opelu (mackerel scad)
bait: Sabiki rigs; very small hooks with minimal bait; also cast-netted in large numbers
rig: Sabiki rig fished mid-water to 60 ft in Hawaiian coastal waters
lures: Tiny silver jigs, sabiki rigs
explanation_cold: Opelu school around Hawaiian harbors, bays, and nearshore seamounts year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round target for live bait; opelu are Hawaii's premier live bait for ahi and other big game — a cast-net full of live opelu is worth its weight in gold on a big-game trip.

name: Uhu (parrotfish)
bait: Small crab pieces, sea urchin, bread bait near coral reef; they scrape algae from coral
rig: Light to medium bottom rig near coral and reef structure
lures: Not commonly caught on lures; small jigs near reef occasionally work
explanation_cold: Uhu are reef-dwelling parrotfish present year-round on Hawaiian coral reefs.
explanation_warm: Year-round target near Hawaiian coral reefs; uhu are highly prized as food fish and were a traditional Hawaiian delicacy — they are regulated and most anglers practice selective harvest.

name: Taape (bluestripe snapper)
bait: Small shrimp, squid strips, tiny pieces of fish near reef structure
rig: Light bottom rig near shallow reef at 10-60 ft; small hooks required
lures: Small jigs in yellow/blue, tiny soft plastic grubs near reef
explanation_cold: Taape (introduced from French Polynesia) are year-round residents on Hawaiian shallow reefs, often forming large schools.
explanation_warm: Year-round abundant species on Hawaiian reefs; easy to catch and good eating — they are an introduced species and there are no bag limits, so harvest is encouraged.

name: Moano (goatfish)
bait: Small shrimp, tiny crabs, sandworms near sand and rubble adjacent to reef
rig: Ultra-light bottom rig near sandy patches on reef at 5-40 ft
lures: Very small jigs tipped with shrimp
explanation_cold: Moano (banded goatfish) are year-round residents on Hawaiian reefs, foraging in sand with their chemosensory barbels.
explanation_warm: Year-round target near Hawaiian sandy reef patches; they taste excellent but require small hooks and light line to land consistently.

name: Atlantic silverside
bait: Tiny pieces of clam, sandworm, or bread; sabiki rigs sized for tiny mouths
rig: Ultra-light float rig or sabiki in tidal creeks and estuaries near grass banks
lures: Micro jigs, tiny sabiki rigs
explanation_cold: Atlantic silversides school in tidal creeks and estuaries fall through spring; they are a foundational baitfish species in the Northeast ecosystem.
