explanation_warm: Spring and summer bring enormous schools of silversides into salt marshes and estuaries; they are the most important live bait for striped bass and bluefish and can be caught by the bucket-full with a sabiki rig.

name: Lumpfish
bait: Worms, small clams, amphipods near rocky structure; lumpfish are not targeted but caught incidentally
rig: Light bottom rig near rocky substrate; caught incidentally while targeting other species
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Lumpfish are cold-water residents that come into shallow water to spawn in early spring; they attach to rocks with their pelvic suction disc.
explanation_warm: Spring spawning brings lumpfish to shallow rocky shores in New England; they are a bizarre bycatch curiosity rather than a targeted species — their roe is commercially harvested as a caviar substitute.

name: Scaled sardine (pilchard)
bait: Cast net is primary method; tiny sabiki hooks work in schooling areas
rig: Cast net or sabiki rig near the surface in bays and inlets
lures: Tiny sabiki-style rigs; primarily a cast-net baitfish
explanation_cold: Scaled sardines school year-round in Florida and the Gulf; they thin out in winter north of Florida.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in Florida bays and Gulf nearshore; the most important live bait for snook, tarpon, and other inshore predators in Florida — a live pilchard free-lined to a tarpon is the ultimate presentation.

name: Monkeyface prickleback
bait: Small crabs, mussels, tiny shrimp; found in rocky intertidal zone
rig: Ultra-light bottom rig in tide pools and rocky intertidal with small hook near bottom
lures: Very small tube jigs, micro soft plastics
explanation_cold: Monkeyface pricklebacks live in rocky intertidal and shallow subtidal habitat year-round along the Pacific coast.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in rocky intertidal zone; a beloved target for kids and beginners fishing rocky California and Oregon coastlines — tasty and surprisingly challenging on light gear.

name: Spotted sand bass
bait: Live anchovies or small baitfish, squid strips near sandy/muddy bottom in bays
rig: Light to medium bottom rig in bays and nearshore areas at 10-60 ft
lures: Soft plastic swimbaits, small paddle-tails on light jig heads near bottom
explanation_cold: Spotted sand bass are bay and estuary residents in Southern California; they overlap with barred sand bass but prefer softer bottom habitat.
explanation_warm: Summer and fall in San Diego Bay and other Southern California coastal bays; sometimes referred to as 'bay bass' and a fun light-tackle target from kayaks and small boats.

name: Squarespot rockfish
bait: Small herring, anchovies, squid strips near shallow rocky reef
rig: Light bottom rig at 20-100 ft on rocky or mixed bottom
lures: Small tube jigs, soft plastic grubs
explanation_cold: Squarespot rockfish are year-round residents on shallow rocky reefs of California; they are often confused with small black rockfish.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall on shallow rocky reefs at 20-80 ft; commonly caught as part of mixed rockfish bags on inshore California trips.

name: Greenstriped rockfish
bait: Squid, herring, anchovies; a mid-depth schooling rockfish
rig: Mid-water dropper loop rig at 100-300 ft over offshore banks
lures: Diamond jigs (100-200g) in silver/green worked mid-water
explanation_cold: Greenstriped rockfish school at 100-350 ft on offshore Pacific banks year-round.
explanation_warm: Party boat rockfish trips in spring and summer frequently encounter greenstriped rockfish on offshore banks; they are part of the mixed rockfish bag.

name: Splitnose rockfish
bait: Squid, herring, small cut fish at medium to deep depths
rig: Bottom to mid-water dropper loop rig at 150-500 ft
lures: Diamond jigs (200-400g) near bottom or mid-water
explanation_cold: Splitnose rockfish inhabit deeper water (150-600 ft) on Pacific offshore banks year-round.
explanation_warm: Caught on deep rockfish trips in spring and summer; part of the mixed rockfish bag on offshore Pacific party boat trips.

name: Pygmy rockfish
bait: Small anchovies, tiny squid strips, tube worms near structure
rig: Light tackle; single hook near rocky reef at 30-120 ft
lures: Very small tube jigs, tiny metal jigs
explanation_cold: Pygmy rockfish are one of the smallest California rockfish, found on shallow to mid-depth rocky reefs year-round.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall near rocky structure at 30-100 ft; often caught as part of mixed nearshore rockfish bags.

name: Weakfish (seatrout)
bait: Peeler crab (best), shrimp, sandworms, spot or croaker on bottom in estuaries and nearshore
rig: Fishfinder rig or Carolina rig at 2-20 ft over sandy bottom in tidal creeks and estuaries
lures: Bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp shrimp, soft plastic paddle tails in white/chartreuse, topwater plugs at dawn
explanation_cold: Weakfish populations have declined sharply; they are most active spring and fall when water temps hit 65-75°F.
explanation_warm: Spring and fall runs in tidal rivers and bays from Virginia to New Jersey are the prime seasons; weakfish are extremely sensitive to freshness — ice immediately for best table quality.

name: Spotted seatrout
bait: Live shrimp (no. 1 bait), live finger mullet, shrimp under a popping cork in grass flats
rig: Popping cork rig with live shrimp or artificial shrimp at 2-6 ft over grass flats; or light jig head
sinker: Popping cork or 1/8-1/4 oz jig head
lures: DOA shrimp, Gulp Shrimp, MirrOlure, Z-Man ShrimpZ under popping cork; topwater plugs at dawn and dusk on flats
explanation_cold: Spotted seatrout are inshore year-round in the South; they move to deeper warm water in winter cold snaps and go dormant when temps drop below 50°F.
explanation_warm: Fall is prime along the entire range; trout stack up on shallow grass flats as shrimp migrate. Use a popping cork with live shrimp or artificial — the 'pop-pause-pop' action is deadly.

name: Fourspot flounder
bait: Sandworms, squid strips, small live killifish near sandy bottom in bays and nearshore
rig: Flounder rig (spreader rig) near sandy or sandy-mud bottom at 5-40 ft
lures: Small bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp minnow; small grubs near the bottom
explanation_cold: Fourspot flounder are a summer visitor to Mid-Atlantic and New England coastal waters; they move offshore in fall and winter.
explanation_warm: Summer and early fall over sandy inshore bottom; often caught alongside summer flounder on the same rigs — similar tactics but fourspot tend to be smaller and less common.

name: Spotfin mojarra
bait: Sandworms, tiny shrimp pieces, clam bits on very small hooks near sandy flats
rig: Ultra-light bottom rig near sandy-bottom flats in shallow bays; size 8-6 hooks required
lures: Very small jig heads with tiny plastics; not a primary lure target
explanation_cold: Spotfin mojarras are shallow-water schooling fish year-round in warm Gulf and SE coastal flats.
explanation_warm: Year-round in shallow warm water; excellent live bait for snook, redfish, and other inshore predators — a cast net is the most efficient way to collect them.

name: Striped mojarra
bait: Tiny shrimp, worms, clam bits on small hooks near grass and sandy areas in bays
rig: Ultra-light rig near sandy/grassy bottom in warm shallow bays
lures: Very small jigs; primarily a bait rather than sport target
explanation_cold: Striped mojarras occupy similar habitat to spotfin mojarra and are often found together in warm shallow coastal waters.
explanation_warm: Year-round in South Florida and Gulf; excellent live bait — valued more as bait than a sportfish but can be fun on ultra-light gear.

name: Blue runner
bait: Small pieces of cut fish, shrimp, or sabiki rigs near reefs and offshore structure
rig: Sabiki rig or light bottom rig near offshore platforms, reef, and buoys
lures: Small metal spoons, sabiki rigs, small jigs; they are aggressive schooling fish
explanation_cold: Blue runners school year-round in Gulf and SE offshore waters; larger fish in fall and winter offshore.
explanation_warm: Year-round near offshore platforms and buoys; blue runners are one of the best live baits for kingfish, amberjack, and cobia — a livewell full of them is worth a lot offshore.

name: Papio (young ulua)
bait: Live baitfish (akule, opelu), small crab, shrimp, squid near reef edges and sandy flats
rig: Light to medium bottom or float rig near reef edges at 5-60 ft
lures: Small metal jigs, soft plastic grubs, topwater poppers near reef edges
explanation_cold: Papio (juvenile giant trevally/ulua complex) are year-round targets in Hawaiian shallow reefs and sandy flats.
explanation_warm: Year-round along Hawaiian shorelines and shallow reefs; papio are the entry-level ulua fishery and perfect training for targeting trophy giant trevally — they hit lures, live bait, and flies.

name: Atlantic blue marlin
bait: Whole rigged ballyhoo, bonito strip, squid, or live bluefish trolled or pitched offshore
rig: Heavy offshore trolling spread; 200-400 lb leader; 50-130 lb class tackle
lures: Skirted lures (blue/white, black/purple), large soft-head lures; primarily a trolling fishery
explanation_cold: Atlantic blue marlin migrate along the Gulf Stream in summer; most common from June through October offshore.
explanation_warm: Peak season is July through September along the Gulf Stream from the Bahamas to Cape Hatteras; blue marlin are IGFA category fish and most are released — a truly bucket-list species.

name: Longbill spearfish
bait: Whole rigged ballyhoo, squid, or small mackerel trolled at 7-9 kts in offshore blue water
rig: Medium offshore trolling spread; 80-200 lb leader; 20-30 lb class tackle
lures: Skirted lures in blue/white and silver; cedar plugs; small soft-head lures
explanation_cold: Longbill spearfish are rare offshore visitors in the Atlantic and Gulf; they are uncommon but encountered during billfish tournaments and offshore trolling trips.
explanation_warm: Summer and early fall in the Gulf Stream; longbill spearfish are the most common Atlantic spearfish but still rarely encountered — a surprising and welcome addition to any offshore spread.

name: Bay anchovy
bait: Tiny sabiki hooks or cast net; they are extremely small (2-4 inches) and primarily used as bait
rig: Sabiki rig near surface in bays, estuaries, and harbors
lures: Tiny sabiki jigs
explanation_cold: Bay anchovies are one of the most abundant forage fish on the East Coast; enormous schools form in bays and estuaries spring through fall.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall schools are visible at the surface in most East Coast estuaries; the most important live bait for striped bass and bluefish in many areas — glass minnow imitation flies are tied specifically to match them.

name: Mummichog
bait: Bread, tiny worm pieces, corn; primarily a bait fish caught by trap or sabiki
rig: Very light float rig in tidal creeks and salt marsh channels near vegetation
lures: Micro jigs; not usually targeted on lures
explanation_cold: Mummichogs are a year-round resident of salt marshes and tidal creeks along the entire East Coast; they are extremely hardy and tolerant of poor water quality.
explanation_warm: Year-round accessible in salt marsh channels; mummichogs are the classic bait-bucket fish — hardy enough to survive in a bucket for hours and irresistible to flounder, striped bass, and weakfish.

name: Striped killifish
bait: Tiny worm pieces, bread, sabiki rigs; primarily a bait species like mummichog
rig: Very light float or bottom rig in tidal flats and estuaries
lures: Micro jigs; primarily a bait-collection target
explanation_cold: Striped killifish occupy sandy-bottom estuaries and tidal flats year-round from Maine to Florida.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in tidal flats; the larger male striped killifish are excellent flounder bait and can be collected in minnow traps baited with bread overnight.

name: Florida gar
bait: Live or dead small fish, frogs, crawfish near the surface in fresh and brackish water
rig: Surface or very shallow float rig with a wire or heavy mono leader (gar have abrasive jaws)
hook_size: 4/0-8/0 treble or single hook on a rope lure
lures: Rope lure (frayed nylon rope twisted over a hook) — gar teeth tangle in the rope; also surface plugs and large streamers
explanation_cold: Florida gar inhabit slow-moving fresh and brackish water throughout Florida and coastal Gulf drainages; they are most active in warm weather.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in Florida freshwater canals, rivers, and coastal brackish areas; gar are a blast on light tackle and the rope lure technique is uniquely effective — no hook needed, the teeth snag in the frayed rope.

name: Chain pickerel
bait: Small live minnows or shiners near weeds and fallen timber in tidal freshwater and brackish ponds
rig: Light float or slip-float rig near weed edges in tidal freshwater and brackish ponds
lures: Small spinners, soft plastic swimbaits, stickbaits, and spoons near vegetation
explanation_cold: Chain pickerel are active year-round including under ice; they prefer cold to cool water and are most aggressive in fall through early spring.
explanation_warm: Fall and spring are peak pickerel seasons in tidal freshwater rivers and brackish ponds behind barrier beaches; they hit lures aggressively and often inhabit the same water as striped bass during spring herring runs.

name: Awa (milkfish)
bait: Specialized dough bait, algae bait, or bread dough near bottom over sandy/muddy flats in fish ponds
rig: Light to medium bottom rig with tiny hook in Hawaiian fishponds or nearshore flats
lures: Not a traditional lure target; small jigs occasionally work
explanation_cold: Milkfish (awa) inhabit Hawaiian inshore waters and traditional fishponds year-round; they are herbivores that graze on algae.
explanation_warm: Year-round target in Hawaiian fishponds; awa are a culturally important species tied to traditional Hawaiian aquaculture — they are excellent eating and are farmed in multigenerational fishponds.

name: Halfbanded rockfish
bait: Squid strips, small herring at 80-250 ft over rocky bottom and banks
rig: Dropper loop rig at 80-250 ft on offshore rocky reef
lures: Diamond jigs (100-200g) in silver/pink worked near bottom
explanation_cold: Halfbanded rockfish inhabit mid-depth rocky reefs on the Pacific coast year-round.
explanation_warm: Part of the mixed rockfish bag on Pacific party boat trips; spring and summer are prime seasons for offshore rockfish trips.

name: Honeycomb rockfish
bait: Squid, anchovies, herring near rocky reef at 50-200 ft
rig: Bottom rig at 50-200 ft near rocky structure
lures: Small tube jigs, metal jigs near rocky bottom
explanation_cold: Honeycomb rockfish are a nearshore Pacific rockfish found year-round on rocky reefs.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in California and Oregon; part of the nearshore rockfish complex bag limit.

name: Speckled rockfish
bait: Small herring, squid strips near offshore rocky banks at 100-350 ft
rig: Dropper loop rig at 100-350 ft over offshore rocky banks
lures: Diamond jigs worked mid-water to bottom on offshore trips
explanation_cold: Speckled rockfish are a mid-depth to deep Pacific rockfish found on offshore banks year-round.
explanation_warm: Party-boat rockfish trips in spring and summer encounter speckled rockfish on offshore banks; part of the mixed rockfish bag.

name: Swordspine rockfish
bait: Squid, small herring near deep rocky reef at 150-500 ft
rig: Heavy dropper loop rig at 150-500 ft on deep offshore banks
lures: Heavy diamond jigs (250-450g) worked near bottom
explanation_cold: Swordspine rockfish are a deep-water Pacific rockfish on offshore banks year-round.
explanation_warm: Caught on deep rockfish drops on Pacific offshore party boats; part of the rockfish aggregate bag limit.

name: Stripetail rockfish
bait: Squid, herring, anchovies at mid to deep depth over banks
rig: Dropper loop rig at 100-400 ft on offshore banks
lures: Diamond jigs, metal jigs in silver worked mid-water
explanation_cold: Stripetail rockfish school mid-water over offshore Pacific banks year-round.
explanation_warm: Caught alongside widow and chilipepper rockfish on mid-water party-boat drifts; part of the rockfish aggregate.

name: Buffalo sculpin
bait: Shrimp, worms, small crabs near rocky intertidal and shallow subtidal areas
rig: Light bottom rig at 5-30 ft near rocky structure
lures: Very small tube jigs near rocky bottom
explanation_cold: Buffalo sculpin are year-round shallow-water residents on Pacific rocky reefs and jetties.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall near rocky Pacific shorelines and jetties; one of the larger Pacific sculpin species, sometimes reaching 14+ inches.

name: Freshwater drum
bait: Crayfish, nightcrawlers, cut shrimp, mussels near sandy or rocky bottom in rivers
rig: Carolina rig or bottom rig in tidal fresh/brackish rivers and impoundments
lures: Blade baits, jigging spoons, and small crankbaits near bottom in current
explanation_cold: Freshwater drum inhabit tidal rivers and brackish-freshwater transition zones year-round in their range.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in tidal freshwater rivers; drum are voracious feeders and the only strictly freshwater member of the drum family — surprisingly hard fighters on medium tackle.

name: Kaku (barracuda, Hawaii)
bait: Live small fish, squid, shiny lures; barracuda are visual hunters that key on flash
rig: Wire leader (30-45 lb) required; medium to heavy spinning or casting with live bait near reef edges
lures: Large diving plugs, metal spoons, and tube lures in silver/chrome; fast retrieves trigger strikes
explanation_cold: Kaku (great barracuda) are year-round residents on Hawaiian reefs and nearshore offshore areas.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Hawaiian coral reef edges and nearshore seamounts; kaku are excellent sport fish on light tackle but the large ones (over 3 lbs) should be released due to ciguatera toxin risk.

name: Gulf pipefish
bait: Very tiny crustaceans; pipefish are not realistically targeted by hook-and-line
rig: Micro hook or net collection only; primarily a scientific interest / accidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Gulf pipefish inhabit seagrass beds and shallow inshore areas year-round in warm Gulf and SE coastal waters.
explanation_warm: Year-round in shallow seagrass beds; pipefish are almost never intentionally targeted but are occasionally snagged accidentally or observed while wade fishing flats — a fascinating member of the seahorse family.

name: Yellow perch (coastal)
bait: Small minnows, nightcrawlers, small jigs near tidal freshwater ponds and rivers behind barrier beaches
rig: Light spinning with split shot and small hook; 4-6 lb line near submerged structure in tidal ponds
lures: 1/32-1/8 oz tube jigs and small grubs; small in-line spinners
explanation_cold: Yellow perch inhabit tidal freshwater ponds and brackish ponds behind barrier beaches year-round; they school up in fall and winter.
explanation_warm: Fall and early spring are peak seasons in tidal back-bay ponds; yellow perch are abundant, easy to catch, and excellent table fare — perfect for family outings with light spinning tackle.

name: Bowfin
bait: Live bluegill, large shiners, crawfish near weeds in slow brackish and freshwater rivers
rig: Heavy float rig or Carolina rig with large live bait near weed mats in tidal freshwater
lures: Large swimbaits, chatterbaits, and topwater frogs over weed mats near dusk; they hit hard
explanation_cold: Bowfin inhabit slow tidal freshwater and brackish swamps and rivers year-round in the Gulf and SE coastal plain; most active in spring through fall.
explanation_warm: Spring through early fall in sluggish tidal rivers and cypress swamps; bowfin are considered a 'trash fish' by some but fight like a demon on medium gear — they are ancient (Jurassic-era lineage) and fascinating to catch.

name: Walleye (coastal)
bait: Live minnows, nightcrawlers, leeches in tidal freshwater sections of large coastal rivers
rig: Jig and live minnow or live bait rig near rocky bottom in tidal river areas
lures: Blade baits, jigging spoons, and paddle-tail jigs in white/yellow near the bottom
explanation_cold: Walleye sometimes occupy the upper tidal freshwater sections of large rivers; they prefer clear, cold to cool water and rocky bottom.
explanation_warm: Spring spawning runs bring walleye into tidal freshwater river sections; light-sensitive and feed best at dawn and dusk.

name: Olive flounder
bait: Anchovies, small herring, shrimp near sandy bottom in Pacific bays and nearshore
rig: Flounder rig near sandy bottom at 10-60 ft in bays
lures: Small Gulp minnow on jig head; small bucktails
explanation_cold: Olive flounder inhabit sandy bays and nearshore areas year-round on the West Coast.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in Pacific bays and estuaries; a common flatfish bycatch on Pacific Coast bottom rigs.

name: Vermilion snapper (beeliners)
bait: Squid, shrimp, cut fish mid-water to bottom on offshore reefs; beeliners school mid-water
rig: Sabiki-style multi-hook rig or single hook at 60-200 ft; let bait flutter mid-water
lures: Small diamond jigs and sabiki rigs worked mid-water on offshore reefs
explanation_cold: Vermilion snapper school mid-water over offshore reefs year-round; most abundant 80-250 ft.
explanation_warm: Year-round on offshore Gulf and SE Atlantic reefs; beeliners are prolific biters and one of the best snapper for the table — a multi-hook dropper rig can produce multiple fish per drop.

name: Little tunny (false albacore)
bait: Live sand eels, small herring, bay anchovies; crash surface bait schools
rig: Light to medium spinning with small lures; 15-20 lb leader ideal
lures: Hogy Epoxy jigs, small metal spoons, sand eel fly patterns; match the hatch exactly
explanation_cold: Little tunny are fall visitors along the entire East Coast from Maine to Florida; the fall run can be spectacular.
explanation_warm: September through November is 'albie season' — they crash bait schools along the coast and are one of the fastest and most exciting fish on light tackle.

name: Dusky rockfish
bait: Herring, squid, small baitfish at depth over offshore banks in Alaska and PNW
rig: Mid-water dropper loop rig at 100-500 ft over offshore Pacific Northwest banks
lures: Heavy diamond jigs (200-400g) worked mid-water
explanation_cold: Dusky rockfish are an important commercial and recreational species in Alaska and the Pacific Northwest; school mid-water over offshore banks.
explanation_warm: Summer season on Alaska and PNW offshore banks; a bread-and-butter species on Alaska offshore trips.

name: Rock hind grouper
bait: Live small fish, squid near shallow rocky reef in the Florida Keys
rig: Medium bottom rig at 20-100 ft near rocky reef and hard bottom
lures: Soft plastic swimbaits and jigs near rocky bottom
explanation_cold: Rock hind grouper inhabit shallow rocky reefs of South Florida and the Florida Keys year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; colorful spotted grouper in the lesser-known grouper species group.

name: Palometa (longfin pompano)
bait: Sand fleas, live shrimp, small pieces of shrimp in the surf
rig: Light surf rig or drift rig near the beach in the surf zone
lures: Small spoons and jigs; occasionally hit small metal lures in the surf
explanation_cold: Palometa are a warm-water surf and nearshore species in South Florida and Caribbean.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall in South Florida and the Keys surf; identified by long trailing fin filaments — a striking and uncommon catch in the US.

name: Florida pompano
bait: Sand fleas (best), live shrimp, coquina clams in the surf wash
rig: Pompano rig (two-hook bottom rig with bright beads) in the surf; fish in the trough
lures: Pompano jigs (1/4-3/4 oz) in yellow, white, or chartreuse; DOA Shrimp near the bottom
explanation_cold: Florida pompano migrate north in spring and south in fall; they patrol tidal inlets and beach surf year-round in South Florida.
explanation_warm: Spring and fall runs along Florida, Georgia, and the Carolinas produce the best pompano surf fishing; sand flea digs at low tide will find your bait — pompano are considered Florida's finest table fish.

name: Permit (nearshore)
bait: Live crab (fiddler or blue), live shrimp near wrecks and nearshore reefs
rig: Light to medium bottom rig with live crab near nearshore wrecks and reefs
lures: Crab imitation soft plastics; hard to catch on lures in this environment
explanation_cold: Nearshore permit inhabit reefs, wrecks, and ledges at 20-80 ft; different fishing scenario from shallow-flat sight-fishing.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall on nearshore Gulf and SE wrecks; permit schooling around artificial reefs can be caught on live crabs — the biggest permit are often offshore rather than on the flats.

name: Inshore lizardfish
bait: Any small fish piece, shrimp; lizardfish are aggressive bottom predators
rig: Light bottom rig on sandy bottom in bays and surf zone
lures: Small soft plastic jigs and minnow imitations near sandy bottom
explanation_cold: Inshore lizardfish inhabit sandy bottom in warm inshore and nearshore areas year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round bycatch on sandy bottom in the Gulf and SE; they are voracious biters with sharp teeth — respected as a nuisance by some and appreciated as a bizarre catch by others.

name: Pacific sand dab
bait: Sandworms, clam strips, squid pieces near sandy bottom at 20-150 ft
rig: Light dropper loop or spreader rig at 20-150 ft over sandy bottom
lures: Small Gulp minnow on jig head near sandy bottom
explanation_cold: Pacific sand dabs are one of the most abundant nearshore flatfish on the West Coast; they school over sandy bottom year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round from piers and small boats; sand dabs are light-tackle favorites and considered the best-tasting Pacific flatfish — the classic California restaurant flatfish.

name: Speckled sand dab
bait: Sandworms, squid strips near sandy bottom at 30-200 ft
rig: Light dropper loop rig at 30-200 ft near sandy bottom
lures: Small Gulp or soft plastic near bottom
explanation_cold: Speckled sand dabs inhabit deeper sandy bottom on the Pacific coast; similar habitat to Pacific sand dab but slightly deeper.
explanation_warm: Part of the sand dab catch on California party boat trips; nearly identical in taste and technique to Pacific sand dab.

name: Butter sole
bait: Sandworms, clam strips, small shrimp near sandy-mud bottom in bays
rig: Light bottom rig at 10-100 ft near sandy bottom
lures: Small Gulp minnow on light jig head
explanation_cold: Butter sole inhabit sandy-bottom bays and nearshore areas year-round on the Pacific coast.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Pacific Northwest bays; a smaller flatfish commonly caught as bycatch while targeting Pacific halibut or starry flounder.

name: Sand sole
bait: Sandworms, squid strips, small shrimp near sandy bottom in Pacific bays
rig: Light bottom rig at 5-80 ft near sandy bottom
lures: Small Gulp or soft plastic near sandy bottom
explanation_cold: Sand sole are a year-round Pacific flatfish on sandy bottom from California to Alaska.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Pacific coastal bays and estuaries; part of the diverse West Coast flatfish mix and caught on the same rigs as Pacific sand dab.

name: Surf smelt
bait: Tiny hooks and sabiki rigs; surf smelt are dip-netted in the surf during spawning runs
rig: Dip net in the surf during smelt runs; sabiki rigs in harbors
lures: Tiny metal jigs and sabiki rigs in harbors
explanation_cold: Surf smelt spawn on gravel beaches in late summer and fall; huge runs concentrate them in the surf.
explanation_warm: Late summer through fall smelt runs on Oregon and Washington beaches; surf smelt dip-netting is a Pacific Northwest tradition — fried whole they are among the finest eating fish on the coast.

name: Night smelt
bait: Tiny sabiki rigs or dip nets during spring spawning runs on gravel beaches at night
rig: Dip net in the surf at night; sabiki rigs near harbors and jetties
lures: Tiny sabiki-style micro jigs
explanation_cold: Night smelt spawn on gravel beaches at night in spring along the Pacific coast.
explanation_warm: Spring night smelt runs on Northern California and Oregon gravel beaches — bring a headlamp and dip net for one of the most fun seasonal fishing events on the Pacific coast.

name: White croaker (tomcod, kingfish)
bait: Sandworms, small clams, shrimp, squid near sandy bottom in bays, harbors, and surf
rig: Light bottom rig at 5-60 ft near sandy bottom
lures: Small soft plastic grubs near the bottom
explanation_cold: White croaker are year-round residents in California and Baja coastal bays; very abundant.
explanation_warm: Year-round from piers in Southern California; one of the most commonly caught pier fish in SoCal — easy to catch but check local consumption advisories in harbors due to sediment contamination.

name: Pacific mackerel
bait: Sabiki rigs near the surface in California coastal waters during warm-water years
rig: Light to medium spinning with sabiki or small metal lure near the surface
lures: Small metal spoons, Crippled Herring jigs, sabiki rigs
explanation_cold: Pacific mackerel are warm-season schooling fish in California coastal waters; abundance varies with El Nino cycles.
explanation_warm: Summer and fall in Southern and Central California during warm-water years; crash baitfish at the surface near piers and in harbors — fast action on light gear.

name: Jack mackerel (Pacific)
bait: Sabiki rigs, small herring or anchovy near the surface; they school offshore and nearshore
rig: Light to medium spinning with sabiki rig or small metal lure
lures: Sabiki rigs, small metal jigs, small chrome spoons
explanation_cold: Pacific jack mackerel are year-round in offshore California waters; they come nearshore seasonally in large schools.
explanation_warm: Year-round offshore; nearshore in summer and fall — they hit sabiki rigs greedily and make excellent live bait for yellowtail, halibut, and seabass.

name: Spotted eagle ray
bait: Oysters, clams, shrimp; spotted eagle rays feed on shellfish and are rarely targeted deliberately
rig: Heavy bottom rig near sandy or shell-rubble bottom; incidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Spotted eagle rays are year-round in warm Gulf and SE coastal waters; they are powerful fighters when hooked incidentally.
explanation_warm: Year-round bycatch near oyster reefs and sandy flats; spectacular when they breach. They have venomous tail spines — handle carefully.

name: Atlantic guitarfish
bait: Shrimp, clams, small fish near sandy bottom; incidental catch on bottom rigs
rig: Medium bottom rig near sandy bottom in shallow bays and nearshore
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Atlantic guitarfish inhabit sandy bottom in warm coastal waters year-round in the South.
explanation_warm: Year-round bycatch in Gulf and SE shallow sandy-bottom areas; shaped like a shark but related to rays — a memorable and beautiful incidental catch.

name: Barndoor skate
bait: Clams, sandworms, squid near deep sandy or gravel bottom; incidental catch
rig: Heavy bottom rig at 60-400 ft over deep sandy-gravel bottom
lures: Not targeted on lures
explanation_cold: Barndoor skates are the largest Atlantic skate; they inhabit deep cold-water sandy and gravelly bottom offshore.
explanation_warm: Deep-water bycatch on New England offshore cod trips; a species of concern — release immediately. Can be 5+ feet across and are impressive to see.

name: Bigeye scad (Atlantic)
bait: Sabiki rigs or cast net near offshore structure, reef, and buoys
rig: Sabiki rig near surface to mid-water around offshore platforms and reefs
lures: Small metal jigs, sabiki rigs
explanation_cold: Atlantic bigeye scad school near offshore structure and reef year-round in the Gulf and SE.
explanation_warm: Year-round near offshore platforms and buoys; excellent live bait for kingfish and amberjack.

name: Round scad
bait: Sabiki rigs near the surface around buoys; very small species
rig: Sabiki rig near surface around offshore markers and buoys
lures: Tiny sabiki rigs
explanation_cold: Round scad school near the surface in warm offshore and coastal waters year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round offshore baitfish; sabiki rigging near any floating object in offshore water will often produce them.

name: French grunt
bait: Shrimp pieces, squid strips, small crab near reef structure
rig: Light bottom rig near coral reef at 5-60 ft
lures: Small soft plastic jigs near reef
explanation_cold: French grunts school densely on Florida Keys and SE Atlantic coral reef year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; make a grunting sound when caught and are excellent live bait for large snapper.

name: Cottonwick grunt
bait: Shrimp, small squid, small crab near coral reef structure
rig: Light bottom rig at 10-80 ft near reef
lures: Small jigs near reef structure
explanation_cold: Cottonwick grunts inhabit tropical reef structures year-round in South Florida and the Florida Keys.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; identified by distinctive black and yellow striping and white tail margin.

name: Caesar grunt
bait: Shrimp, small crab, squid near reef structure in the Keys
rig: Light bottom rig at 10-80 ft near coral and rocky reef
lures: Small jigs near reef
explanation_cold: Caesar grunts are tropical reef fish found year-round in the Florida Keys and South Florida.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Florida Keys reef; blue-striped with yellow fins and part of the diverse grunt community under coral heads.

name: Oio (bonefish, Hawaii)
bait: Small shrimp, crab, and worm imitations near sandy and muddy tidal flats
rig: Light spinning or fly rod on Hawaiian tidal flats; sight-fishing presentation is critical
lures: Crazy Charlie, Gotcha, EP shrimp flies; small shrimp-imitation jigs for spin gear
explanation_cold: Oio are year-round residents on Hawaiian sand and mud flats; they are sight-fished in very shallow water.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Hawaiian tidal flats — especially Kaneohe Bay; oio are Hawaii's premier flats sportfish almost exclusively caught on fly or light spinning gear.

name: Omilu (bluefin trevally)
bait: Live small fish, shrimp, and crabs near reef edges and nearshore rocky areas
rig: Medium spinning or casting with live bait near reef edges; or hard lures cast fast
lures: Topwater poppers, metal jigs, and fast-retrieved plugs near reef
explanation_cold: Omilu are year-round predators on Hawaiian reef flats and nearshore rocky areas; they hunt aggressively at dawn and dusk.
explanation_warm: Year-round but most active in warmer months; omilu hit poppers explosively and are significantly more accessible than trophy ulua.

name: Kole (surgeonfish)
bait: Algae bait, dough bait, or very small pieces of urchin near rocky reef
rig: Ultra-light bottom rig or float rig near rocky shallow reef
lures: Not typically a lure target
explanation_cold: Kole (goldring surgeonfish) are year-round grazers on Hawaiian rocky and coral reef; herbivores feeding primarily on algae.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Hawaiian rocky reef; sharp scalpel-like tail spine — handle carefully. Culturally significant as a traditional Hawaiian food fish.

name: Atlantic menhaden
bait: Cast net is by far the most effective; sabiki rigs in a pinch; they filter-feed and rarely bite hooks
rig: Cast net over feeding schools; sabiki rig in schools
lures: Not a traditional lure target
explanation_cold: Atlantic menhaden form enormous schools migrating along the East Coast spring through fall; the most ecologically important baitfish on the Atlantic coast.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall massive bunker schools migrate the East Coast; a cast-net full of fresh bunker is the single most effective bait for trophy striped bass and bluefish.

name: Gizzard shad
bait: Cast net or dip net; gizzard shad are filter feeders that rarely bite conventional baits
rig: Cast net over schools in tidal rivers and reservoirs
lures: Not a lure target; bait-collection species only
explanation_cold: Gizzard shad inhabit tidal freshwater rivers and reservoirs year-round throughout the East and Gulf coasts.
explanation_warm: Year-round in tidal freshwater areas; the primary baitfish for large catfish, stripers, and bass in tidal rivers.

name: Barred sand bass
bait: Live anchovies or squid strips near sandy bottom in Southern California bays and nearshore kelp
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 15-80 ft over sandy bottom near kelp edge
lures: Soft plastic swimbaits on jig heads; small spoons near sand-kelp interface
explanation_cold: Barred sand bass are a warm-season target in Southern California; most abundant July through October.
explanation_warm: Summer and fall in Southern California nearshore; 'bar bass' are a staple of SoCal light-tackle fishing — accessible from kayaks and excellent eating.

name: Striped burrfish
bait: Any small bottom bait — shrimp, clam, worm; burrfish eat shellfish with their fused beak
rig: Light bottom rig on sandy or grassy bottom in bays and inlets
lures: Not a lure target; bait only
explanation_cold: Striped burrfish inhabit shallow-water seagrass beds and sandy bottom year-round in warm SE and Gulf coastal areas.
explanation_warm: Year-round bycatch in warm inshore waters; inflate into a ball covered in short spines when threatened — memorable accidental catch on bottom rigs.

name: Balloonfish
bait: Shrimp, clam bits, small crab near reef and rocky bottom
rig: Light bottom rig near reef and hard bottom at 5-40 ft
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Balloonfish are a porcupinefish relative found year-round in South Florida and the Keys near reef.
explanation_warm: Year-round near South Florida reef; inflate dramatically when caught with dangerous spines — release carefully with pliers.

name: Sharpnose puffer
bait: Shrimp, clam, small worms on tiny hooks near sandy flats and seagrass
rig: Ultra-light bottom rig near sandy bottom and seagrass with small hooks
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Sharpnose puffers inhabit shallow seagrass beds and sandy flats year-round in warm Gulf and SE waters.
explanation_warm: Year-round bycatch on light tackle; small (3-5 in) but aggressive biters that make a squeaking sound when caught.

name: Fringed filefish
bait: Small crabs, shrimp, amphipods near seagrass and floating sargassum
rig: Very light rig near sargassum and seagrass; caught incidentally
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Fringed filefish inhabit seagrass beds and floating sargassum year-round in warm SE and Gulf waters.
explanation_warm: Year-round around floating sargassum; filefish change color to match surroundings perfectly — a fascinating bycatch.

name: Leatherjacket (Atlantic)
bait: Shrimp, small fish, and tiny pieces of squid near reef and sandy flats
rig: Light bottom or float rig near sandy or rocky nearshore areas
lures: Small jigs and tiny spoons
explanation_cold: Atlantic leatherjackets are a tropical species found near reef and sandy nearshore areas in warm SE and Gulf waters.
explanation_warm: Year-round in South Florida and the Gulf; interesting bycatch with rough skin and small mouth on light inshore tackle.

name: Leopard shark (Pacific)
bait: Clams, pile worms, squid, and live mudsuckers near sandy-mud bottom in bays
rig: Medium bottom rig at 5-30 ft in bays near sandy-mud bottom
lures: Occasionally taken on cut bait near bottom; not a lure species
explanation_cold: Leopard sharks are year-round residents in California bays and nearshore; most abundant in SF Bay and major SoCal bays.
explanation_warm: Year-round but most active spring through fall in California bays; leopard sharks gather in large groups in shallow warm water — a favorite for kayak anglers on sandy flats.

name: Soupfin shark
bait: Whole squid, mackerel fillet, large pile worms near sandy-mud bottom in bays and nearshore
rig: Medium-heavy bottom rig at 10-60 ft; 60-80 lb leader
lures: Not typically targeted on lures
explanation_cold: Soupfin sharks inhabit California and Pacific Northwest bays and nearshore; can reach 6+ feet.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in California bays and nearshore; heavily overfished in the 1930s-40s for their livers, populations have recovered and they are a popular large-shark target.

name: Gray smoothhound
bait: Pile worms, clams, squid near sandy-mud bottom in estuaries and bays
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 5-30 ft in bays near soft bottom
lures: Not targeted on lures; bait only
explanation_cold: Gray smoothhound sharks inhabit Pacific estuaries and coastal bays year-round; slender sharks reaching about 5 ft.
explanation_warm: Year-round in California estuaries and bays; common bycatch for leopard shark anglers — will hit virtually any fresh bait on the bottom.

name: Brown smoothhound
bait: Pile worms, squid, small crabs, shrimp near soft bottom in Pacific bays
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 5-30 ft near soft bottom
lures: Not targeted on lures
explanation_cold: Brown smoothhound sharks inhabit nearshore Pacific waters; nearly identical in habits to gray smoothhound.
explanation_warm: Year-round in California coastal bays; closely related to the gray smoothhound and often caught together.

name: Pacific electric ray
bait: Small fish, squid near sandy bottom in shallow to mid-depth Pacific coastal areas; incidental catch
rig: Medium bottom rig at 5-100 ft near sandy bottom; incidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Pacific electric rays inhabit sandy-bottom coastal areas from California to Alaska; can deliver a powerful electric shock.
explanation_warm: Occasional bycatch year-round; Pacific electric rays deliver a strong electric shock — never handle directly. Cut the leader and release.

name: Pacific tomcod
bait: Pile worms, shrimp, small clams near the bottom in bays, estuaries, and nearshore Pacific waters
rig: Light bottom rig at 5-60 ft near soft bottom
lures: Small soft plastic jigs tipped with worm or shrimp
explanation_cold: Pacific tomcod inhabit shallow coastal waters from California to Alaska; most abundant in colder months.
explanation_warm: Fall through spring in Pacific Northwest bays and estuaries; a classic winter fish for pier anglers in WA and OR — hits small baits readily and excellent table fare.

name: Eulachon (smelt)
bait: Dip net in rivers during spring spawning runs; tiny sabiki rigs in estuaries
rig: Dip net in rivers during spawning run; tiny sabiki rigs at river mouths
lures: Tiny micro jigs near river mouths
explanation_cold: Eulachon (oolichan or candlefish) make spring spawning runs into Pacific Northwest rivers; so oily they were historically dried and burned as candles.
explanation_warm: February through April in Pacific Northwest rivers and estuaries; dip-netting a spawning run is one of the most culturally rich fishing experiences on the Pacific coast.

name: Black croaker (xieb)
bait: Sandworms, clam strips, shrimp near rocky or sandy bottom in Southern California bays and nearshore
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 5-50 ft near rocky-sandy bottom
lures: Small soft plastic grubs near the bottom
explanation_cold: Black croaker inhabit rocky and sandy nearshore areas and kelp bed edges in Southern California.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall in Southern California nearshore; much less common than white croaker and a prized catch — makes a deep thudding sound when landed.

name: Silver hake (whiting)
bait: Sandworms, small squid, cut clam, small fish near sandy bottom at 60-300 ft
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 60-300 ft; multi-hook spreader
lures: Diamond jigs and small metals at depth
explanation_cold: Silver hake (whiting) migrate inshore in fall and winter; they form dense schools near the bottom.
explanation_warm: Fall through early spring in the Mid-Atlantic and New England; silver hake school near sandy bottom and can be caught rapidly — one of the Northeast's most underrated eating fish.

name: Offshore hake
bait: Squid, cut fish, clam strips at depth on deep rocky-sandy bottom
rig: Heavy deep-drop rig at 200-600 ft over deep hard bottom
lures: Large diamond jigs at depth
explanation_cold: Offshore hake inhabit deep offshore waters year-round; come shallower in winter.
explanation_warm: Winter through spring on deep New England offshore trips; caught in quantity on the same trips targeting offshore cod and haddock.

name: Atlantic tripletail
bait: Live shrimp, small crabs, small fish near floating debris and crab trap buoys
rig: Light to medium spinning or fly rod; cast live shrimp to a visible fish near surface debris
lures: Small paddle tail swimbaits, DOA shrimp, or surface flies cast to visible fish
explanation_cold: Atlantic tripletail are warm-season visitors; they lie on their sides near floating debris and crab trap buoys, ambushing prey.
explanation_warm: Late spring through fall in SE and Gulf coastal waters; tripletail are a sight-fishing species — motoring slowly through nearshore waters and spotting them near crab buoys is a unique experience.

name: Goldface tilefish
bait: Squid, cut fish, shrimp at depth 200-700 ft near hard clay or coral bottom
rig: Heavy deepdrop rig at 200-700 ft; electric reel recommended
lures: Large deepdrop lures with glow sticks
explanation_cold: Goldface tilefish inhabit deep-water clay and coral bottom in the Gulf and SE Atlantic year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round deepdrop target; goldface tilefish build burrows in deep Gulf clay bottom — electric reels are nearly mandatory at 400+ ft.

name: Blackline tilefish
bait: Squid, cut fish, shrimp at depth near hard or clay bottom
rig: Heavy deepdrop rig at 200-600 ft
lures: Large deepdrop lures
explanation_cold: Blackline tilefish are a close relative of golden tilefish found in the Gulf of Mexico at moderate depths.
explanation_warm: Year-round deepdrop; inhabit similar habitat to golden tilefish and are excellent eating.

name: Pilotfish
bait: Small fish, squid near sharks, large rays, sea turtles, and floating debris offshore
rig: Light spinning; incidental catch near offshore vessels and large animals
lures: Small jigs near offshore floating debris
explanation_cold: Pilotfish associate with large marine animals in warm offshore waters; rarely specifically targeted.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall in warm offshore waters; pilotfish swim alongside sharks and rays — an unusual and memorable catch.

name: Blue tang (Atlantic)
bait: Algae, small invertebrates; not commonly targeted
rig: Very light rig near reef; rarely targeted
lures: Not a lure target; occasionally bycatch
explanation_cold: Blue tang are a brilliant electric-blue surgeonfish on Florida and Caribbean reef year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; sharp scalpel spine at tail base — handle carefully.

name: Ocean surgeon
bait: Algae-based baits or small invertebrates near reef; incidental catches
rig: Very light rig near shallow reef
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Ocean surgeons are a brownish surgeonfish found near Florida and Gulf reef year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near reef; herbivores rarely targeted — most are released after an incidental catch.

name: Doctorfish
bait: Algae-based baits near reef and hard bottom
rig: Ultra-light rig near shallow reef
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Doctorfish are a surgeonfish found on Florida and Caribbean reef near rubble and hard bottom.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; among the most common surgeonfish in shallow Caribbean-type reef environments.

name: Foureye butterflyfish
bait: Small worms and crustaceans near reef; rarely caught on hook and line
rig: Very light rig near coral reef; almost always bycatch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Foureye butterflyfish are year-round residents on Florida Keys and SE Atlantic coral reef.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; named for the false eyespot on their tail — almost always encountered while snorkeling rather than fishing.

name: Hogfish (Atlantic)
bait: Live shrimp, small crabs, and sea urchin pieces near reef and rocky bottom at 10-100 ft
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 10-100 ft near reef structure
lures: Not typically a lure target; live or fresh dead shrimp is best
explanation_cold: Hogfish are a wrasse species that use their long snout to root shellfish from reef rubble; they are considered the finest-eating reef fish by many Florida anglers.
explanation_warm: Best in cooler months when hogfish are more active near shallow reef; hogfish are a prized target for spearfishers and bottom anglers alike — they won't bite cut fish, only live or freshly dead shellfish.

name: Spanish hogfish
bait: Shrimp pieces, small crabs, small invertebrates near reef and hard bottom
rig: Light bottom rig at 10-80 ft near reef and rocky structure
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Spanish hogfish are a smaller wrasse found on Florida and Caribbean reef year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; Spanish hogfish are colorful purple-and-gold fish and excellent eating — they are smaller than Atlantic hogfish and often caught as bycatch on shrimp bait.

name: Rock beauty
bait: Very difficult to target on bait; occasionally small sponge or algae-based baits near reef
rig: Ultra-light rig near reef; incidental catch only
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Rock beauty are a striking black-and-yellow angelfish on Florida Keys and Caribbean reef; they feed primarily on sponges and are nearly impossible to catch on conventional bait.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; rock beauty are more commonly observed by divers and snorkelers than caught by anglers — mostly an incidental bycatch on tiny hooks.

name: French angelfish
bait: Very difficult on bait; occasionally small sponge pieces or algae-based bait near reef
rig: Ultra-light rig near reef; incidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: French angelfish are large, dark, circle-marked angelfishes on Florida Keys and Caribbean coral reef.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; French angelfish are sponge-feeders and are almost always caught incidentally by snapper anglers fishing small baits near reef.

name: Queen angelfish
bait: Very difficult; occasionally small pieces of sponge or algae near coral reef
rig: Ultra-light rig near coral reef
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Queen angelfish are arguably the most beautiful fish on the Florida Keys reef — vivid blue and yellow with a spotted crown.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys deep reef; queen angelfish are sponge-feeders and nearly impossible to catch deliberately — an accidental catch is considered very lucky.

name: White seaperch
bait: Pile worms, shrimp, small clams near rocky jetties, piers, and kelp in Pacific coastal waters
rig: Light rig near jetties, piers, and rocky structure at 5-40 ft
lures: Small soft plastic jigs on 1/8-1/4 oz heads near structure
explanation_cold: White seaperch are year-round residents near rocky shores, jetties, and kelp from Southern California to Oregon.
explanation_warm: Year-round from piers and jetties; white seaperch are one of the most common catch-from-shore species on the Pacific coast — they hit small baits and jigs readily on light tackle.

name: Weke ula (goatfish)
bait: Shrimp, sandworms, small crabs near sandy bottom and reef flats
rig: Light bottom rig near sandy bottom and reef flats at 5-40 ft
lures: Small shrimp-imitation jigs near sandy bottom
explanation_cold: Weke ula (yellowfin goatfish) are year-round residents on Hawaiian sandy bottom and reef flats; they use chin barbels to probe sand for prey.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Hawaiian sandy flats and reef edges; weke ula are a prized Hawaiian food fish and particularly sought by local anglers for traditional preparations.

name: Nenue (chub)
bait: Bread balls, dough bait, small pieces of musubi, or tiny pieces of algae near rocky reef
rig: Light float or bottom rig near rocky reef and shoreline; bread bait is traditional
lures: Not a lure target; bread ball bait is the most effective
explanation_cold: Nenue (rudderfish/Hawaiian chub) school near rocky reef and shorelines year-round in Hawaii.
explanation_warm: Year-round near rocky Hawaiian shorelines; nenue are fished with bread balls thrown into the water to chum them up — a beloved local style of fishing especially popular with families.

name: Amaama (striped mullet, Hawaii)
bait: Algae, dough bait, micro-bread balls near shallow sandy flats and estuaries; cast net is most effective
rig: Cast net in shallow estuaries and fishponds; light float rig with bread bait
lures: Not typically a lure target
explanation_cold: Amaama (striped mullet) are year-round in Hawaiian coastal waters and fishponds; they run in schools that are traditionally netted.
explanation_warm: Year-round but best in cooler months; amaama are deeply embedded in Hawaiian cultural fishing history — traditionally harvested with throw nets in coastal fishponds. They are excellent eating.

name: Kumu (squirrelfish, Hawaii)
bait: Small shrimp, small fish, squid at night near rocky reef caves and crevices
rig: Light bottom rig fished at night near rocky reef at 10-60 ft
lures: Small glow jigs at night near reef
explanation_cold: Kumu (squirrelfish) are nocturnal reef fish, similar to menpachi; they inhabit rocky reef caves and are active at night.
explanation_warm: Night fishing near Hawaiian rocky shorelines and reef; kumu are large-eyed nocturnal hunters that come out of reef caves after dark — excellent eating and well worth the nighttime trip.

name: Clown wrasse
bait: Shrimp pieces, small crab, invertebrates near reef and rubble
rig: Light rig near reef and rubble; incidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Clown wrasse are colorful tropical wrasse on Florida Keys reef and Caribbean structure year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; phase-changing fish that look completely different as juveniles vs adults — an interesting incidental catch on small hooks.

name: Atlantic Spanish mackerel
bait: Small live or dead baitfish, cut strips trolled or free-lined near the surface
rig: Light to medium trolling or casting; 30-50 lb fluorocarbon leader; wire trace optional
lures: Clarkspoon, Got-Cha plug, silver spoon trolled 4-8 knots; or small jigs cast into schooling fish
explanation_cold: Atlantic Spanish mackerel migrate the East Coast in spring and fall; massive schools run nearshore and inside inlets chasing baitfish.
explanation_warm: Spring and fall migration runs bring huge schools nearshore; one of the most accessible and exciting light-tackle gamefish on the East Coast.

name: Longtail tuna
bait: Small live fish, squid, trolled lures near the surface offshore
rig: Medium to heavy trolling or casting offshore; 80-100 lb leader
lures: Small to medium skirted trolling lures, feathers, and tuna-style jigs
explanation_cold: Longtail tuna are an offshore pelagic occasionally encountered in warm SE Atlantic and Gulf waters.
explanation_warm: Summer offshore; most common near the Bahamas and Greater Antilles — an exciting accidental catch during offshore trolling trips.

name: Pacific whiting (hake)
bait: Squid strips, cut herring, small anchovy at depth near mid-water and bottom
rig: Medium to heavy bottom or mid-water rig at 60-400 ft
lures: Large diamond jigs worked at depth
explanation_cold: Pacific whiting form enormous mid-water schools off the Pacific coast in summer and fall; the most abundant groundfish in the Pacific.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall in Pacific coastal waters; recreationally caught on deep jigs by party boat anglers in Washington and Oregon.

name: Blacksmith (Pacific)
bait: Small crustaceans and plankton near kelp in Southern California; rarely caught deliberately
rig: Light float rig near kelp; incidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Blacksmith are a deep-blue damselfish that school in midwater columns above Southern California kelp beds.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Southern California kelp; blacksmiths form dense schools around kelp beds — an incidental catch while fishing for other species.

name: Garibaldi (California state fish)
bait: FULLY PROTECTED — it is illegal to catch, possess, or harm garibaldi in California
rig: None; fully protected
lures: None; fully protected
explanation_cold: The garibaldi is the California state marine fish; it is brilliant orange and fully protected by law.
explanation_warm: Do not target garibaldi — they are fully protected and violations carry significant fines. If accidentally hooked, release immediately.

name: Plainfin midshipman
bait: Pile worms, small fish, shrimp near shallow rocky shoreline; nocturnal species
rig: Light bottom rig near rocky intertidal at night; incidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Plainfin midshipman are nocturnal fish of the Pacific intertidal; males produce a loud buzzing hum to attract females during spawning.
explanation_warm: Spring through summer near rocky Pacific tidal zones at night; midshipmen hum loudly under rocks during spawning (May-August) — a surreal experience. Mild venom in dorsal spines.

name: Pollock (Atlantic)
bait: Jigs, small metal lures, sandworms, and cut herring near the surface or mid-depth
rig: Light to medium spinning or conventional; often caught near the surface in fall
lures: Norwegian jigs, diamond jigs, small soft plastic tails — pollock are aggressive lure-strikers
explanation_cold: Atlantic pollock school in large numbers near the surface and mid-water in New England fall and winter; they are aggressive strikers.
explanation_warm: Fall through spring in New England inshore and offshore; pollock are one of the most fun inshore fish of the New England fall season — they will aggressively hit metal jigs near the surface and fight hard on light tackle.

name: Witch flounder
bait: Clam strips, sandworms, squid strips near sandy-mud bottom at 100-400 ft
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 100-400 ft near deep sandy bottom
lures: Small Gulp jigs tipped with bait
explanation_cold: Witch flounder (gray sole) inhabit deep sandy-mud bottom in New England offshore waters; they are excellent eating.
explanation_warm: Fall through winter on New England offshore trips; witch flounder (or 'gray sole') are considered some of the finest eating flatfish in the Northwest Atlantic — a welcome bycatch on deep cod trips.

name: American plaice
bait: Clam strips, sandworms near sandy bottom at 100-400 ft
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 100-400 ft over deep sandy bottom
lures: Small Gulp tipped with bait near bottom
explanation_cold: American plaice inhabit deep sandy-mud bottom in New England and Canadian waters; similar to yellowtail flounder but larger.
explanation_warm: Fall through spring on New England offshore trips; American plaice (dab) are excellent eating and frequently taken alongside haddock and cod on deep bank trips.

name: Greenland halibut (turbot)
bait: Large squid, herring, or clams near deep cold-water bottom at 300-1500 ft
rig: Very heavy bottom rig at 300-1500 ft in deep cold water; electric reel almost mandatory
lures: Large diamond jigs at depth
explanation_cold: Greenland halibut (turbot) inhabit very deep cold-water bottom in New England, Canadian, and Arctic waters.
explanation_warm: Deep cold-water specialty; Greenland halibut are primarily a commercial species and are rarely targeted recreationally in the US — a remarkable accidental catch on extremely deep winter trips.

name: Three-line grunt
bait: Shrimp, squid, small crabs near reef and rocky structure at 10-80 ft
rig: Light bottom rig near reef and rocky structure
lures: Small jigs near reef
explanation_cold: Three-line grunt inhabit tropical reef and rocky structure in South Florida and the Keys year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; three-line grunts school tightly around coral heads and are part of the diverse grunt complex.

name: Belted sandfish
bait: Small shrimp, small fish near sandy bottom in shallow Gulf and SE waters
rig: Light bottom rig near sandy bottom in shallow bays
lures: Very small jigs near sandy bottom
explanation_cold: Belted sandfish are a small serranid found near sandy shallow bottom in warm Gulf and SE Atlantic waters.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall in warm shallow sandy areas; belted sandfish are a colorful small fish rarely targeted deliberately — mostly caught incidentally on ultra-light tackle.

name: Vermilion snapper
bait: Squid, cut fish, live shrimp near reef and rocky structure at 60-300 ft
rig: Medium bottom rig at 60-300 ft near reef; double-dropper loop or spreader
lures: Small vertical jigs and diamond jigs near reef structure
explanation_cold: Vermilion snapper inhabit mid-depth reef structure in the Gulf and SE Atlantic year-round; they form dense schools.
explanation_warm: Year-round near offshore reef; vermilion snapper (b-liners) school in large numbers over rocky bottom — small baits on multi-hook rigs can produce dozens quickly.

name: Yelloweye snapper
bait: Squid, cut fish near moderate-depth reef and hard bottom at 100-400 ft
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig at 100-400 ft near reef
lures: Large diamond jigs near reef
explanation_cold: Yelloweye snapper inhabit moderate-depth reef and hard bottom in the Gulf and SE Atlantic.
explanation_warm: Year-round near offshore reef; less commonly targeted than red or vermilion but excellent eating.

name: Wenchman snapper
bait: Squid, cut fish near deep rocky bottom at 300-900 ft
rig: Heavy deepdrop rig at 300-900 ft near deep reef
lures: Large deep-drop lures
explanation_cold: Wenchman snapper inhabit deep reef in the Gulf and SE Atlantic; resemble vermilion snapper but are deeper-dwelling.
explanation_warm: Deepdrop specialty year-round; plentiful over deep hard bottom and excellent eating.

name: Longspine porgy
bait: Small crustaceans, clams, squid near deep reef at 100-400 ft
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig at 100-400 ft near deep reef
lures: Small diamond jigs near deep reef
explanation_cold: Longspine porgy inhabit deep reef in SE Atlantic; identified by very long dorsal spines.
explanation_warm: Year-round on SE offshore deep reef; a common bycatch on snapper trips in the Carolinas.

name: Permit (offshore)
bait: Live crabs, live shrimp near offshore wrecks and reef structure at 10-60 ft
rig: Light to medium live-bait rig near reef and wreck structure
lures: Crab imitation flies and DOA crab lures near wrecks and reef
explanation_cold: Offshore permit congregate around offshore wrecks, ledges, and reef in SE and Gulf waters.
explanation_warm: Year-round near offshore structure; even offshore permit can be highly selective — one of the ultimate light-tackle challenges.

name: Goliath grouper
bait: Fully protected in US waters — release immediately if caught; do not target
rig: Release immediately
lures: Release immediately if caught
explanation_cold: Goliath grouper are fully protected in US waters; they can reach 800 lbs and are the largest grouper in the Atlantic.
explanation_warm: Goliath grouper must be immediately released — do not remove from the water. Commonly seen stealing caught fish. A thrilling encounter but do not target them.

name: Gulf kingfish (sea mullet)
bait: Sand fleas, sand worms, shrimp in the surf over sandy bottom
rig: Light surf rig at 5-20 ft in the surf zone near troughs and sandbars
lures: Small pompano-style jigs with sand flea trailers
explanation_cold: Gulf kingfish are year-round surf fish on the Gulf Coast; school over sandy bottom and are excellent eating.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Gulf surf; the most common sea mullet on the Gulf Coast — excellent eating and easy to catch on sand fleas from the beach.

name: Northern kingfish (sea mullet)
bait: Sand fleas, bloodworms, sandworms, clam bits in the surf over sandy bottom
rig: Light surf or spinning rig at 5-20 ft in the surf zone
lures: Small pompano-style jigs; occasional small bucktail
explanation_cold: Northern kingfish run Mid-Atlantic and NE beaches from spring through fall; they school in the surf over sandy bottom.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall on Mid-Atlantic and NE beaches; one of the most underrated eating fish on the East Coast — sweet white flesh and easy to catch in the surf on bloodworms.

name: Southern kingfish (sea mullet)
bait: Sand fleas, sandworms, shrimp in the surf over sandy bottom
rig: Light surf or spinning rig at 5-20 ft in the surf zone
lures: Small pompano-style jigs
explanation_cold: Southern kingfish inhabit SE Atlantic and Gulf Coast surf zones year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round in SE surf and nearshore; nearly indistinguishable from northern kingfish in the overlap zone and caught on the same rigs.

name: Atlantic threadfin
bait: Cast net near the surface in coastal bays and inlets
rig: Cast net over surface schools; sabiki rig
lures: Not typically a lure target; baitfish species
explanation_cold: Atlantic threadfin are coastal baitfish that school near the surface in warm SE and Gulf waters.
explanation_warm: Year-round in warm SE coastal waters; excellent live bait for snook, tarpon, and inshore predators.

name: Tripletail (Gulf)
bait: Live shrimp, small fish near floating crab buoys and offshore structure
rig: Light spinning or fly; cast to visible fish near surface debris and buoys
lures: DOA shrimp, small paddletail swimbaits, or surface flies cast to visible fish
explanation_cold: Gulf tripletail are seasonally abundant in warm Gulf coastal waters; sight-fished near crab trap buoys and floating debris.
explanation_warm: Late spring through fall in Gulf coastal waters; cruise nearshore in a shallow-draft boat scanning crab buoys for tripletail lying sideways near the surface.

name: Yellowtail rockfish
bait: Live anchovies, squid strips, cut herring near rocky reef at 60-300 ft
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig at 60-300 ft near rocky reef; dropper loop
lures: Lead-head jigs with soft plastic tails; knife jigs near reef structure
explanation_cold: Yellowtail rockfish inhabit mid-depth rocky reef from California to Alaska; they school in large numbers and are among the most commonly caught rockfish on Pacific party boats.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Pacific rocky reef; yellowtail rockfish form large schools at mid-depth and are a staple catch on West Coast party boat trips — they hit jigs and bait readily and are excellent eating.

name: Cowcod
bait: Squid, cut herring near deep rocky reef at 300-1200 ft; cowcod conservation areas restrict access
rig: Heavy deep-drop rig at 300-1200 ft; check for cowcod conservation area closures before fishing
lures: Large diamond jigs near deep rocky bottom
explanation_cold: Cowcod are a large slow-growing deepwater rockfish off Southern California; they are heavily protected.
explanation_warm: Cowcod are prohibited from retention in California waters and in federally designated Cowcod Conservation Areas. Release immediately if caught. Check current CDFW and NMFS closure maps before deep-water rockfish fishing.

name: Greenspotted rockfish
bait: Squid, cut herring near rocky reef and ledges at 60-300 ft
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig at 60-300 ft near rocky reef
lures: Soft plastic jigs and knife jigs near reef structure
explanation_cold: Greenspotted rockfish inhabit rocky reef at moderate depth on the Pacific coast; common on Southern California party boat trips.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Southern California party boat trips; greenspotted rockfish are part of the mixed-rockfish bag and are excellent eating with firm white flesh.

name: Sharpchin rockfish
bait: Squid, small fish near rocky bottom at 100-600 ft
rig: Heavy bottom rig at 100-600 ft
lures: Knife jigs at depth
explanation_cold: Sharpchin rockfish inhabit deep rocky bottom on the Pacific coast; a common deep-water rockfish species.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Pacific deep-water trips; sharpchin rockfish are part of the mixed-rockfish bag.

name: Redbanded rockfish
bait: Squid, cut herring near very deep rocky bottom at 600-1500 ft
rig: Very heavy deep-drop rig at 600-1500 ft; electric reel recommended
lures: Very large diamond jigs at extreme depth
explanation_cold: Redbanded rockfish inhabit very deep water on the Pacific coast; they are one of the deepest-dwelling rockfish species.
explanation_warm: Extreme-depth specialty on Pacific offshore trips; redbanded rockfish are bright red with distinctive bands and have very large eyes adapted to the deep — a remarkable deep-drop catch.

name: Puddingwife wrasse
bait: Shrimp, small crabs, invertebrates near reef and hard bottom
rig: Light bottom rig at 10-80 ft near reef
lures: Small jigs near reef structure
explanation_cold: Puddingwife are a large colorful wrasse on SE Atlantic and Florida Keys reef year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; dramatically color-changing from juvenile (orange with white spots) to adult (bright green and blue).

name: California moray
bait: Squid, cut fish near rocky reef crevices; incidental catch
rig: Medium bottom rig near rocky reef; morays attack baits near crevices
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: California moray eels inhabit rocky reef and crevices in Southern California nearshore waters.
explanation_warm: Year-round in SoCal rocky reef; sharp teeth — cut the leader if accidentally hooked. Do not attempt to handle.

name: Green moray
bait: Squid, cut fish near rocky reef crevices; incidental catch
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig near reef
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Green moray eels are year-round residents in rocky reef throughout SE Atlantic and Florida Keys.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; very sharp teeth — cut the leader if accidentally hooked.

name: Spotted moray
bait: Squid, cut fish near reef crevices; incidental catch
rig: Medium bottom rig near reef crevices
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Spotted moray eels inhabit shallow reef and rocky areas in SE and Gulf waters.
explanation_warm: Year-round near SE reef; smaller than green morays but equally sharp-toothed — cut the leader rather than handling.

name: Chain moray
bait: Small crabs, shrimp near shallow reef; incidental catch
rig: Light rig near shallow reef
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Chain morays are a smaller moray found in shallow SE reef areas year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near shallow Florida Keys reef; distinctive yellow-and-brown chain-link pattern — cut leader if hooked.

name: Silver perch (Atlantic)
bait: Shrimp, small fish, clam bits near seagrass and sandy bottom in coastal bays
rig: Ultra-light bottom or float rig near seagrass and shallow sandy bottom
lures: Very small jigs near seagrass
explanation_cold: Silver perch are year-round residents in SE and Gulf coastal bays; they are small but make excellent live bait.
explanation_warm: Year-round in SE and Gulf coastal bays; silver perch are a common bycatch on light inshore tackle — prized as live bait for speckled trout and redfish.

name: Coho salmon (Pacific)
bait: Herring, sand lance, squid; trolled hoochies, Apex lures, or spoons in ocean
rig: Medium trolling or mooching rig at 20-100 ft; flasher-fly or spoon
lures: Hoochie squid flies on flasher; silver spoons; Apex lures trolled 2-3 knots
explanation_cold: Coho (silver) salmon return to Pacific rivers and bays fall through winter; they school in ocean nearshore in summer.
explanation_warm: Ocean season July-October; coho are the most acrobatic salmon — they leap repeatedly when hooked. Rivers peak September-November.

name: Chum salmon
bait: Pink or orange marabou flies, Kwikfish near river mouths and tidal estuaries
rig: Medium to heavy spinning or fly rod near river mouths during fall run
lures: Pink/chartreuse marabou jigs, Comet flies, and bright-colored spoons
explanation_cold: Chum (dog) salmon return to Pacific estuaries and rivers in fall; they are aggressive fighters that hit bright-colored lures.
explanation_warm: September through December near Pacific river mouths; underrated fighters that hit flies and jigs aggressively near tidal water.

name: Pink salmon
bait: Small pink spoons, pink jigs, small herring near river mouths; odd-year peaks
rig: Light to medium spinning near river mouths and tidal areas during summer run
lures: Small pink spoons (Pixee, Crocodile), pink marabou jigs, Comet flies
explanation_cold: Pink (humpy) salmon have a strict 2-year cycle and return in enormous numbers in odd years; the most abundant Pacific salmon.
explanation_warm: July-September in odd years; runs can be so thick that every cast produces a fish — the most underrated Pacific salmon on light tackle.

name: Sockeye salmon
bait: Small red or pink flies, small spoons in rivers during spawning run; rarely feed in salt water
rig: Light to medium fly or spinning in rivers during summer run
lures: Small red/pink Comet flies, tiny spoons; sockeye rarely feed in fresh water
explanation_cold: Sockeye salmon return to Pacific Northwest rivers in summer; they are the most prized salmon for eating.
explanation_warm: July-September; notoriously difficult to hook — flossing or drifting small flies near their mouths is the primary technique. The finest salmon for smoking.

name: Dolly Varden
bait: Salmon eggs (single egg or cluster), small spoons, and streamers near stream bottom
rig: Light to medium spinning or fly rod in streams and glacier-fed rivers
lures: Small spoons (Pixee, Kastmaster), egg-sucking leech flies, and beads near salmon redds
explanation_cold: Dolly Varden (a char) inhabit cold Pacific streams year-round and feed heavily on salmon eggs during fall runs.
explanation_warm: Fall through early winter near salmon-bearing streams; dead-drifting a single salmon egg or pink bead near the bottom is the classic technique.

name: Wahoo (Pacific)
bait: Live baitfish, whole mackerel, trolled high-speed lures in warm offshore Pacific
rig: Heavy high-speed trolling; 60-100 lb fluorocarbon or wire leader; 30-50 lb class
lures: High-speed trolling lures (Marauders, Ilanders), rigged ballyhoo at 12-20 knots
explanation_cold: Pacific wahoo are found in warm offshore California waters during warm-water years; the fastest fish in the ocean.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall during warm-water years off Southern California; blazing speed runs that strip 200+ yards of line instantly.

name: Mahi-mahi (Pacific)
bait: Live flyingfish, small yellowtail, trolled lures near floating debris offshore
rig: Medium to heavy trolling or casting near floating structure; 50-80 lb fluorocarbon leader
lures: Trolled skirted lures; soft plastics and metals cast to visible fish near sargassum
explanation_cold: Pacific mahi-mahi are warm-season visitors in Southern California offshore waters; they congregate near floating debris.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall off Southern California in warm years; spectacular jumpers that school under floating debris.

name: Yellowfin tuna (Pacific)
bait: Live sardines, anchovies, squid near surface schools offshore
rig: Medium to heavy baitcasting or spinning for live bait; 50-80 lb fluorocarbon leader
lures: Surface iron (Tady, Salas, Yo-Zuri) and poppers
explanation_cold: Pacific yellowfin tuna range offshore in warm California waters near temperature breaks.
explanation_warm: Late summer through fall off Southern California; 30-200+ lb fish caught on the same live-bait trips as bluefin tuna out of San Diego.

name: Pacific bluefin tuna
bait: Live sardines, anchovies, squid near the surface; kite fishing with live flyingfish
rig: Heavy baitcasting or spinning; 40-80 lb fluorocarbon; 30-50 lb class conventional
lures: Flat-fall jigs, surface iron (Tady 45, Salas 6X), and stick baits near tuna schools
explanation_cold: Pacific bluefin tuna range the open Pacific and come near Southern California in summer and fall; giants exceed 500 lbs.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall off San Diego and Baja; a premier target with large numbers appearing near Southern California in recent years.

name: Pacific sailfish
bait: Live baitfish, trolled lures; primarily found in Baja/Mexico offshore
rig: Medium to heavy offshore trolling; 50-80 lb class conventional
lures: Skirted sailfish lures trolled at 7-9 knots; pitch baits to raised fish
explanation_cold: Pacific sailfish are warm-water billfish more common off Mexico and Baja than mainland California.
explanation_warm: Occasionally encountered off Southern California in very warm years; most Pacific sailfish action is off Cabo San Lucas.

name: Wahoo (Atlantic)
bait: Live baitfish, whole rigged mackerel, high-speed trolled lures offshore
rig: Heavy high-speed trolling; 80-100 lb wire or fluorocarbon leader; 30-50 lb class
lures: High-speed trolling lures (Marauders, Ilanders), rigged ballyhoo at 12-20 knots
explanation_cold: Wahoo range the Gulf Stream and warm offshore Atlantic waters; known as the fastest fish in the ocean.
explanation_warm: Year-round near the Gulf Stream with peaks in fall and winter; the holy grail of offshore trolling — their initial run is stunning and their flesh is exceptional.

name: Uku (green jobfish)
bait: Live fish, squid, cut bait near offshore rocky bottom and reef structure at 50-300 ft
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig at 50-300 ft near rocky bottom
lures: Large soft plastic jigs and butterfly jigs near reef structure
explanation_cold: Uku (green jobfish) are year-round residents on Hawaiian offshore rocky bottom and reef at moderate depth.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Hawaiian offshore reef; uku are a highly prized food fish and a quality sportfish — they are aggressive strikers on jigs worked at mid-depth near rocky structure.

name: Kahala (amberjack, Hawaii)
bait: Live fish, squid near offshore structure and reef at 30-200 ft
rig: Heavy live-bait rig or jigging at 30-200 ft near offshore structure
lures: Large vertical jigs and swimbaits near deep reef
explanation_cold: Kahala (amberjack) are powerful offshore jacks found on Hawaiian deep reef and offshore structure year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Hawaiian offshore structure; kahala are the Hawaiian equivalent of greater amberjack — powerful fish that immediately run for structure and are difficult to stop.

name: Mu (bigscale soldierfish)
bait: Small shrimp, small fish, squid near rocky reef caves at night
rig: Light bottom rig near rocky reef at night at 5-60 ft
lures: Small glow jigs at night near reef
explanation_cold: Mu (bigscale soldierfish) are nocturnal reef fish similar to menpachi; they inhabit rocky reef and caves year-round in Hawaii.
explanation_warm: Night fishing near Hawaiian rocky reef; mu have very large scales and large eyes adapted for nocturnal hunting — a respected food fish.

name: Ehu (squirrelfish snapper)
bait: Squid, cut fish near deep rocky reef at 100-500 ft
rig: Heavy bottom rig at 100-500 ft near rocky deep reef
lures: Large butterfly jigs near deep reef
explanation_cold: Ehu (squirrelfish snapper) are a deep-reef Hawaiian snapper; they are one of the most prized deep-water food fish in Hawaii.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Hawaiian deep reef; ehu are considered one of the finest-eating Hawaiian fish — their bright orange-red flesh has rich flavor and their deep habitat means they are only caught by serious deep-drop anglers.

name: Onaga (longtail snapper)
bait: Squid, cut fish near very deep rocky reef at 400-1200 ft
rig: Very heavy deepdrop rig at 400-1200 ft; electric reel mandatory
lures: Large deepdrop lures with glow sticks
explanation_cold: Onaga (longtail red snapper) are a Hawaii deepwater specialty; they inhabit very deep rocky reef and are one of the most prized fish in the Hawaiian islands.
