explanation_warm: Year-round on Hawaiian very deep reef; onaga are the most prestigious fish served at traditional Hawaiian celebrations — deep-drop fishing (400-1200 ft) is required with electric reels. The signature fish of Hawaiian seafood cuisine.

name: Lehi (silver jaw snapper)
bait: Squid, cut fish near deep rocky reef at 200-800 ft
rig: Heavy deepdrop rig at 200-800 ft
lures: Large deepdrop lures
explanation_cold: Lehi (silver jaw snapper) inhabit deep rocky reef in Hawaiian waters year-round; they are part of the Hawaiian deep-drop 'Opakapaka-Lehi-Onaga-Ehu' snapper complex.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Hawaiian deep reef; lehi are one of the four premium Hawaiian bottomfish — together with onaga, ehu, and opakapaka they represent the most sought-after deepwater fish in Hawaii.

name: Nairagi (striped marlin, Hawaii)
bait: Live baitfish, rigged ballyhoo or mackerel trolled offshore
rig: Heavy offshore trolling; 80-130 lb class conventional or standup
lures: Large skirted marlin lures trolled 7-10 knots
explanation_cold: Nairagi (striped marlin) are year-round in Hawaiian offshore waters; they are the dominant billfish species in Hawaiian waters.
explanation_warm: Year-round offshore Hawaii with summer peak; nairagi are incredibly acrobatic and tailwalk dramatically — almost universally catch-and-release by Hawaiian tournament anglers.

name: Darkblotched rockfish
bait: Squid, cut herring near deep rocky bottom at 200-800 ft
rig: Heavy bottom rig at 200-800 ft near deep rocky reef
lures: Large diamond jigs at depth
explanation_cold: Darkblotched rockfish are a deep-dwelling rockfish inhabiting rocky bottom along the Pacific coast; they are a rebuilding stock under PFMC management.
explanation_warm: Deep-water bycatch on Pacific offshore rockfish trips; darkblotched rockfish count toward the general shelf rockfish bag limit. Check for any area closures.

name: Pacific grenadier
bait: Squid, cut fish near very deep rocky-sandy bottom at 500-2000 ft
rig: Very heavy deep-drop rig at 500-2000 ft; electric reel required
lures: Large deep jigs at extreme depth
explanation_cold: Pacific grenadier (rattail) inhabit very deep rocky bottom along the Pacific coast; they are rarely targeted recreationally.
explanation_warm: Extreme-depth incidental catch on Pacific deep-drop trips; grenadiers have a long tapering tail and huge head — distinctive deep-sea fish occasionally brought up on sablefish gear.

name: Spiny dogfish (Pacific)
bait: Herring, squid, small fish near the bottom in bays, nearshore, and offshore
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 10-400 ft; they school in huge numbers
lures: Not a lure target; bait only
explanation_cold: Pacific spiny dogfish are the most abundant shark on the Pacific coast; they school in massive numbers and can be a nuisance on bottom rigs.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Pacific coastal waters; spiny dogfish have a venomous dorsal spine — handle carefully. They school in such numbers that they can completely take over a fishing spot.

name: Pacific angel shark
bait: Small fish, squid near sandy bottom at 5-100 ft; incidental catch
rig: Medium bottom rig near sandy bottom in Southern California
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Pacific angel sharks bury in sandy bottom and ambush prey; they were once abundant in Southern California bays but are now a protected species.
explanation_warm: Pacific angel sharks are protected in California — release immediately if caught. They are a prohibited species and must not be retained.

name: Bat ray (Pacific)
bait: Clams, oysters, shrimp, pile worms near sandy-mud bottom in bays
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig at 5-30 ft in bays and nearshore
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Bat rays are the largest ray in Pacific bays; they inhabit sandy-mud bottom in California and Pacific Northwest coastal bays year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round in California bays and nearshore; bat rays are strong fighters and common bycatch for leopard shark anglers — they have a venomous tail spine; handle carefully.

name: Banded guitarfish
bait: Small fish, squid, shrimp near sandy bottom in shallow Southern California bays
rig: Light to medium bottom rig near sandy-bottom bays at 5-30 ft
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Banded guitarfish are found near sandy bottom in Southern California bays and coastal areas; they are a shark-ray hybrid in body shape.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Southern California nearshore; banded guitarfish are a beautiful incidental catch on bay bottom rigs — shaped like a shark but clearly ray-like when seen up close.

name: Kelp bass
bait: Live anchovies, live squid, swimbaits near kelp and rocky reef in Southern California
rig: Light to medium spinning or baitcasting near kelp at 10-60 ft
lures: Swimbaits on light jig heads, Kastmasters, and small spoons near kelp canopy
explanation_cold: Kelp bass are a year-round resident of Southern California kelp beds and rocky reef; they are the most popular inshore sportfish in SoCal.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Southern California kelp; kelp bass ('calico bass') are the bread-and-butter species for local anglers — they fight hard, hit a wide variety of lures, and are excellent eating. The most targeted inshore gamefish in Southern California.

name: Rock wrasse
bait: Shrimp, small crabs, invertebrates near rocky reef and kelp
rig: Light bottom rig near rocky reef and kelp at 5-60 ft
lures: Small soft plastic grubs near rocky bottom
explanation_cold: Rock wrasse inhabit rocky reef and kelp beds in Southern California and Baja year-round; they change color dramatically between sexes.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Southern California rocky reef and kelp; rock wrasse are colorful and fun on light tackle — males and females look like completely different species.

name: Señorita wrasse
bait: Small invertebrates near kelp and rocky reef; notorious bait-stealers
rig: Light rig near kelp; incidental catch
lures: Not a practical target
explanation_cold: Señorita wrasse are extremely common in Southern California kelp beds year-round; they are the most abundant fish in the SoCal kelp forest.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Southern California kelp; señoritas are notorious bait thieves that steal small baits before target species can find them. They are long, cigar-shaped, and brownish-orange.

name: Walleye pollock
bait: Squid, herring, small fish in mid-water at 100-600 ft offshore
rig: Medium to heavy mid-water or bottom rig at 100-600 ft
lures: Diamond jigs and knife jigs worked at depth
explanation_cold: Walleye pollock are the most abundant fish in the North Pacific; they form enormous mid-water schools and are the basis of the major commercial fishery in Alaska.
explanation_warm: Fall through spring in Pacific Northwest and Alaska coastal waters; walleye pollock form huge mid-water schools near bottom and are caught on jigs and bait in deep water — the fish in most fish sticks and fast-food fish sandwiches.

name: Sablefish (Pacific)
bait: Squid, large herring, salmon belly near deep rocky-sandy bottom at 300-1500 ft
rig: Very heavy bottom rig at 300-1500 ft; electric reel strongly recommended
lures: Large diamond jigs at extreme depth
explanation_cold: Sablefish (black cod) inhabit very deep Pacific offshore waters year-round; they are among the most valuable fish in the Pacific.
explanation_warm: Year-round in deep Pacific offshore waters; sablefish are one of the most prized fish for smoking — their extremely high fat content gives them a butter-like texture. Deep drop fishing requires heavy gear and often electric reels.

name: Black sea bass (Atlantic)
bait: Clams, squid, crabs near rocky bottom, wrecks, and reef at 20-120 ft
rig: Medium bottom rig at 20-120 ft near rocky structure and wrecks
lures: Small jigs and soft plastics near structure; diamond jigs
explanation_cold: Black sea bass range from New England to Florida; one of the most popular bottom fish on the Mid-Atlantic coast.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall on Mid-Atlantic party boats; aggressive biters and excellent eating — the most sought-after bottom fish on New England and Mid-Atlantic party boat trips.

name: Bank sea bass
bait: Squid, shrimp, cut bait near rocky reef and hard bottom at 40-200 ft
rig: Medium bottom rig at 40-200 ft near rocky and hard bottom
lures: Small jigs near rocky structure
explanation_cold: Bank sea bass inhabit rocky and hard bottom in the SE Atlantic from the Carolinas south; closely related to black sea bass.
explanation_warm: Year-round on SE offshore reef; a smaller version of black sea bass, common on Carolinas and Georgia offshore trips.

name: Rock sea bass
bait: Shrimp, squid, small crabs near rocky and hard bottom at 20-150 ft
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 20-150 ft near rocky bottom
lures: Small jigs near reef
explanation_cold: Rock sea bass inhabit rocky and hard bottom in SE coastal waters; one of the smaller sea bass species.
explanation_warm: Year-round on SE rocky bottom; a common bycatch on light-tackle trips in the Carolinas and Georgia.

name: Spot (Atlantic)
bait: Sandworms, bloodworms, small shrimp near sandy-mud bottom in coastal bays
rig: Light bottom rig at 3-30 ft in bays and nearshore over sandy or muddy bottom
lures: Tiny soft plastic grubs; small Gulp Sandworm near bottom
explanation_cold: Spot are one of the most abundant inshore fish on the Mid-Atlantic coast; they run in huge schools in bays and rivers each fall.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in Mid-Atlantic coastal waters; fall spot runs are a beloved annual event — they move through bays in large schools and are easy to catch on bloodworms. Excellent panfish.

name: Sheepshead (Atlantic)
bait: Live fiddler crabs, oysters, barnacles, shrimp near docks, pilings, and rocky structure
rig: Light to medium rig near dock pilings, jetties, and rocky structure at 5-30 ft
lures: Small jigs tipped with shrimp near structure
explanation_cold: Sheepshead inhabit hard structure throughout the SE and Gulf year-round; nicknamed 'convict fish' for their black-and-white stripes.
explanation_warm: Best in late winter and spring when they aggregate near structure; notoriously difficult to hook — strong jaws crush shells and they steal bait without telegraphing the bite.

name: Dog snapper
bait: Live fish, large shrimp, squid near reef and rocky structure at 20-120 ft
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig at 20-120 ft near reef structure
lures: Large jigs and swimbaits near reef structure
explanation_cold: Dog snapper are a large tropical snapper on SE Atlantic and Florida Keys reef; wary and harder to catch than other snappers.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; solitary and cautious, often hovering under deep ledges. Excellent eating.

name: Mahogany snapper
bait: Shrimp, squid, small fish near reef at 20-100 ft
rig: Medium bottom rig at 20-100 ft near reef structure
lures: Small jigs near reef
explanation_cold: Mahogany snapper inhabit SE Atlantic and Florida Keys reef year-round; they school on shallow to mid-depth reef.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; smaller than red snapper but excellent eating — often caught alongside mutton and lane snapper.

name: Glasseye snapper
bait: Small fish, squid near deep reef at night at 30-200 ft
rig: Light to medium bottom rig near deep reef; more active at night
lures: Small glow jigs near reef at night
explanation_cold: Glasseye snapper are nocturnal reef fish with very large eyes on moderate-depth SE reef.
explanation_warm: Best at night near Florida Keys reef; emerge from reef crevices after dark — named for their very large reflective eyes.

name: Graysby
bait: Small fish, shrimp near shallow reef at 10-80 ft
rig: Light bottom rig at 10-80 ft near rocky reef
lures: Small jigs near reef structure
explanation_cold: Graysby are a small tropical grouper on Florida Keys and SE Atlantic reef year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; small (under 1 lb) spotted groupers that hit baits aggressively near reef rubble.

name: Coney grouper
bait: Small fish, shrimp, squid near shallow reef at 10-100 ft
rig: Light to medium bottom rig at 10-100 ft near reef
lures: Small jigs near reef structure
explanation_cold: Coney grouper are a colorful small grouper on Florida Keys and SE Atlantic reef; they occur in multiple color phases.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; colorful from yellow-spotted to bicolor phases — small but hard-fighting and excellent eating.

name: Caribbean reef shark
bait: Live or cut fish near reef and offshore structure; incidental catch
rig: Heavy offshore bottom or live-bait rig near reef
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Caribbean reef sharks inhabit Florida Keys and SE Atlantic offshore reef year-round; they are among the most common large sharks on tropical reef.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef and offshore structure; Caribbean reef sharks are cautious around divers but can be aggressive when bait is present — always exercise caution and release quickly.

name: Blue catfish (tidal)
bait: Cut shad, cut herring, chicken liver, clams in tidal freshwater rivers
rig: Heavy bottom rig with heavy sinker in tidal rivers at 5-40 ft near channel
lures: Large swimbaits occasionally; primarily bait
explanation_cold: Blue catfish are an introduced invasive species in many Mid-Atlantic tidal rivers; they have reached enormous sizes (80+ lbs) in the James, Potomac, and Chesapeake Bay tributaries.
explanation_warm: Year-round in tidal Chesapeake Bay tributaries; blue catfish are now the dominant predator in many Mid-Atlantic tidal rivers. Cut shad soaked on the bottom produces trophy fish. Harvest is actively encouraged due to their invasive status.

name: Channel catfish (tidal)
bait: Chicken liver, cut shad, nightcrawlers, punch bait in tidal freshwater rivers
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig in tidal freshwater rivers
lures: Not a primary lure target; bait-fishing species
explanation_cold: Channel catfish inhabit tidal freshwater rivers throughout the Mid-Atlantic and SE coast year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round in tidal freshwater rivers; channel catfish are the classic tidal river catfish — they hit chicken liver and punch bait readily and grow to 20+ lbs in productive rivers.

name: Skilletfish
bait: Tiny shrimp, worms near oyster beds; incidental catch on ultra-light tackle
rig: Ultra-light rig near oyster reefs; incidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Skilletfish are tiny clingfish that attach to oyster shells and hard substrate in Mid-Atlantic estuaries; they are rarely caught deliberately.
explanation_warm: Year-round near oyster beds in Mid-Atlantic estuaries; one of the smallest fish encountered by anglers — more often seen clinging to oyster shells than caught on hook and line.

name: Striped cusk-eel
bait: Small shrimp, worms near sandy bottom; nocturnal incidental catch
rig: Light bottom rig near sandy bottom at night; incidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Striped cusk-eels are eel-like fish that burrow in sandy bottom in SE and Gulf coastal waters; nocturnal and rarely targeted.
explanation_warm: Night bycatch in warm SE and Gulf coastal waters; striped cusk-eels emerge from sand burrows after dark and grab baits unexpectedly — they resemble eels but are unrelated.

name: Northern puffer
bait: Sandworms, clam, shrimp near sandy and muddy bottom in bays
rig: Light bottom rig near sandy bottom in bays and nearshore
lures: Tiny soft plastic jigs
explanation_cold: Northern puffer inhabit sandy bottom in Mid-Atlantic and NE coastal bays in summer; they inflate when threatened.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall in Mid-Atlantic bays; northern puffer (blowfish or sugar toads) are an underrated eating fish when skinned and cleaned as 'sea squab' — light sweet meat like chicken tenders.

name: Skipjack tuna (Atlantic)
bait: Live baitfish, small squid, trolled cedar plugs and small lures offshore
rig: Light to medium trolling or casting offshore; 30-50 lb leader
lures: Cedar plug, small skirted lures, Rapalas trolled 6-8 knots
explanation_cold: Skipjack tuna school in offshore Atlantic waters in warm months; the most abundant tuna in the world.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall near the Gulf Stream; hit trolled lures aggressively — prized as live bait for marlin.

name: Cobia (juvenile)
bait: Live eels, live crabs, live pinfish near surface structure and rays
rig: Medium to heavy live-bait rig near surface-migrating cobia in spring
lures: Large paddletail swimbaits and soft plastic eels rigged weightless near the surface
explanation_cold: Juvenile and sub-adult cobia migrate along the Mid-Atlantic coast in spring; a highly prized sight-fishing target.
explanation_warm: Spring migration along Mid-Atlantic and SE beaches; cobia follow cownose rays north in May-June and are sight-fished from tower boats — one of the greatest light-tackle experiences on the East Coast.

name: Atlantic blacktip shark
bait: Cut fish, whole bonito, large squid near sandy bottom and nearshore surf
rig: Heavy surf or spinning rig; 100 lb leader
lures: Large spoons and swimbaits for feeding sharks in the surf
explanation_cold: Atlantic blacktip sharks are one of the most common inshore sharks on the SE and Gulf coast; spectacular jumpers.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall nearshore; iconic for their leaping behavior — they spiral out of the water when hooked. Thrilling encounters in the surf.

name: Black sea bass (Pacific)
bait: Live anchovies, squid, cut bait near rocky reef and kelp at 20-100 ft
rig: Medium bottom rig near rocky reef in Southern California at 20-100 ft
lures: Large swimbaits and jigs near rocky bottom and kelp
explanation_cold: Pacific black sea bass are a massive, slow-growing grouper-like species protected in California; they can reach 500+ lbs.
explanation_warm: Pacific black sea bass are FULLY PROTECTED in California — it is illegal to take or possess them. Release immediately. They inhabit Southern California kelp beds and are one of the largest bony fish encountered by divers.

name: Gray tilefish
bait: Squid, crabs, shrimp near deep clay-sandy bottom at 80-400 ft
rig: Heavy deepdrop rig at 80-400 ft near clay and sandy bottom
lures: Large deepdrop lures
explanation_cold: Gray tilefish inhabit moderate-depth clay and sandy bottom in the Gulf and SE Atlantic year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round on SE and Gulf deepdrop trips; gray tilefish are smaller than golden tilefish but easier to access at shallower depths — excellent eating.

name: California corbina
bait: Sand crabs (mole crabs), bloodworms, clam strips in the Southern California surf zone
rig: Light surf rig at 5-20 ft in the surf zone; long gentle casts near shoreline
lures: Small soft plastic grubs mimicking sand crabs worked slowly near the bottom in the surf
explanation_cold: California corbina are the premier surf species in Southern California; they are wary, selective, and require skill to catch.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall in Southern California surf; corbina are the holy grail for SoCal surf anglers — they are very selective and spooky, usually picked off by sight-fishing in clear shallow water with sand crab bait or small lures.

name: Redfish (red drum) juvenile
bait: Live shrimp, live crabs, cut mullet near oyster reefs, grass flats, and tidal creeks
rig: Light to medium inshore rig near structure; free-line or popping cork with shrimp
lures: Gold spoon, paddle-tail swimbait, topwater plug, and DOA shrimp near grass flats and oyster reef
explanation_cold: Juvenile and slot redfish (red drum) are the backbone of SE and Gulf inshore fishing; they inhabit grass flats, oyster reefs, and tidal creeks year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round in SE and Gulf inshore waters; redfish are the most popular inshore gamefish in the SE — they copper-colored back and distinctive tail spot make them unmistakable. Tailing reds on a shallow flat are a thrilling sight-fishing target.

name: Tarpon (juvenile)
bait: Live shrimp, live finger mullet, small crabs in tidal creeks, ditches, and backwater lagoons
rig: Light to medium spinning near tidal creek mouths and backwater lagoons
lures: Small topwater plugs, DOA shrimp, and small streamers near creek mouths
explanation_cold: Juvenile tarpon inhabit warm tidal creeks, backwater canals, and shallow lagoons year-round in SE and Gulf coastal areas.
explanation_warm: Year-round in warm SE and Gulf backwater areas; juvenile tarpon in small creeks are more accessible than migratory adult tarpon — they leap spectacularly even at 5-10 lbs and give a preview of why tarpon are called the Silver King.

name: Pacific spadefish
bait: Shrimp, squid, small invertebrates near structure and buoys in Southern California
rig: Light rig near surface structure, buoys, and kelp in Southern California
lures: Small jigs near floating structure
explanation_cold: Pacific spadefish are rarely encountered; Atlantic spadefish are more common. Incidental catch near structure.
explanation_warm: Occasionally seen near buoys and offshore structure in SoCal; mostly incidental.

name: Pacific jack mackerel
bait: Small live baitfish, anchovies near the surface and mid-water from piers and boats
rig: Light spinning or sabiki near schooling fish; free-lined small live anchovy
lures: Small spoons, small jigs, and sabiki rigs worked near surface schools
explanation_cold: Pacific jack mackerel school in enormous numbers off California; they are a forage species also called 'horse mackerel'.
explanation_warm: Year-round off California piers and nearshore; jack mackerel form dense schools and hit small lures and sabiki rigs readily — a fun fast-action species for beginners.

name: Pacific barracuda
bait: Live anchovies, sardines, small baitfish near kelp and rocky bottom in Southern California
rig: Light to medium spinning near kelp; free-lined live bait or fast retrieved spoon
lures: Kastmaster spoons, small chrome jigs, and pencil plugs retrieved fast near the surface
explanation_cold: Pacific barracuda inhabit Southern California nearshore waters in summer and fall; they arrive with warm water.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall in Southern California nearshore; 'cuda school near kelp and hit fast-retrieved spoons and live bait — excellent on light tackle. Very good eating when fresh.

name: Halfmoon perch
bait: Kelp, small invertebrates, shrimp near rocky reef and kelp beds in Southern California
rig: Light rig near rocky reef and kelp
lures: Small grubs near rocky bottom
explanation_cold: Halfmoon perch (catalina perch) are common around rocky reef and kelp in Southern California; they are bluish with a distinctive half-moon shaped tail.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Southern California rocky reef; halfmoon are a frequent catch near kelp beds and rocky structure — fun on ultra-light tackle.

name: Brown shark (sandbar)
bait: Cut fish, large squid near sandy bottom nearshore
rig: Heavy rig; 200 lb leader
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Brown shark is a common name for the sandbar shark on the Mid-Atlantic coast.
explanation_warm: Same as sandbar shark — a prohibited species in the Atlantic. Release immediately.

name: Kingfish (Northern/Southern)
bait: Bloodworms, sandworms, sand fleas, shrimp in the surf and bays
rig: Light two-hook bottom rig in the surf and bay
lures: Small grubs and Gulp Sandworm near bottom
explanation_cold: Northern and Southern kingfish (sea mullet) are a popular Mid-Atlantic and SE surf and bay species; they bite hard and are excellent panfish.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in Mid-Atlantic and SE surf; kingfish run in schools and are easy to catch on bloodworms and cut bait — a staple of pier and surf fishing up and down the coast.

name: Bluefish (small)
bait: Live baitfish, cut bunker near surface schools; voracious striker
rig: Light to medium spinning near surface feeding schools
lures: Metal spoons, poppers, Gotcha plugs near feeding fish
explanation_cold: Smaller bluefish (under 3 lbs) school near the surface and provide fast light-tackle action throughout their range.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall from Maine to Florida; small bluefish school in bays and nearshore blitzing bait — any metal spoon or small surface plug thrown into the school produces instant results.

name: Yellowfin grouper
bait: Live fish, shrimp, squid near tropical reef at 15-120 ft
rig: Medium live-bait rig near coral reef and rocky bottom
lures: Large swimbaits near reef structure
explanation_cold: Yellowfin grouper inhabit Florida Keys and SE Atlantic tropical reef year-round; they have distinctive yellow-tipped pectoral fins.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; yellowfin grouper are wary and targeted near deep coral ledges — they have vivid yellow fin margins and are excellent eating.

name: Atlantic pollock
bait: Clams, squid, cut herring, jigs near rocky bottom at 50-300 ft
rig: Medium to heavy rig at 50-300 ft; also caught jigging
lures: Large diamond jigs worked near bottom
explanation_cold: Atlantic pollock are a cold-water bottom fish from New England to the Maritimes; faster and more aggressive than cod.
explanation_warm: Fall through spring on NE party boats; pollock hit jigs aggressively and fight harder than cod — superb light-tackle bottom fish. Excellent eating.

name: Tautog (Mid-Atlantic)
bait: Green crabs, rock crabs, clams near rocky jetties, wrecks, and mussel beds
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig right at rocky structure; minimal weight
lures: Not a lure target; bait-only species
explanation_cold: Tautog (blackfish) are year-round Mid-Atlantic and NE residents near rocky structure; powerful crushing jaws for hard-shelled prey.
explanation_warm: Spring and fall at rocky structure; must fish literally on the rocks. Green crab is the go-to bait. Excellent white flaky meat.

name: Red snapper (Gulf)
bait: Live or cut fish, squid near rocky reef and artificial reef at 40-200 ft
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig at 40-200 ft near rocky structure
lures: Large jigs near rocky structure
explanation_cold: Red snapper are the most prized reef fish in the Gulf; their populations have recovered significantly under strict management.
explanation_warm: Short federal season (usually July-August in Gulf); check current NOAA season dates before fishing. Outstanding table fare — they hit baits aggressively near the bottom.

name: Blacknose shark
bait: Cut fish, squid near nearshore sandy bottom; incidental catch
rig: Heavy nearshore shark rig; 100 lb leader
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Blacknose sharks are a small coastal shark common in SE and Gulf nearshore waters.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall nearshore; smaller than blacktip sharks — incidental catch on shark rigs. Practice catch-and-release.

name: Spotted seatrout (Gulf)
bait: Live shrimp under a popping cork, live finger mullet near grass flats
rig: Light to medium inshore rig with popping cork or soft plastic jig head
lures: Mirrolure, DOA shrimp, soft plastic paddle-tails, and topwater plugs near grass flats
explanation_cold: Spotted seatrout are the most popular inshore gamefish in the Gulf; they inhabit grass flats and oyster reefs year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round in SE and Gulf grass flats; hitting a topwater plug at dawn is a quintessential SE experience. School near submerged grass and oyster bars.

name: Crevalle jack (small)
bait: Live baitfish, live shrimp near the surface near structure in bays and nearshore
rig: Light to medium spinning near surface schooling fish
lures: Metal spoons, topwater plugs, and jigs near schooling fish
explanation_cold: Juvenile crevalle jacks school in bays and nearshore from the SE through Mid-Atlantic in summer.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall inshore; jack schools crash baitfish near the surface — pound for pound one of the hardest-fighting fish in coastal waters.

name: Tarpon (adult)
bait: Live mullet, live crabs, live pinfish, large streamers near passes, channels, and flats
rig: Medium to heavy casting or fly tackle; 100 lb shock leader
lures: Large streamers (Puglisi, Tarpon Toad), large swimbaits near rolling fish
explanation_cold: Adult tarpon are the premier light-tackle gamefish in Florida and the Gulf; they migrate along the coast in huge pods in spring and summer.
explanation_warm: Spring through summer migration along FL and Gulf coasts; tarpon (Silver King) are the holy grail of inshore fishing — they jump spectacularly, run 100+ yards in seconds, and reach 200 lbs. Primarily catch-and-release.

name: Wahoo (East)
bait: Large trolled lures, ballyhoo near offshore structure and dropoffs
rig: Heavy trolling rig at 7-16 knots; 300 lb mono or wire leader
lures: High-speed skirted lures, Ilander combos, large Rapalas trolled at 12-16 knots
explanation_cold: Wahoo are among the fastest fish in the ocean; they inhabit offshore tropical waters and are prized for sport and table.
explanation_warm: Year-round near SE and Gulf offshore structure; the bite is an instantaneous shock and the run is explosive. Excellent eating.

name: Sailfish (Atlantic)
bait: Trolled ballyhoo, live bait near warm offshore current and color changes
rig: Light to medium trolling tackle; 100-200 lb leader
lures: Rigged ballyhoo, small skirted lures; live bait under kite for sailfish
explanation_cold: Atlantic sailfish are the most abundant billfish; they concentrate in winter off SE Florida.
explanation_warm: Best November through April off SE Florida; sailfish are nearly always released. Kite fishing with live bait off Miami is world-famous.

name: Dolphinfish (mahi) school
bait: Small trolled lures, flying fish, live baits near offshore weedlines
rig: Light to medium trolling or casting offshore; 30-80 lb leader
lures: Small skirted lures, small Rapalas, Mahi bombs near weed lines
explanation_cold: School dolphinfish (mahi-mahi) school near offshore weedlines and debris in huge numbers.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall near offshore weedlines; school mahi travel in massive packs near sargassum — non-stop action casting small lures.

name: Longfin albacore
bait: Chunked butterfish, squid, and trolled lures offshore in cold water
rig: Medium trolling or live-bait rig; 50-100 lb leader
lures: Small skirted lures, cedar plugs, and metal jigs trolled or cast to breaking fish
explanation_cold: Longfin albacore are a cold-water tuna that appears offshore NE and Mid-Atlantic in summer and fall.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall offshore NE and Mid-Atlantic; prized for canning and sashimi — hit trolled lures eagerly. Excellent eating.

name: Pacific bluefin tuna (juvenile)
bait: Anchovies, sardines, small trolled lures offshore Southern California
rig: Medium to heavy casting or trolling near offshore surface schools; 50-100 lb leader
lures: Flat-fall jigs, iron jigs, small skirted lures cast to breaking fish
explanation_cold: Pacific bluefin tuna juveniles appear off Southern California and the Pacific Northwest annually.
explanation_warm: July through October off Southern California and Pacific Northwest; schools appear nearshore and are sight-fished with surface iron and live bait — one of the most exciting events in West Coast fishing.

name: Dorado (Pacific mahi)
bait: Flying fish, small baitfish, trolled lures near offshore weed lines
rig: Light to medium trolling or casting offshore
lures: Small Rapalas, skirted lures near sargassum and debris lines
explanation_cold: Dorado (Pacific mahi-mahi) appear seasonally off Southern California and Baja in warm-water years.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall in warm-water years off SoCal and Baja; electric blue-green and gold colors — excellent eating.

name: Pacific yellowtail (amberjack)
bait: Live sardines, anchovies, squid, large swimbaits near kelp and rocky offshore islands
rig: Medium to heavy casting or live-bait rig near kelp paddies and rocky islands
lures: Surface iron jigs, swimbaits, and large poppers near kelp and rocky structure
explanation_cold: Pacific yellowtail (California yellowtail) are a premier gamefish off Southern California and Baja; related to amberjack and fight extremely hard.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Baja, spring through fall off Southern California; yellowtail near kelp paddies sight-fished with live bait and surface iron — the SoCal equivalent of East Coast striper fishing.

name: Permit (flats)
bait: Live crabs near sandy flats and reef edges; the ultimate sight-fishing target
rig: Light fly or spinning near tailing and cruising permit on flats
lures: Crab fly imitations and small jigs mimicking crabs
explanation_cold: Permit are the holy grail of flats fishing; they inhabit sand flats and reef edges in the Florida Keys and Gulf year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Florida Keys flats; incredibly intelligent and wary — a flats permit on fly is considered the pinnacle of inshore fishing.

name: Bonefish (flats)
bait: Live shrimp, small crabs near sandy flats
rig: Light fly or spinning near tailing bonefish on shallow flats
lures: Crazy Charlie, Gotcha, small crab and shrimp flies sight-fished on flats
explanation_cold: Bonefish are the iconic flats gamefish of the Florida Keys; catch-and-release only in Florida.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Florida Keys flats; sight-fished on shallow sand and marl flats — incredibly fast and powerful for their size. Almost exclusively catch-and-release.

name: Snook (inshore)
bait: Live pilchards, live shrimp, live pinfish near mangrove edges, passes, and bridges
rig: Light to medium inshore rig near mangrove edges and bridge pilings
lures: DOA lures, swimbaits, topwater plugs near mangrove edges
explanation_cold: Snook are the premier inshore gamefish in Florida and the Gulf Coast; they ambush prey near mangrove edges and tidal passes.
explanation_warm: Year-round in warm SE inshore waters; structure-oriented — lurk in ambush just inside mangrove edges and under bridges. Live pilchards free-lined into snook holes produce explosive strikes.

name: Flounder (winter)
bait: Sandworms, clam strips near sandy-mud bottom in coastal bays and harbors
rig: Light to medium bottom rig in coastal bays at 5-30 ft
lures: Small jigs tipped with worm near the bottom
explanation_cold: Winter flounder inhabit NE coastal bays and harbors from fall through spring; populations have declined significantly in the Mid-Atlantic.
explanation_warm: Fall through spring in NE and Mid-Atlantic coastal bays; gather in bay channels in cold months — sandworms on the bottom near submerged eelgrass is the classic technique.

name: Longnose gar (tidal)
bait: Frayed rope lure that entangles teeth, or live/cut fish in tidal rivers
rig: Light to medium in tidal rivers; frayed nylon rope lure or live baitfish
hook_size: No hook needed for rope lure
lures: Frayed nylon rope lure worked slowly near surface
explanation_cold: Longnose gar inhabit tidal freshwater rivers throughout the Mid-Atlantic and SE; elongated beaks and diamond-scale armor.
explanation_warm: Late spring through summer in tidal rivers; frayed rope lure catches in their teeth since scales deflect hooks — a fascinating prehistoric catch.

name: Bowfin (tidal)
bait: Large lures, cut fish in shallow tidal backwater and swamps
rig: Heavy spinning or baitcasting in shallow backwater; heavy fluorocarbon leader
lures: Large swimbaits, spinnerbaits, frogs in heavy cover
explanation_cold: Bowfin (mudfish, swamp bass) inhabit tidal backwater swamps and slow rivers; primitive fish from an ancient lineage.
explanation_warm: Spring through summer in tidal backwater swamps; incredibly powerful — guard nests aggressively and bite lures fearlessly. A surprising and memorable catch.

name: Pink salmon (Pacific)
bait: Small spinners, pink lures, small spoons near river mouths and estuaries
rig: Light spinning near tidal zones and river mouths
lures: Pink Pixee, Mepps spinners, small spoons in pink or chartreuse
explanation_cold: Pink salmon (humpback) run in massive numbers on odd years in Washington; the most abundant Pacific salmon.
explanation_warm: July through September near river mouths; pinks run in phenomenal numbers and hit small lures eagerly — on strong run years you can catch dozens in a morning.

name: Sockeye salmon (Pacific)
bait: Small red or pink lures near river mouths; difficult to catch on hook and line
rig: Light to medium spinning or fly near tidal river mouths
lures: Small red/pink Buzz Bombs, sockeye flies, and small spoons near river mouths
explanation_cold: Sockeye salmon are the most commercially valuable Pacific salmon; they feed on plankton and are challenging to catch recreationally.
explanation_warm: June through August near river mouths; notoriously difficult on hook and line — feed on plankton. Small red flies near their mouths is the best bet. Premium eating fish.

name: Chum salmon (Pacific)
bait: Fluorescent lures, streamers near river mouths and tidal zones
rig: Medium spinning or fly near tidal zones and lower rivers
lures: Chartreuse or orange streamers, large flies, fluorescent spoons
explanation_cold: Chum salmon (dog salmon) run in fall in the Pacific Northwest and Alaska; large and aggressive fighters.
explanation_warm: September through November near river mouths; chum develop fangs as they enter freshwater — fight extremely hard on medium gear. Better catch-and-release than table fare.

name: Steelhead (tidal)
bait: Roe, shrimp, sand shrimp in tidal and lower river zones during winter runs
rig: Light to medium drift rig or float rig in tidal and lower river reaches
lures: Large spoons, streamers, and Corkies near the bottom in tidal river runs
explanation_cold: Winter steelhead are sea-run rainbow trout returning to PNW rivers from winter through spring; the pinnacle of Pacific Northwest sportfishing.
explanation_warm: November through March in tidal and lower river reaches; powerful, acrobatic fighters that can leap several feet. The ultimate PNW freshwater experience.

name: Dolly Varden (tidal)
bait: Small spinners, spoons, and salmon eggs near tidal rivers in PNW and Alaska
rig: Light to medium spinning near tidal rivers and estuaries
lures: Mepps spinners, small spoons, Pixee lures
explanation_cold: Dolly Varden are char that move between saltwater and freshwater in the Pacific Northwest and Alaska; they follow salmon runs.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall in PNW and Alaska tidal rivers; follow salmon upstream and feed on their eggs — surprising fighters on salmon rigs.

name: Speckled trout (Gulf)
bait: Live shrimp under a popping cork near grass flats and oyster reefs
rig: Light to medium popping cork rig or soft plastic jig head
lures: Mirrolure Lil John, DOA shrimp, Paul Brown Corky, and topwater plugs at dawn
explanation_cold: Speckled trout (spotted seatrout) are the most popular inshore fish in the Gulf; inhabit grass flats and oyster reefs year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Gulf grass flats; topwater explosions at dawn over grass flats are the quintessential Gulf inshore experience.

name: Redfish (slot size)
bait: Live shrimp, gold spoon, crab near grass flats and oyster reef edges
rig: Light to medium inshore rig on grass flats; popping cork or free-line
lures: Gold Johnson Sprite spoon, Gulp Shrimp, and topwater plug near grass flat edges
explanation_cold: Slot redfish (18-27 in in most Gulf states) are the prime keeper-size red drum inhabiting Gulf grass flats and oyster reefs.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Gulf and SE inshore; tailing redfish with tail waving in the air while rooting for crabs is one of the most exciting sights in inshore fishing. Gold spoon near tailing fish.

name: Treefish rockfish
bait: Shrimp, squid, small crabs near rocky reef and kelp at 10-150 ft
rig: Light to medium bottom rig near rocky reef
lures: Small jigs near rocky structure
explanation_cold: Treefish are a colorful rockfish with distinctive yellow, black, and white striping found on rocky reef in Central and Southern California.
explanation_warm: Year-round on California rocky reef; treefish are one of the most visually striking rockfish — bright stripes make them unmistakable. Fun to catch on light tackle near kelp.

name: Pacific halibut (small)
bait: Herring, squid, large anchovies near sandy bottom in nearshore and offshore at 30-200 ft
rig: Medium to heavy sliding sinker rig near sandy bottom
lures: Large swimbaits and herring-imitating jigs near sandy bottom
explanation_cold: Pacific halibut are a prized flatfish found from Central California north to Alaska; smaller fish (under 20 lbs) are common nearshore.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in Pacific Northwest nearshore; smaller halibut are aggressive biters on herring and large jigs — excellent eating and one of the most popular nearshore targets in WA and OR.

name: Topsmelt
bait: Tiny bits of bait, algae, bread near pier pilings and surface in bays
rig: Ultra-light float rig near surface; sabiki near pier pilings
lures: Tiny sabiki rigs near pier pilings
explanation_cold: Topsmelt are abundant small fish common near piers, pilings, and bay margins throughout California.
explanation_warm: Year-round at California piers and bays; topsmelt school in large numbers near pier pilings and are easily caught on tiny hooks — popular beginner fish and excellent live bait.

name: Sharpnose surfperch
bait: Pile worms, small shrimp, tiny crabs near rocky reef and sandy areas
rig: Ultra-light rig near rocky areas and sandy bottom at 5-50 ft
lures: Tiny soft plastic grubs
explanation_cold: Sharpnose surfperch are a small surfperch found on sandy and rocky bottom along the Pacific coast.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Pacific nearshore sandy and rocky areas; sharpnose surfperch are quick biters that school near the bottom — perfect ultralight species.

name: Silver surfperch
bait: Pile worms, amphipods, small shrimp in surf and nearshore
rig: Ultra-light surf or spinning rig in the surf zone
lures: Tiny soft plastic grubs in the surf
explanation_cold: Silver surfperch are a small but common surfperch in the surf zone and nearshore Pacific coast.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in Pacific surf and nearshore; silver surfperch run in schools in the surf — fun on ultra-light tackle.

name: Lingcod (small)
bait: Live rockfish, herring, squid near rocky reef at 20-300 ft
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig near rocky reef
lures: Large swimbaits and jigs worked near bottom on rocky reef
explanation_cold: Smaller lingcod under 22-24 inches (legal minimum varies) are frequently encountered on Pacific rocky reef; lingcod are voracious predators that will follow hooked rockfish to the surface.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall near Pacific rocky reef; even sub-legal lingcod are exciting — they will bite almost anything and follow hooked fish aggressively. Larger fish must be released; check current size limits.

name: Spiny lobster (Pacific)
bait: Dive-caught only; not a rod-and-reel species — caught by hand or hoop net at night
rig: Hoop net at night near rocky reef and kelp in Southern California
lures: Not a hook-and-line species; hoop nets and diving
explanation_cold: California spiny lobster (red rock lobster) is a premier shellfish target in Southern California; they are caught at night by divers and hoop nets, not rod and reel.
explanation_warm: October through March in Southern California nearshore; spiny lobster season is one of the most anticipated events in SoCal fishing — opening night sends thousands of divers and hoop-netters into the water at once. Excellent eating.

name: Red drum (adult)
bait: Live crabs, cut mullet, large live shrimp near surf, inlets, and nearshore structure
rig: Medium to heavy surf or inshore rig near structure and deep holes
lures: Large swimbaits, gold spoons, and topwater plugs near breaking surf
explanation_cold: Adult red drum (bull reds) are oversized fish above the slot that congregate in nearshore and surf areas.
explanation_warm: Fall through spring in surf and nearshore; bull reds over the slot must be released in most states — but they fight like freight trains. Chasing them in the surf is one of the ultimate East Coast experiences.

name: Striped bass (small)
bait: Live eels, clams, bunker, sandworms near rocky points, jetties, and surf
rig: Light to medium surf or casting rig near rocky structure
lures: Bomber Long A, soft plastic eels, bucktail jigs near structure
explanation_cold: Schoolie striped bass under 28 inches are abundant in Mid-Atlantic and NE coastal waters from spring through fall.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in Mid-Atlantic and NE surf; schoolie stripers hit plugs, soft plastics, and live bait eagerly. Great sport on light tackle.

name: Summer flounder (fluke)
bait: Live minnows, Gulp Alive shrimp, squid strips drifted near sandy bottom
rig: Drifting bottom rig at 10-60 ft; bucktail jig with Gulp or squid strip
lures: Bucktail jig with Gulp Shrimp or squid strip drifted across sandy bottom
explanation_cold: Summer flounder (fluke) are the premier bottom fish in the Mid-Atlantic; they migrate inshore each spring.
explanation_warm: May through September in Mid-Atlantic bays and nearshore; fluke attack a bucktail+Gulp combination aggressively — the classic NJ and NY doormat chase. Excellent eating.

name: Cobia (adult)
bait: Live eels, large live crabs, live spot near surface near offshore structure and buoys
rig: Medium to heavy live-bait rig near surface; free-line or split shot
lures: Large soft plastic eels and swimbaits cast to cobia near surface structure
explanation_cold: Adult cobia are large, powerful fish found near offshore structure, buoys, and wrecks throughout the SE and Mid-Atlantic.
explanation_warm: Spring through summer offshore and nearshore; large cobia near channel markers and wrecks — sight-fishing and casting a live eel to a cobia is one of the most exciting experiences in coastal fishing.

name: Ballyhoo
bait: Tiny hooks near surface; also rigged as whole-bait for offshore trolling
rig: Light float rig near surface; or rigged whole for offshore trolling
lures: Tiny sabiki near surface; primarily used rigged whole for offshore trolling
explanation_cold: Ballyhoo are abundant small baitfish in SE and Gulf nearshore; the most commonly used offshore trolling bait.
explanation_warm: Year-round in SE and Gulf nearshore; the primary rigged bait used for offshore trolling for marlin, sailfish, and mahi. Caught near the surface on tiny hooks.

name: Gray snapper
bait: Live shrimp, small baitfish, squid near mangrove edges, reef, and dock pilings
rig: Light to medium rig near mangroves, docks, and reef at 5-80 ft
lures: Small jigs and soft plastics near mangrove edges and dock pilings
explanation_cold: Gray snapper (mangrove snapper) are one of the most abundant snapper in SE and Gulf inshore and nearshore waters year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near mangroves, docks, and reef; gray snapper are intelligent and leader-shy — use long fluorocarbon leaders and finesse presentations. One of the most fun inshore species in FL.

name: Tiger grouper
bait: Live fish, squid near coral reef and rocky structure at 10-120 ft
rig: Medium live-bait rig at 10-120 ft near coral reef
lures: Large swimbaits near reef structure
explanation_cold: Tiger grouper are a tropical grouper found on Florida Keys and SE Atlantic coral reef year-round; they have distinctive tiger-stripe markings.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; tiger grouper are colorful and aggressive biters on live bait near coral ledges — their banded markings make them one of the most visually striking grouper.

name: Bluestriped grunt
bait: Shrimp, small crabs near shallow reef and seagrass at 5-80 ft
rig: Light bottom rig near shallow reef and grass beds
lures: Small jigs near reef
explanation_cold: Bluestriped grunt are common on shallow SE Atlantic reef and seagrass beds; they have distinctive blue horizontal stripes.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; bluestriped grunt school near coral heads — their brilliant blue stripes make them one of the most colorful reef fish. Good panfish eating.

name: Hardhead catfish
bait: Cut shrimp, cut fish, clams near sandy-mud bottom in bays, surf, and nearshore
rig: Light to medium bottom rig near soft bottom in bays and surf
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Hardhead catfish are extremely abundant in Gulf and SE coastal waters; they are considered a nuisance by many anglers but are edible.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Gulf and SE coastal waters; hardhead catfish swarm baits and will take any bait intended for other species — they have venomous dorsal and pectoral spines that cause painful wounds. Handle with extreme care.

name: Atlantic torpedo ray
bait: Cut fish, squid near sandy bottom; incidental catch
rig: Medium bottom rig near sandy bottom; incidental
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Atlantic torpedo rays are electric rays capable of delivering powerful electric shocks; they inhabit sandy bottom from New England to the Gulf.
explanation_warm: Incidental catch near sandy bottom; torpedo rays can deliver 220-volt electric shocks — do NOT touch if caught. Cut the leader and release at the waterline. They have no tail spine.

name: Blue tang
bait: Algae near reef (herbivore); occasionally shrimp or bread near shallow reef
rig: Light rig near shallow reef; incidental catch on tiny baits
lures: Not a practical target
explanation_cold: Blue tang are an iconic reef fish in the Florida Keys and SE Atlantic; they are primarily herbivores and rarely caught on hook and line.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; blue tang are one of the most recognizable reef fish (the 'Dory' fish) — they nibble algae off coral and are rarely caught on hook and line. Release immediately.

name: Ocean surgeonfish
bait: Algae near reef (herbivore); incidental on bread or tiny baits
rig: Light rig near reef; incidental catch
lures: Not a practical target
explanation_cold: Ocean surgeonfish are a common surgeonfish on Florida Keys and SE Atlantic reef; they have a razor-sharp spine at the tail base.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; ocean surgeonfish have a scalpel-like spine at the base of the tail that can inflict deep cuts — handle with extreme caution if caught. Release immediately.

name: Remora
bait: Bait near surface attached to large fish; incidental catch
rig: Any rig — caught incidentally when attached to large sharks, rays, and marlin
lures: Not a target
explanation_cold: Remoras are sucker-fish that attach to large marine animals; they are rarely caught independently on hook and line.
explanation_warm: Incidental catch offshore and nearshore; remoras detach from host fish and may bite a bait near the surface. An odd and unexpected catch.

name: Gulf kingfish
bait: Sand crabs, shrimp, bloodworms in the surf zone
rig: Light surf rig at 5-20 ft in the surf zone
lures: Small grubs and Gulp near bottom in surf
explanation_cold: Gulf kingfish are a surf species in the Gulf and SE; closely related to the Northern kingfish (sea mullet).
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in Gulf and SE surf; Gulf kingfish are an underrated surf panfish that run in schools in the surf zone — bloodworms and cut shrimp produce bites.

name: Cardinal soldierfish
bait: Small shrimp, small fish near deep reef crevices at night at 15-150 ft
rig: Light rig near deep reef at night
lures: Tiny glow jigs near reef at night
explanation_cold: Cardinal soldierfish are nocturnal reef fish with very large eyes; they hide in reef crevices during the day and emerge at night.
explanation_warm: Best at night near Florida Keys reef; soldierfish are bright red with enormous eyes — they emerge from crevices and coral caves after dark and are occasionally caught on small baits.

name: Southern kingfish
bait: Bloodworms, shrimp, sand crabs in the surf zone and bays
rig: Light surf rig at 5-20 ft in surf and bays
lures: Small grubs near bottom in surf
explanation_cold: Southern kingfish (sea mullet) range from the Chesapeake south through the Gulf; nearly identical to Northern kingfish.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in SE and Gulf surf; run in schools and bite bloodworms eagerly — a beloved surf panfish throughout the SE and Gulf.

name: Atlantic spadefish
bait: Clams, shrimp, jellyfish tentacles near offshore buoys, wrecks, and platforms
rig: Light to medium rig near surface structure; offshore buoys and wrecks
lures: Tiny jigs near buoys; clam on tiny hook
explanation_cold: Atlantic spadefish school near offshore structure, buoys, and wrecks throughout the SE and Gulf in summer.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall near offshore buoys and wrecks; school in massive numbers but are highly selective — clam on a tiny hook is the classic technique.

name: Pacific sierra mackerel
bait: Live anchovies, small baitfish, fast-retrieved lures near surface off Baja and SoCal
rig: Light to medium spinning near surface schools
lures: Small spoons and skirted jigs retrieved fast near surface
explanation_cold: Pacific sierra mackerel appear seasonally off Southern California and Baja in warm water; fast, ferocious strikers.
explanation_warm: Late summer through fall in warm-water years off Baja and SoCal; hit lures at blistering speed — excellent eating, prized in Mexico.

name: Queenfish
bait: Anchovies, sardines near the surface in Southern California bays and nearshore
rig: Light spinning near surface schools in bays
lures: Small spoons and jigs near surface schools
explanation_cold: Queenfish are an abundant summer species in Southern California bays; they school near the surface and hit lures eagerly.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall in Southern California bays; form large surface schools — a fast-action light-tackle species.

name: Sargo
bait: Mussels, clams, shrimp near rocky reef and kelp at 5-60 ft in Southern California
rig: Light rig near rocky reef and kelp
lures: Small grubs near rocky bottom
explanation_cold: Sargo are found on rocky reef and kelp in Southern California; they feed on invertebrates near rocky structure.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Southern California rocky reef; common around rocky jetties and kelp beds — good panfish.

name: Salema
bait: Algae, small invertebrates near kelp and reef — primarily herbivorous
rig: Ultra-light near kelp and rocky bottom
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Salema are a small schooling fish with horizontal yellow stripes found near kelp in Southern California.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Southern California kelp; school near kelp in large numbers. Historically noted for causing ichthyoallyeinotoxism (hallucinogenic fish poisoning) when consumed in large quantities due to their diet.

name: Leatherjacket (filefish)
bait: Small shrimp, clams, squid near weed lines, floating debris, and nearshore
rig: Light rig near surface-floating debris and nearshore structure
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Filefish (leatherjackets) associate with floating weed lines and offshore debris; caught incidentally nearshore.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall near floating structure; bizarre-looking with sandpaper-rough skin — steal baits without getting hooked and are an interesting incidental catch.

name: Burfish (spiny boxfish)
bait: Clams, crabs, shrimp near shallow sandy and rocky bottom; incidental
rig: Light bottom rig; incidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Striped burfish inhabit SE and Gulf coastal waters; they inflate when threatened.
explanation_warm: Year-round in SE and Gulf coastal waters; puff up when caught and have incredibly strong jaws — handle carefully and release quickly.

name: Mutton hamlet
bait: Small fish, shrimp near shallow reef at 10-80 ft
rig: Light to medium bottom rig near shallow coral reef
lures: Small jigs near reef
explanation_cold: Mutton hamlet are a small, colorful hamlet grouper on SE Atlantic and Florida Keys reef year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; mutton hamlet are small (under 1 lb) hamlet grouper with rich reddish colors — an interesting incidental catch on light tackle near shallow reef.

name: Cabezon (large)
bait: Crabs, squid, mussels, small fish near rocky reef at 5-150 ft
rig: Medium bottom rig directly on rocky reef; minimal weight
lures: Large swimbaits and crabs near rocky bottom
explanation_cold: Cabezon are the largest sculpin in the Pacific; they inhabit rocky reef from Baja to Alaska year-round.
explanation_warm: Fall through spring on Pacific rocky reef; ambush predators — their roe is toxic (bright red and poisonous) but the white flesh is excellent eating.

name: Wolf eel
bait: Clams, crabs, sea urchins, squid near rocky reef crevices at 10-200 ft
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig near rocky reef and crevices
lures: Not a typical lure target
explanation_cold: Wolf eels are large eel-like fish (a sculpin relative) found on Pacific rocky reef; they live in dens and form monogamous pairs.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Pacific rocky reef; mate for life and both parents guard eggs. Excellent eating despite fearsome appearance. Powerful jaws can crush a hand — handle carefully.

name: Pacific hake
bait: Squid, herring, small fish near mid-water and bottom at 100-500 ft
rig: Medium bottom or mid-water rig at 100-500 ft
lures: Diamond jigs and knife jigs worked at depth
explanation_cold: Pacific hake (whiting) are highly abundant mid-water fish in the Pacific Northwest; the basis of a major commercial fishery.
explanation_warm: Fall through spring offshore Pacific Northwest; form large schools and are easily caught on jigs — excellent battered and fried.

name: C-O sole
bait: Shrimp, worms, small crabs near sandy-mud bottom in bays and nearshore
rig: Light bottom rig near sandy-muddy bottom
lures: Small grubs near bottom
explanation_cold: C-O sole are a small flatfish in Pacific bays; named for C-shaped and O-shaped marks on their tail.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Pacific coastal bays; distinctive C and O tail markings. Caught incidentally on bay bottom rigs.

name: Longfin sanddab
bait: Shrimp, worms, small crabs near sandy bottom at 5-120 ft
rig: Light bottom rig near sandy bottom
lures: Small grubs near sandy bottom
explanation_cold: Longfin sanddabs are a small flatfish on sandy bottom along the California coast.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Pacific sandy bottom; delicious panfish — lightly fried whole or filleted, considered a delicacy.

name: Speckled sanddab
bait: Shrimp, worms near sandy bottom at 5-100 ft
rig: Light bottom rig near sandy bottom
lures: Small grubs near sandy bottom
explanation_cold: Speckled sanddabs are a small flatfish on sandy bottom along the Pacific coast.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Pacific sandy bottom; delicious eating — same approach as Pacific sanddab.

name: Horn shark
bait: Sea urchins, clams, crabs near rocky reef and kelp at 5-150 ft; incidental
rig: Medium bottom rig near rocky reef; incidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Horn sharks are small, sluggish sharks on California rocky reef; they lay spiral corkscrew egg cases.
explanation_warm: Year-round on California rocky reef; have two venomous dorsal spines — handle carefully. Nocturnal. Release immediately if caught.

name: Swellshark
bait: Small fish, squid near rocky reef and kelp at 5-150 ft; incidental
rig: Light to medium bottom rig near rocky reef; incidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Swellsharks are a catshark that inflates its body when threatened; they inhabit California rocky reef year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round on California rocky reef; inflates stomach with water when threatened and wedges in crevices — fascinating defensive behavior. Release immediately.

name: Smoothhound shark
bait: Squid, shrimp, small crabs near sandy-mud bottom in bays and nearshore
rig: Light to medium bottom rig in bays and nearshore
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Gray and brown smoothhound sharks are common in Pacific coastal bays year-round; closely related to leopard sharks.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Pacific coastal bays; school near the bottom in bays — slender, fast-swimming sharks common as bycatch on bottom rigs.

name: Big skate
bait: Clams, worms, squid near sandy-mud bottom in bays and nearshore
rig: Medium to heavy bottom rig near sandy-mud bottom
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Big skate are the largest skate in the Pacific; they inhabit sandy-mud bottom from California to Alaska.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Pacific nearshore; the edible 'wings' are common in Pacific Northwest fish and chips.

name: Longnose skate
bait: Worms, clams, small fish near sandy-rocky bottom at 5-200 ft
rig: Medium bottom rig near sandy-rocky bottom
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Longnose skate inhabit deep sandy and rocky bottom on the Pacific coast; identified by their elongated pointed snout.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Pacific nearshore and offshore; edible wing meat similar to big skate.

name: California skate
bait: Worms, clams, shrimp near sandy bottom in bays and nearshore
rig: Light to medium bottom rig near sandy bottom
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: California skate inhabit sandy bottom in California bays and nearshore year-round.
explanation_warm: Year-round in California coastal bays; common incidental catch on bay bottom rigs. Edible wing meat.

name: Albacore (Pacific)
bait: Squid, anchovies near the surface offshore Pacific Northwest and California
rig: Medium trolling or casting; 30-50 lb leader
lures: Cedar plugs, feathers, and small skirted lures trolled at 5-8 knots
explanation_cold: Pacific albacore are a prized tuna that school offshore from California to British Columbia each summer and fall.
explanation_warm: July through October offshore Pacific coast; albacore schools are found 20-80 miles offshore following the warm-water edge — they hit trolled cedar plugs and cast jigs eagerly. The best-eating tuna for canning.

name: Skipjack (Pacific)
bait: Small baitfish, squid near the surface offshore in warm California current water
rig: Light to medium casting or trolling offshore; 20-40 lb leader
lures: Small metal jigs, feathers, and cedar plugs cast or trolled near surface schools
explanation_cold: Skipjack tuna appear offshore in warm water off California and the Pacific Northwest in summer and fall.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall offshore California and Pacific Northwest; skipjack school with albacore and yellowfin — they are aggressive surface feeders and excellent live bait for marlin.

name: Oceanic bonito
bait: Small baitfish, anchovies near the surface offshore Southern California
rig: Light to medium spinning or trolling near surface schools
lures: Small spoons, jigs, and feathers near surface breaking fish
explanation_cold: Oceanic bonito (plain bonito) are a pelagic schooling fish offshore California in warm months.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall offshore Southern California; bonito school near the surface and hit small lures readily — a fast-action species on light tackle.

name: Pacific saury
bait: Caught incidentally on tiny hooks; primarily used as bait
rig: Light rig near surface; sabiki for bait
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Pacific saury are elongated, needle-like forage fish that appear offshore in the Pacific Northwest in summer and fall.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall offshore; Pacific saury appear in large schools near the surface and are used as bait. Occasionally caught incidentally.

name: California flying fish
bait: Not a rod-and-reel target; observed offshore in warm California current water
rig: Not applicable — not a hook-and-line species
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: California flying fish leap and glide above the water surface for distances up to 1,000 ft; they appear in warm California current water offshore.
explanation_warm: Summer offshore Southern California; California flying fish are a spectacular sight offshore — they leap to escape predators and can glide hundreds of feet. Not a hook-and-line target but sometimes dip-netted at night with a light.

name: Striped bass (adult)
bait: Live eels, live bunker, large poppers, swimmer plugs near rocky structure, inlets, and surf
rig: Medium to heavy surf or boat casting near rocky structure and sandy beaches
lures: Super Strike Needle, Bomber plug, large pencil popper, soft plastic eel on jig head, large bucktail
explanation_cold: Adult striped bass are the premier inshore gamefish of the Northeast US; they migrate along the coast annually and are the focus of a massive recreational fishery.
explanation_warm: Spring and fall migration in surf and nearshore; large stripers (30+ in) require large baits and heavy tackle — live eels near rocky points at night and large plugs in white water are the classic approaches. Strictly regulated due to stock decline.

name: Hybrid striped bass
bait: Live shad, live baitfish, surface lures near open water in reservoirs and tidal rivers
rig: Light to medium spinning near schooling fish; popping corks and live bait
lures: Topwater plugs, chrome spoons, swimbaits near surface schooling fish
explanation_cold: Hybrid striped bass (sunshine bass) are a cross between striped bass and white bass; they are stocked in reservoirs and inhabit some tidal rivers.
explanation_warm: Spring through fall in reservoirs and tidal rivers; hybrid stripers crash shad schools near the surface creating explosive surface feeding — chrome spoons thrown into the melee produce instant hookups. Excellent eating.

name: Alligator gar
bait: Large live fish, large cut fish in tidal rivers, bayous, and large slow-moving rivers
rig: Heavy spinning or baitcasting in tidal rivers; heavy cable or braided leader
lures: Large swimbaits and chunky lures near the surface in slow-moving rivers; frayed rope lure
explanation_cold: Alligator gar are the largest gar species, reaching over 8 feet and 300 lbs; they inhabit Gulf Coast rivers, bayous, and tidal areas.
explanation_warm: Spring through summer in Gulf Coast tidal rivers and bayous; alligator gar are prehistoric giants — they roll at the surface and can be sight-fished in slow tidal rivers. Heavily scaled and powerful; an unforgettable encounter.

name: Spotted gar
bait: Small fish, frayed rope lure in shallow tidal backwaters, swamps, and bayous
rig: Light to medium rig in shallow tidal backwater; frayed nylon rope lure
hook_size: No hook needed for rope lure
lures: Frayed nylon rope lure worked slowly near surface
explanation_cold: Spotted gar inhabit warm tidal backwaters and shallow rivers in Gulf Coast states; they are smaller than alligator gar.
explanation_warm: Spring through summer in Gulf tidal backwater; spotted gar are a common encounter in slow bayous and backwaters — frayed rope lure works by entangling their teeth. A fascinating primitive catch.

name: Shortnose gar
bait: Small fish, frayed rope lure in tidal rivers and coastal plains streams
rig: Light spinning; frayed rope lure or small live baitfish
hook_size: No hook needed for rope lure
lures: Frayed nylon rope lure near surface
explanation_cold: Shortnose gar inhabit tidal rivers and coastal plains streams from the Mid-Atlantic south through the Gulf.
explanation_warm: Spring through summer in tidal river zones; shortnose gar are widely distributed but seldom targeted — frayed rope lure is the classic catch technique.

name: Yellow perch (tidal)
bait: Bloodworms, small minnows, nightcrawlers near the bottom in tidal rivers and estuaries
rig: Ultra-light to light rig near the bottom in tidal river zones
lures: Small tube jigs and soft plastic grubs near the bottom
explanation_cold: Yellow perch move into tidal river zones in spring and fall in Mid-Atlantic coastal areas; they are a beloved panfish.
explanation_warm: Spring and fall in tidal creeks and river tributaries; yellow perch are schooling fish that stack up in tidal pools in early spring — blood worms and small jigs near the bottom produce fast action. Outstanding eating.

name: Swordfish (Atlantic)
bait: Large squid, bonito strips deep-dropped at 1000-2000 ft overnight or near surface at dawn
rig: Very heavy 130-class or deep-drop rig; 400 lb leader or wire; electric reel for deep-drop
lures: Not a lure target; bait only
explanation_cold: Atlantic swordfish inhabit offshore waters from New England to the Gulf; targeted by deep-dropping overnight and drifting near surface at dawn near canyon edges.
explanation_warm: Summer through fall near Mid-Atlantic and NE canyon edges; swordfish (broadbill) are the ultimate blue-water trophy. HMS permit required. Deep-dropping at 1500 ft with squid and light sticks is most reliable.

name: Opah (Atlantic)
bait: Squid, small fish; incidental deep-water catch at 300-1500 ft
rig: Heavy deep-drop or trolling rig; incidental catch
lures: Not a typical target
explanation_cold: Opah (moonfish) are appearing with increasing frequency in the Atlantic; incidentally caught on swordfish deep-drop gear.
explanation_warm: Incidental on Atlantic deep-drop swordfish trips; the only fully warm-blooded fish — bright red meat with rich, lobster-like flavor.

name: Wahoo (Gulf)
bait: Large trolled lures, ballyhoo, rigged mullet near offshore structure and humps
rig: Heavy trolling at 12-18 knots; wire or 300 lb fluorocarbon leader
lures: High-speed skirted lures trolled near Gulf offshore humps and rigs
explanation_cold: Gulf wahoo are present year-round near offshore oil rigs, reefs, and humps throughout the Gulf of Mexico.
explanation_warm: Year-round in Gulf offshore waters near rigs and reef humps; wahoo are particularly abundant in the Gulf — strike at lightning speed. A single clean wahoo fillet is considered one of the finest fish in the Gulf.

name: Crevalle jack (adult)
bait: Large live baitfish, large lures near the surface in bays, inlets, and nearshore
rig: Medium to heavy spinning near surface schools and structure
lures: Large topwater plugs, large spoons, and big swimbaits near surface schooling fish
explanation_cold: Adult crevalle jacks are one of the strongest inshore fish on the SE and Gulf coast; they school in large pods attacking baitfish near the surface.
explanation_warm: Year-round in SE and Gulf inshore; big jacks (10-30 lbs) are pound-for-pound one of the hardest-fighting fish in coastal waters — will break rods and burn drag on medium tackle.

name: Slippery dick
bait: Shrimp, small invertebrates near sandy bottom adjacent to reef at 3-100 ft
rig: Light bottom rig near sandy bottom adjacent to reef
lures: Small grubs near sandy reef base
explanation_cold: Slippery dick are an extremely common wrasse on sandy bottom near SE and Gulf reef; they are frequent bycatch.
explanation_warm: Year-round near SE reef; slippery dick are notoriously good at stealing bait — they dart in and steal shrimp before target species get it. Edible but rarely targeted intentionally.

name: Spotted drum
bait: Shrimp, small crabs, worms near rocky reef and coral at 5-100 ft; incidental catch
rig: Light rig near rocky reef at night
lures: Tiny jigs near reef at night
explanation_cold: Spotted drum are a striking nocturnal reef fish with distinctive white spots and long dorsal filaments; they inhabit SE Atlantic reef and the Florida Keys.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; spotted drum are one of the most beautiful reef fish — long trailing dorsal fin and bold white spots on a black body. Juveniles have even longer streamers. Mainly caught at night.

name: Jackknife fish
bait: Shrimp, small crabs near shallow reef at night; incidental catch
rig: Light rig near shallow reef at night
lures: Not a typical target
explanation_cold: Jackknife fish are a strikingly marked drum related to the spotted drum; they inhabit SE Atlantic shallow reef.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; jackknife fish have dramatic black-and-white stripes and an extremely long dorsal fin — a spectacular sight near reef at night.

name: Highhat
bait: Shrimp, small invertebrates near shallow reef at night; incidental
rig: Light rig near reef at night; incidental catch
lures: Not a typical target
explanation_cold: Highhat are a striped drum related to spotted drum and jackknife fish; they inhabit SE Atlantic shallow reef.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; highhat have dramatic black-and-white vertical stripes — they are nocturnal and an exciting incidental catch at night near reef.

name: Cubbyu
bait: Shrimp, small crabs, worms near mangrove edges and nearshore structure
rig: Light bottom rig near mangrove edges and structure
lures: Small jigs near structure
explanation_cold: Cubbyu (reef croaker) are a small drum found near mangrove edges and nearshore structure in SE and Gulf coastal waters.
explanation_warm: Year-round in SE and Gulf nearshore; cubbyu are a small, easily overlooked drum that are caught incidentally near mangroves and structure — they make a distinctive drumming sound.

name: Reef squirrelfish
bait: Small shrimp, small fish near coral reef at night; incidental catch
rig: Light rig near reef at night
lures: Small glow jigs at night
explanation_cold: Reef squirrelfish are a common nocturnal squirrelfish on SE Atlantic coral reef; they are bright red with large eyes.
explanation_warm: Best at night near Florida Keys reef; squirrelfish hide in reef crevices during the day and emerge to feed at night — bright red color with enormous eyes. Occasionally caught on small baits.

name: Longspine squirrelfish
bait: Small shrimp near coral reef at night; incidental catch
rig: Light rig near reef at night
lures: Small glow jigs at night
explanation_cold: Longspine squirrelfish have extremely long dorsal spines; they inhabit SE Atlantic coral reef and are nocturnal.
explanation_warm: Best at night near Florida Keys reef; similar to reef squirrelfish but with dramatically elongated dorsal spines. An interesting and colorful incidental night catch.

name: Tilefish (blueline)
bait: Squid, crabs, shrimp near clay bottom at 200-600 ft; shallow enough for conventional gear
rig: Heavy bottom rig at 200-600 ft; conventional reel works without electric assist
lures: Large deep jigs with glow sticks
explanation_cold: Blueline tilefish are a smaller tilefish inhabiting clay and sandy bottom at 200-600 ft; they are more accessible than golden tilefish.
explanation_warm: Year-round on Mid-Atlantic clay bottom; blueline tilefish are one of the most accessible deep-water species — found shallower than golden tilefish, no electric reel required. Excellent eating.

name: Atlantic sturgeon (catch-release)
bait: Bloodworms, clams, small crayfish near sandy-mud bottom in tidal rivers and bays
rig: Heavy bottom rig near tidal river bottom; incidental catch
lures: Not a lure target
explanation_cold: Atlantic sturgeon are a federally protected species in tidal rivers along the East Coast; they are incidentally caught on bottom rigs in tidal rivers.
explanation_warm: Atlantic sturgeon are FEDERALLY PROTECTED — do not target, retain, or harm them. Release immediately if caught accidentally. They can reach over 10 feet and 800 lbs — a prehistoric giant. Report any incidentally caught fish to NOAA.

name: Banded butterflyfish
bait: Coral polyps, worms; incidental tiny hook near shallow reef
rig: Ultra-light near shallow reef; incidental
lures: Not a target
explanation_cold: Banded butterflyfish are one of the most recognizable reef fish in the Florida Keys; bold black-and-white bands.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; spectacular banded fish that pair for life on coral heads. Release immediately if caught.

name: Reef butterflyfish
bait: Coral polyps, small invertebrates; incidental near shallow reef
rig: Ultra-light near reef; incidental catch
lures: Not a target
explanation_cold: Reef butterflyfish are a colorful Florida Keys reef fish; yellow body with chevron marks.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; rarely targeted. Release immediately.

name: Neon goby
bait: Parasites from fish; cleaning station species — not a hook-and-line target
rig: Not a hook-and-line target
lures: Not a target
explanation_cold: Neon goby operate cleaning stations on coral heads removing parasites from reef fish.
explanation_warm: Year-round at Florida Keys reef cleaning stations; large grouper and morays queue for parasite removal. Not a hook-and-line species.

name: Cleaning goby
bait: Parasites from fish; cleaning station species
rig: Not a hook-and-line target
lures: Not a target
explanation_cold: Cleaning gobies operate cleaning stations on SE Atlantic reef; remove ectoparasites from reef fish.
explanation_warm: Year-round at Florida Keys reef; not a target for anglers.

name: Sharknose goby
bait: Parasites, tiny plankton near coral; cleaning station
rig: Not a hook-and-line target
lures: Not a target
explanation_cold: Sharknose gobies are a cleaning station goby on SE Atlantic and Caribbean reef.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; encountered by divers at coral cleaning stations.

name: Spotted goatfish
bait: Shrimp, worms, small crabs near sandy bottom adjacent to reef at 3-100 ft
rig: Light bottom rig near sandy bottom
lures: Small grubs near sandy bottom
explanation_cold: Spotted goatfish probe sandy bottom with chin barbels; common on SE and Gulf reef-adjacent sandy areas.
explanation_warm: Year-round near SE and Gulf reef; use barbels like fingers to feel for buried prey — they change color rapidly. Fascinating to watch near reef.

name: Yellow goatfish
bait: Shrimp, worms, small crabs near sandy bottom adjacent to reef at 5-80 ft
rig: Light bottom rig near sandy bottom adjacent to reef
lures: Small grubs near bottom
explanation_cold: Yellow goatfish have a distinctive yellow body and are common on SE Atlantic reef-adjacent sandy bottom.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; bright yellow with a dark lateral stripe, school on sandy patches near coral. Excellent eating.

name: Red goatfish
bait: Shrimp, worms near sandy-rocky bottom at 5-120 ft
rig: Light to medium bottom rig near sandy-rocky bottom
lures: Small grubs near bottom
explanation_cold: Red goatfish are a common goatfish on SE Atlantic and Gulf reef and adjacent sandy bottom.
explanation_warm: Year-round on SE and Gulf reef; bright red, use barbels to probe sand for prey — good eating.

name: Bigeye (reef)
bait: Small fish, shrimp near deep reef at night at 20-200 ft
rig: Light to medium bottom rig near deep reef at night
lures: Small glow jigs at night
explanation_cold: Bigeyes are nocturnal reef fish with extremely large eyes; they hide in reef crevices during the day.
explanation_warm: Best at night near Florida Keys deep reef; bright red with enormous eyes — emerge from crevices after dark.

name: Sailors choice
bait: Shrimp, worms, squid near sandy bottom adjacent to reef at 5-80 ft
rig: Light bottom rig near sandy bottom and reef
lures: Small jigs near reef base
explanation_cold: Sailors choice are a grunt that school on sandy bottom adjacent to reef throughout the SE and Gulf.
explanation_warm: Year-round near SE and Gulf reef; common reef panfish with distinctive dark spots — good eating like other grunts.

name: Latin grunt
bait: Shrimp, small crabs, worms near shallow reef at 5-60 ft
rig: Light bottom rig near reef
lures: Small jigs near reef
explanation_cold: Latin grunt are a shallow-water grunt common on SE Atlantic reef; they have bold yellow stripes.
explanation_warm: Year-round near Florida Keys reef; school around coral heads — a colorful reef panfish.

name: Porcupinefish
bait: Crabs, clams, sea urchins near rocky reef and sandy bottom; incidental catch
rig: Light to medium bottom rig near reef; incidental
lures: Not a lure target
